talks.title: How to Write Great Bug Bounty & Pentest Report (Proof of Concepts)
talks.teaser: Walks through the core parts of a bug bounty or pentest report, using weak credentials and a file read as worked examples.
talks.summary:
Good vulnerability reports matter whether they go to a bug bounty program or into a formal penetration test deliverable, and the core structure is largely the same for both. The talk lays out five elements: a descriptive title that states the issue and where it lives, a description that sets the scene and any prerequisites, a step-by-step proof of concept that a stranger could follow, an honest impact statement, and remediation guidance or references. It also argues that a short video can help when a flaw is complex, such as a chained attack or a race condition.

The speaker applies this to two examples. The first is a weak password on an admin panel that grants only read-only access, where the report has to avoid overstating severity because the account cannot change data. The second is a local file read that exposes a configuration file containing a hash that can be cracked, which leads to admin access and, potentially, command execution through a scripting feature. For each section, the speaker drafts text by hand and then compares it with output from an AI-assisted reporting tool, keeping the wording that reads more clearly and adding recommendations the draft had missed, such as an account lockout policy and restricting access to the admin download endpoint.

The takeaway is to write for a reader who knows nothing about the target. Before submitting, reproduce the issue using only the written steps, because any gap there will also block triagers and customer security teams. Where the impact has not been tested, describe it as potential rather than confirmed.

talks.title: Understanding ⛔️403 Bypass Techniques⛔️ (With Examples)
talks.teaser: Walks through practical techniques for getting past 403 Forbidden responses using headers, path tricks and encoding.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the habit of moving on after a 403 Forbidden response. Such bypasses exist because modern applications stack front-end code, APIs, gateways and middleware, and each layer may assume another one handles access control. Legacy and internal endpoints that end up exposed add more openings, so reconnaissance of the server and architecture comes first, since a 403 on IIS may need a different approach than one behind nginx and a CDN.

Where a lab reports an unknown client IP, spoofing headers such as X-Forwarded-For with local or VPN addresses is tried, comparing responses for any change. Dot-slash segments and path traversal can reach a blocked admin path that a string filter misses, and requests should go through curl or an intercepting proxy because browsers normalize paths first. For APIs, switching version numbers such as v1 or v1.1 can expose legacy endpoints, found through web archives or GitHub. Hidden endpoints may respond to URL-encoding the leading slash, double-encoding the percent sign, or encoding one letter, and combining traversal, normalization and encoding often works best.

A pentest on a Windows server shows the case-sensitivity point: Windows paths ignore letter case, so changing capitals can slip past a filter that a Linux server would enforce. The takeaway is to try simple variations first, consider the operating system, and watch error messages for hints that a bypass is working.

talks.title: How To Write A Pentest Report That Gets Your Findings Fixed
talks.teaser: Shows how a pentester structures a report, from executive summary to technical findings, so that fixes actually get made.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that a penetration test only helps when the client understands and acts on the findings, and that many reports fail by being too technical for executives or too vague for engineers. The speaker, who has written reports for clients from small startups to large enterprises, walks through a section-by-section structure. The front matter covers company and client details, a confidentiality statement and document control with version history and contacts. The overview and methodology sections set out the timeline, assessment type, access method, frameworks and phases, and a scope table records what was and was not tested.

The executive summary holds an opener, a testing summary with finding counts by severity, key observations on strengths and systematic weaknesses, and strategic recommendations. Findings use CVSS ratings. Each technical finding gets a consistent ID, a specific title, affected hosts, a description with evidence, numbered reproduction steps and concrete remediation. Two examples show this: an LDAP credential exposure tied to eight IP addresses and the paths it opened up, and a path traversal flaw in a Windows install of Splunk Enterprise, documented with the exact affected version, the vulnerable endpoint and vendor updates to apply.

The second half demonstrates a reporting platform that keeps reusable templates, narrative sections and finding write-ups, links related findings into an attack path, and exports a Word document with generated tables. The main takeaway is to write each finding so someone can verify and fix it without follow-up questions, and to reuse templates so that routine findings take less time to document.

talks.title: The Blueprint to Your First $1,000+ Bounty
talks.teaser: Lays out a week-by-week plan for bug bounty newcomers to earn a first $1,000 payout by going deep on one program.
talks.summary:
The video sets out a goal of landing a first bug bounty payout of $1,000 or more, presented as a stepping stone before larger milestones. The speaker argues that most hunters stall because they jump between many programs and run the same automated scanners as everyone else, collecting small rewards without going deep enough to find valuable issues. The recommended approach is to pick one program and learn its business and features well.

The talk then covers how to test with a clear objective, such as taking over an account, reaching internal networks, or exposing sensitive data, and matching the hunting style (for example XSS, SSRF, IDOR, or information disclosure) to the application's core logic. Tools should only improve efficiency, and a cheap virtual server is enough to start. The four-week plan covers choosing a program with a large attack surface in week one, setting up accounts with different permission levels and reading documentation in week two, and systematically testing one feature per day while noting odd behaviour in week three. In week four, the hunter combines those observations to break application logic and writes reports that show business impact.

The speaker closes by noting that the timeline assumes one to two hours a day alongside other commitments, and encourages viewers to start immediately and treat consistent daily effort as the key to a first large payout.

talks.teaser: Lays out a roadmap for growing bug bounty earnings from first payouts toward six figures, covering targets, niches and bug classes.
talks.summary:
The talk lays out a route from a first bug bounty payout to a six-figure income, using milestones of $1,000, then $10,000, then $100,000. The speaker argues that target choice matters most: strong programs pay well and have a large, fast-changing attack surface, with Amazon, T-Mobile, TikTok and Epic Games given as examples. Invite-only tiers and live hacking events can follow for researchers who report valuable bugs professionally.

Once a target is chosen, the speaker recommends going deep on how the company makes money, which parts would hurt most if abused, and how its stack and deployment work, while following CVEs and write-ups for that stack. The vulnerability types highlighted include XSS chained into account takeover, blind XSS that can fire in internal admin panels, and SSRF that pivots from cloud metadata into internal services. Authorization checks, such as whether admin functions respond to logged-out requests, and 403 bypasses are also worth testing across every application a company owns.

The closing advice is to value consistent medium and high findings, since they add up and build momentum. Reports act as a professional reputation, so impact should be explained clearly, and a downgraded or undervalued report should be handled calmly, because burned bridges cost more than any single bounty.

talks.title: This Bug Got Me A $30,000 Bounty
talks.teaser: Shows how to pull data out of a blind command injection using DNS, HTTP and timing-based techniques.
talks.summary:
This bug bounty walkthrough covers a command execution flaw in a functionality on a public program, found together with a collaborator. The command output never came back to the browser, so the blind injection needed other ways to leak results. The demo uses a stock-checking feature in a practice lab, with the same problem.

The first method sends command output in an outbound HTTP POST with curl to a server the tester controls, which works when curl is available. The second places the output into a DNS lookup as a subdomain, which helps when HTTP is blocked but DNS is not. Spaces and special characters break this method, so only the first word of a command may arrive. When a firewall blocks all outbound traffic, the speaker switches to a timing channel. A bash if statement checks one character of the command output at a time, and sleep delays the response when the guess is correct. Running this through Caido with a list of candidate characters, then sorting responses by how long they took, recovers the username one letter at a time.

The takeaway is that blind command injection can still leak data through out-of-band DNS or HTTP, or through response timing, even with no visible output. Testers should check which outbound channels are open, and they should test payloads against character restrictions before relying on them.

talks.title: Hacking Websites With A Zip File (Zip Slip)
talks.teaser: Shows how zip slip path traversal in archive uploads overwrites server files, using a Tomcat example and a real pentest case.
talks.summary:
Zip slip is a file upload flaw where archive entries carry path traversal sequences, such as repeated "../" in their names. When the server extracts an uploaded archive without checking those paths, the uploaded file can replace an existing file somewhere else on the system, as long as the target already exists. The speaker explains this and builds a small Python script, first drafted with a chatbot, that packs a chosen file into a zip with a set number of traversal segments.

The demo runs against a local Tomcat application where a test file in a directory is replaced by an uploaded archive, confirmed from inside the container. The harder case comes from a pentest with no visible paths: the speaker guesses traversal depths across several archives and none work at first. An invalid input that triggers a Java stack trace leaks the application's webapps path, which lets the speaker target an example JSP page and replace it with a shell.

The talk closes by noting that overwriting configuration files, such as one holding an authorization key, can be more useful than replacing web content. The practical takeaway is to look for any upload that gets unzipped and to test whether a write can land on a file the attacker can later reach.

talks.title: Hacking GitLab Instances For A $5,000 Bounty (2 Examples)
talks.teaser: Walks through finding and abusing exposed self-hosted GitLab instances, from public API enumeration to leaked tokens and code push.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through what an attacker can do after finding a publicly reachable self-hosted GitLab instance. Registration and default logins are a quick first check, and even when the web interface is locked down, the REST API v4 often exposes project lists, repository URLs and commit authors without signing in. The speaker presents two real-world cases, both drawn from bug bounty and disclosure programs.

In the first case, cloning a publicly visible project and reviewing its source and configuration files exposed a hidden, organization-specific internal panel. Access was granted on request, and that panel then passed the user's GitLab session on to other internal applications, which trusted the login without a separate check. The second case started with a broad API query that listed every repository URL, and the results were cloned in bulk and scanned with TruffleHog. A leaked file contained a build account's access token; checking it against the users endpoint confirmed it was valid, and the token allowed cloning a project and pushing a change to it.

The takeaway is that self-hosted CI/CD and developer tools should be reviewed for exposed endpoints and misconfiguration, because write access to a repository can lead to code that is later deployed into production. The speaker suggests scanning repositories for secrets, reviewing Dockerfiles for hints about the stack, and checking public API routes, and points to CI/CD Goat as a practice environment for these pipeline techniques.

talks.title: Scanning All Vulnerability Disclosure Programs For Automated API Hacking
talks.teaser: Shows how Swagger Jacker finds and tests exposed API specs across many bug bounty programs and builds wordlists from them.
talks.summary:
The host presents a recon workflow built around Swagger Jacker, an open-source Go tool from Bishop Fox. He explains that exposed Swagger or OpenAPI JSON files can reveal an API's full set of endpoints, which makes them valuable even when the file is not a vulnerability on its own. He describes collecting roughly 800 domains from HackerOne vulnerability disclosure programs, splitting them into batches, and scanning them with Nuclei for common swagger file paths.

He then walks through the tool's modes. The automate option requests every endpoint listed in a set of spec URLs and reports the status of each, so responses that return 200 can be picked out quickly. A header option lets a tester attach leaked credentials to check whether they authenticate against APIs across an infrastructure. The prepare option outputs ready-made curl commands for each call, which can then be fed into tools such as httpx or Nuclei. Extracting the endpoint names from the specs produces a custom wordlist, and a brute-force mode searches common paths when no spec is found.

He notes that the dataset was gathered for content and is messy, and that a wordlist built for a single target would be far cleaner. The main lesson is that an exposed Swagger file is a strong recon lead even without a vulnerability, since it maps an API's endpoints for later testing. He closes by offering his bug bounty data and asking viewers for tool suggestions for future videos.

talks.title: Running Nuclei On All My Bug Bounty Programs
talks.teaser: Covers a large-scale Nuclei template scan across HackerOne bug bounty subdomains and what it did and did not find.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through a large scan of every HackerOne bug bounty program the presenter could access. Subdomains were gathered with subfinder, which produced roughly 250,000 unique hosts. They were saved to one file and split into batches of about 10,000 lines, so the work could be spread across a VPS and avoid serverless function timeouts. Public Nuclei templates were then run against the batches in three phases.

The first phase focused on exposed panels, such as GlobalProtect, Pulse Secure and WordPress login pages, so they could be revisited when a new vulnerability is disclosed. The second phase reviewed misconfiguration results, where products like Grafana, Tomcat and GitLab stood out as targets for manual testing. The third phase ran vulnerability templates. Those results were mostly noisy and were not treated as real findings, and a scan of NASA's vulnerability disclosure program produced leads but no vulnerabilities.

The scan did not yield any confirmed vulnerabilities across the programs. The main consequence was an abuse notice from AWS caused by the volume of requests, which the presenter said was a reason to avoid this approach at scale. The practical takeaway is that Nuclei templates are more useful for lead generation, such as finding exposed panels and misconfigured third-party tools, than for finding bugs, since automated vulnerability scanning in bug bounty is heavily saturated.

talks.title: Live Recon: Hacking With STOK
talks.teaser: Coverage of Live Recon: Hacking With STOK from the conference program.
talks.summary:
Live Recon: Hacking With STOK is a practical reconnaissance stream featuring NahamSec and security researcher STOK (Fredrick Stoksund) analyzing large-scale bug bounty program data from HackerOne and Bugcrowd using the Trickest platform. The primary focus is lead generation and methodology for identifying promising targets and vulnerabilities within bug bounty programs.

## Overview
NahamSec partners with Trickest to scan nearly every major bug bounty program, resulting in massive datasets covering organizations like Yahoo, Quora, Binance, Stanford, Snapchat, and others. The stream demonstrates practical techniques for filtering and analyzing this data to identify interesting attack vectors. The data is available free at checkers.io.

## Key Methodologies
STOK emphasizes a deep-dive, manual approach rather than automation at scale. His primary strategy involves: (1) selecting targets with depth rather than pursuing numerous subdomains; (2) creating multiple user accounts to test for IDORs and authentication issues; (3) monitoring targets for changes over time; (4) looking for what breaks systems rather than what works. He describes this as "falling in love with a target" and comparing it to re-watching a TV series—you notice small changes others miss.

## Technical Analysis Approach
The core recon methodology involves filtering HTTP responses by status codes to identify anomalies. Rather than treating 404s, 403s, and 500s as dead ends, STOK advocates sorting by content length to find rare responses. Standard error pages typically have consistent sizes; outliers indicate something unusual occurred—often application logic or JavaScript files revealing additional functionality. Error pages returning 403 with substantial data frequently contain useful information like embedded scripts pointing to other endpoints.

## Practical Techniques Demonstrated
- **Content Length Filtering**: Sorting by response size to isolate anomalies; treating rare sizes as high-value targets
- **403 Analysis**: Examining forbidden pages for embedded JavaScript or error messages that reveal application structure
- **Redirect Chain Mapping**: Following 302/307 redirects to identify internal portals, staging environments, or different infrastructure
- **Swagger/API Documentation Hunting**: Looking for swagger.io, openapi, or api/docs endpoints that provide API specifications
- **JavaScript File Inspection**: Using browser DevTools or view source to extract API endpoints, roles, and functionality
- **Wayback Machine Integration**: Cross-referencing Internet Archive data to find historical endpoints and functionality
- **Match/Replace Techniques**: Modifying API responses (e.g., changing `false` to `true`, switching user roles) to access restricted features
- **Fuzzing Organization IDs**: Iterating through org parameters to discover other organizations or accounts
- **Basic Auth Testing**: Attempting default credentials or password spraying against 401-protected endpoints

## Real-World Examples
The stream walks through several targets including Daimler, Marriott, MongoDB internal portals, and others. Notable findings include redirect chains revealing internal infrastructure, org ID parameters susceptible to fuzzing, login pages permitting registration or password resets, and APIs behind authentication proxies (Okta, etc.) that may expose functionality through JavaScript inspection.

## Key Insights
- Most successful hacking combines hunches, experience, and data analysis
- Automation handles volume but manual investigation yields quality findings
- Different skill sets and approaches lead to different discoveries—there's no single "correct" way
- Deep knowledge of a single target often outperforms shallow scanning of many targets
- Error responses and edge cases often reveal more than successful requests
- Swagger documentation is particularly valuable for API security testing
- Internal asset discovery (corp, intra, dev subdomains) frequently surfaces testing/staging environments with fewer security controls

## Tools and Platforms
Trickest (primary data analysis tool), Burp Suite (Intruder, match/replace), Splunk (large dataset analysis), browser DevTools, Wayback Machine, grep for pattern matching.

## Future Work
STOK mentions preparing a presentation at Black Hat with Jonah (FFUF creator) on a novel tool related to bit-flip squatting. He plans to participate in Def Con and the H1702 competition after taking time to recover from previous burnout. He emphasizes the importance of avoiding burnout by hacking for curiosity and fun rather than purely financial motivation.

talks.title: Live Recon: Hacking Tinder's Bug Bounty Program (with @Rhynorater)
talks.teaser: Follows a live reconnaissance session on a public bug bounty target, from gathering historical URLs to filtering leads.
talks.summary:
This livestream follows a hunter through reconnaissance against a public bug bounty program, with the target chosen during the broadcast. The session starts with DNS and host data for the target's domains, then moves to historical URLs pulled from web archives. The hunter explains why archived paths are useful: they show routes real users have visited, which saves guessing.

The middle of the session covers filtering noise. Using ffuf, the hunter matches on status codes, then removes redirects by size or regex so that a single sign-on redirect does not hide other results. Unusual responses such as 500 errors and JSON-formatted 404s are flagged as worth a closer look. The hunter also trims a long list of archived links by dropping plain HTTP entries, images and static files, keeping parameterised URLs that may expose XSS, business logic or cookie handling issues. JavaScript files are reviewed for hidden endpoints, feature flags and beta hosts, and staging or QA environments are discussed as places where features and weaker controls may appear.

Near the end, the hunter describes cookie injection, where a reflected value containing a semicolon can add cookie attributes such as a path, letting an attacker influence how a browser stores and sends cookies. A 403 bypass plugin with header and path variations is then run against a protected host. The takeaway is a repeatable workflow: collect, filter by signal, and test the most unusual results first.

talks.teaser: Walks through practical ways to find API flaws, from leaked credentials and header-based auth bypass to content-type issues.
talks.summary:
The talk covers the API vulnerability types the speaker looks for first. Standard web bugs from the OWASP Top 10, such as XSS, IDOR and SSRF, also apply to APIs, but the focus here is on API-specific checks. The first area is authentication. When a login wall blocks access, the speaker suggests searching public GitHub repositories and Postman workspaces for leaked keys or hardcoded credentials, and using Google dorking to find them. Another route is testing whether the application trusts forwarded-IP headers such as X-Forwarded-For, which can get past an IP allowlist. In one case shared by a colleague, adding such a header changed the error message, which led to a login and then to fuzzing that uncovered more vulnerable endpoints.

The second area is authorization. The speaker recommends checking whether sensitive endpoints, including ones that use POST, still respond when the session cookie or bearer token is removed, since unauthenticated access to data such as a user list can raise the severity of a report. For role-based flaws, the approach is to list every function and test it with each user level, from admin down to a regular user, to see which actions a lower role can perform. The speaker admits this is slow manual work, but argues that it is how better bugs are found.

The final area is content type. An API that returns JSON normally does not render HTML, but if an endpoint serves HTML under a JSON or other non-HTML type, or reflects input inside a response, cross-site scripting may become possible. The method is to find endpoints that return HTML, work out how user input can reach the response, and fuzz parameters or error paths that echo input back. The main takeaway is to read response headers and role boundaries closely, not just the main function of each endpoint.

This video is a reading list of cybersecurity books the host has found valuable, aimed mainly at people who want to get into web hacking and bug bounties. It starts with The Web Application Hacker's Handbook, which is dated but gives a grounding in the basics, older techniques and the client-side attacks that other books often skip. Next is Bug Bounty Bootcamp by Vickie Li, which covers choosing a program, reconnaissance and more modern vulnerability classes such as open redirects, clickjacking, XSS, IDOR and SQL injection.

Real-World Bug Hunting by Peter Yaworski is recommended for its walkthroughs of disclosed HackerOne reports, each with an overview, a summary and a takeaway. Hacking APIs by Corey Ball follows, covering API reconnaissance, API-specific flaws, Postman and documentation, with hands-on practice in Juice Shop. Black Hat GraphQL comes next, explaining how GraphQL queries are built before covering tooling, lab setup and attacks; the host says they have not finished it yet.

The list then moves beyond web work. Black Hat Python is presented as a guide to using Python for offensive tasks such as Burp extensions and network analysis, and the host notes that much of it remains valid despite its age. The Hacker Playbook by Peter Kim walks through building a lab, finding credentials and attacking, and the first edition is suggested as a starting point. The video ends by asking viewers whether they want more book videos, including non-technical ones.

talks.title: Day in the Life of an Ethical Hacker/Penetration Tester
talks.teaser: Walks through the four phases of a typical penetration test, from scoping with a client to writing the final report.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through the day-to-day work of a penetration tester across the four phases of a typical engagement, which usually spans two to four weeks. The first phase is scoping: meeting the client to settle what is in scope, whether the test is internal, external or web application, the rules of engagement, and why the client wants it, such as for compliance. Those notes become a proposal with estimated hours.

The exploitation phase is the core of the test. An automated scanner runs first, and each finding shows its severity and where it was found, so it can be copied into a report. The speaker deprioritises checks a scanner already covers well, such as reflected cross-site scripting and content discovery, and spends more time on stored XSS and multi-step logic flaws, like bypassing a signup flow, which need human judgement. Proxy tools such as Burp Suite support the manual work.

Reporting is the least favourite phase. Each finding needs a description, reproduction steps, remediation advice and impact, and an AI assistant can help clarify them. For the executive summary, the speaker feeds an AI model finding titles and criticality levels, without exploit details, then edits the draft. The engagement closes with a retest after the client applies fixes, reporting any bypasses still present. The takeaway is that pentesting involves scoping, judgement, clear writing and verification as much as hacking.

talks.title: #NahamCon2024: .js Files Are Your Friends | @zseano
talks.teaser: Shows how JavaScript files expose hidden endpoints, parameters and secrets that help guide manual bug bounty testing.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that a website's JavaScript files often contain most of its client-side logic, including API endpoints for features an ordinary account cannot see, such as premium or restricted functions. Using a hacker platform's sign-in page as an example, the speaker shows how endpoints listed in these files reveal functionality a normal user cannot reach, and how a denied response can still confirm that an endpoint exists.

The method moves from a Burp Professional extension that passively scans for endpoints to a browser bookmarklet that lists every endpoint referenced by the page being viewed. The speaker finds the matching script in developer tools, reads the expected request method and data format, and builds raw requests to test. Error messages such as method not allowed or a missing parameter guide the next guess. An AI assistant can help interpret unclear code. The speaker stresses focusing on one feature, such as a checkout flow, where hidden endpoints for shipping details or age checks may suggest IDOR or injection points.

For broader coverage, the speaker filters a scope for JavaScript URLs and runs a secret finder script with customised regular expressions to hunt for hardcoded keys and secrets. Such secrets are less common but are often easy to find and less likely to be duplicates. The takeaway is to spend time on JavaScript, understand why each endpoint exists, and go deep on a single target.

The speaker, a bug bounty hunter marking ten years in the field, shares what he would do differently if he were starting in cyber security today. He came in without a formal security background, learning to build and break web applications at the same time. He suggests that a structured course or certificate first gives newcomers the basics of computing, networking and the internet, and shows them the different career paths available.

The middle of the talk argues for learning both sides of the field. Understanding how blue teams build defenses and what they look for helps an attacker avoid detection, and understanding how developers build applications helps a tester anticipate the assumptions they make. On coding, he separates scripting for automating everyday tasks from full programming, and says that a learner who can read and write code gains an edge, especially when the source code of a target is public or available in a company's repositories.

He ends with visibility and people. He recommends publishing projects on GitHub, writing up research, and taking part in online CTFs and training platforms that provide completion certificates or leaderboards, since project-based work shows employers what a person can build. His final advice is to join communities, online and in person, including groups in adjacent niches. Those connections provide support during setbacks and people to share wins with.

talks.title: #NahamCon2024: Modern WAF Bypass Techniques on Large Attack Surfaces
talks.teaser: Covers WAF bypasses on large attack surfaces, from request body size limits to serverless fuzzing at scale.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Shubham Shah explores practical, modern Web Application Firewall (WAF) bypass strategies on large enterprise attack surfaces. Rather than focusing on complex, meticulously crafted payload mutations or traditional methods like origin IP discovery, Shah advocates for keeping bypass techniques simple and scalable. The presentation focuses on exploiting inherent WAF architectural limitations, utilizing cloud serverless compute for distributed testing, and abusing reverse proxy trust relationships.

### Key Topics
- **WAF Inspection Limits:** Exploiting default maximum request body size thresholds in major WAF vendors.
- **Automated Body Padding:** Using a specialized Burp Suite extension to push malicious payloads past inspection limits.
- **Distributed Fuzzing via Serverless Compute:** Distributing reconnaissance, vulnerability scanning, and fuzzing traffic across thousands of dynamic IP addresses using AWS API Gateway and serverless fleets.
- **WAF-via-WAF Bypasses:** Circumventing origin protections by funneling requests to known origin IPs through an attacker-controlled WAF account.
- **HTTP/2 Cleartext (h2c) Smuggling:** Bypassing internal WAF layers and reverse proxies using h2c smuggling.

### Technical Details
- **Request Body Size Limits:** For performance reasons, most WAFs only inspect a bounded prefix of request bodies (e.g., POST, PUT, PATCH requests). For example, AWS WAF defaults to inspecting 8 KB on ALBs/AppSync (up to 64 KB on CloudFront/API Gateway), Azure defaults to 128 KB, Akamai inspects the first 8 KB by default (configurable up to 128 KB), and Cloudflare inspects 128 KB (with up to 500 MB on enterprise plans). Anything sent past these limits is ignored by the inspection engine. Shah created a Burp Suite plugin, **no WAF please**, which context-awarely pads bodies with dummy data (XML comments, JSON dummy keys/values, or URL-encoded junk) so the actual payload executes cleanly beyond the inspection threshold.
- **IP Rotation and API Gateways:** Shah discusses using the **IP Rotate** Burp plugin and **fireprox** to route HTTP traffic via AWS API Gateway instances across multiple regions, leveraging AWS's dynamic outbound IP pool to circumvent IP-based WAF rate limits.
- **Mass Serverless Execution with Shadow Clone:** To overcome the high cost and bandwidth limits of proxy pools when testing large attack surfaces, Shah leverages **Shadow Clone**. This tool distributes commands across serverless functions (like AWS Lambda, where free tiers offer up to 1 million monthly invocations). Demonstrated workflows include:
  1. Resolving live hosts across massive target lists using `httpx` split into 40 assets per worker.
  2. Checking live assets for specific vulnerabilities (such as a path traversal payload matching a specific response string) without triggering Akamai IP bans.
  3. Running singular Nuclei templates (e.g., Swagger discovery) across an attack surface with low split thresholds and guardrails.
  4. Rapid directory and file brute forcing with `ffuf` where each request originates from a unique IP in serverless infrastructure.
- **Alternative Bypass Vectors:**
  - *Bypassing WAF via WAF:* When backends rely on shared authenticated TLS certificates or whitelist WAF IP ranges (e.g., historical Cloudflare setups), an attacker who identifies the origin IP can point their own Cloudflare account's DNS to that origin IP, lower security controls to minimum, and route payloads through the trusted WAF network.
  - *h2c Smuggling:* Useful against AWS ALBs or custom reverse proxy/WAF architectures to smuggle requests past WAF inspection rules and rate limits.

### Takeaways
Security testers do not need to spend excessive hours crafting obscure payload encodings when testing body-based endpoints; understanding size inspection thresholds provides a reliable bypass. Furthermore, serverless platforms provide high IP variability for fuzzing and scanning without prohibitive proxy costs. On defense, organizations must understand their WAF's body inspection caps, deploy strict per-zone origin authentication certificates, and recognize that WAFs are friction points rather than absolute boundaries.

talks.title: Hacking WordPress Sites for up to $10,000!
talks.teaser: Shows how to find and exploit an arbitrary file deletion flaw in a WordPress plugin for bug bounty payouts.
talks.summary:
Bug bounty hunters can earn money from WordPress plugins, because Wordfence runs a program that pays for flaws in plugins and themes. Which targets a researcher can submit against depends on their tier, which rises with the number of active installs. WordPress plugins are open source, so anyone can download one, open it in an editor and review the code. The talk stresses matching the plugin version listed on the target site, usually found in its readme file, since a newer release may have already fixed a bug.

The walkthrough uses a practice site with a form plugin. Checking a plugin's public page and its history of reported vulnerabilities gives ideas for patterns worth testing. In this case, a previously reported flaw in a file removal routine did not validate the file path it received. Changing one parameter in a POST request could delete any file on the server whose absolute path is known. The speaker removes the index.php file on the practice site to show the effect, warning that deleting core files can break a site. They also describe a similar gap found during a past penetration test, where access to the source code later led to the database.

The takeaways are to confirm the plugin version, study earlier reports for similar mistakes, and report confirmed issues to the bounty program or to the client in a penetration test. The full solution to the practice challenge is left for viewers to work out.

talks.title: Your Mental Health Matters
talks.teaser: Coverage of Your Mental Health Matters from the conference program.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this personal talk, security researcher and bug bounty hunter Ben Sadeghipour (known online as NahamSec) opens up about his mental health struggles, burnout, and personal journey toward healing. Driven by an intense desire to build his community, Ben overworked himself by streaming security content up to four days a week on top of a full-time job. This excessive workload, combined with the isolation of the COVID-19 pandemic and the breakdown of his marriage resulting in a divorce around his 30th birthday, led to severe anxiety, depression, and unhealthy coping mechanisms such as alcohol reliance.

### Key Topics
- **Overworking and Burnout:** How excessive streaming schedules and tunnel vision strained personal relationships and deteriorated mental well-being.
- **Seeking Help and Therapy:** Overcoming the stigma of therapy and recognizing the need for external professional support rather than managing emotional crises alone.
- **Environmental Reset:** The importance of curating one's physical space (rearranging furniture and living areas) and social circle to foster personal healing.
- **November Challenge & Habit Building:** Using personal discipline challenges to quit alcohol and adopt wellness habits, such as daily exercise, reading, and meditation.
- **Actionable Coping Mechanisms:** Practical tools including journaling, daily to-do lists, guided meditation, physical workouts, and dietary improvements to process difficult emotions.

### Technical Details
While the talk focuses on lifestyle and mental health rather than software vulnerabilities or exploits, Ben outlines a structured daily regimen and personal framework designed to counter depression and anxiety:
- **Interval Running & Meditation:** Ben began physical conditioning with interval running (alternating 30 seconds of jogging with 90 seconds of walking). A discussion with fellow creator STÖK revealed that counting intervals functioned as mindfulness, prompting Ben to adopt structured 5–10 minute guided meditation sessions using audio apps to regulate breathing and anxiety.
- **Structured Three-Part Morning Journaling:** To process thoughts without resorting to alcohol or overthinking, Ben implemented a morning writing habit focusing on: (1) noting what he is grateful for, (2) articulating specific intrusive thoughts or sources of sadness (such as processing his divorce), and (3) creating a prioritized to-do list.
- **Micro-Accomplishments & Daily Routine:** Starting each morning by making his bed, preparing breakfast, and completing meditation established early momentum and self-efficacy.
- **Dietary Adjustments:** Cutting out fast food (defined as drive-through meals) and processed foods to eliminate physical sluggishness and support mood stability.

### Takeaways
Ben stresses that struggling with trauma and mental health is normal and that difficult experiences can build personal character if approached constructively. Rather than escaping through alcohol or denial, individuals should confront uncomfortable feelings and establish consistent daily routines. He urges viewers to seek outside help when needed, go outside for physical activity, practice mindfulness, and establish manageable daily habits. Additionally, Ben announced a charitable campaign pledging $1 per comment on the video, along with sponsorship funds from NahamCon (scheduled for May 24th), toward mental health and suicide prevention charities.

talks.title: Turning a $500 bounty into $30,000+
talks.teaser: Coverage of Turning a $500 bounty into $30,000+ from the conference program.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, the speaker explains how security researchers and bug bounty hunters can escalate standard Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) findings beyond simple `alert(1)` proof-of-concepts to demonstrate maximum critical impact. While an `alert(1)` confirms arbitrary JavaScript execution in a victim's browser, relying on it often results in standard or medium-severity payouts. The presentation outlines three key techniques to turn routine XSS findings into critical account takeovers and higher bug bounties, highlighted by the speaker's real-world experience turning an XSS into a $30,000 bounty during a HackerOne live hacking event.

### Key Topics
- **Limitations of Traditional XSS Impact:** The default assumption that an attacker can easily dump session cookies via `document.cookie` often fails in modern web applications due to expiration policies, cookie restrictions, and rapid rotation.
- **Technique 1: Session & Cookie Extraction:** The conventional method of dumping cookies and sending them to an attacker-controlled listener, while common in legacy applications, often lacks maximum impact today.
- **Technique 2: Modifying Account Data or Adding Organization Users:** Exploiting application workflows without direct cookie access by changing user details (e.g., swapping email addresses and immediately triggering password reset flows) or adding attacker-controlled administrative users to SaaS organizations.
- **Technique 3: API Token and Key Exfiltration via Background Requests:** Monitoring network calls (such as `/api/me` or `/me`) to identify endpoints that return sensitive JSON data, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), or API keys, and scripting background requests to exfiltrate these credentials.
- **Real-World Escalation Case Study:** An account of how an initial reflected XSS was chained with a Content Security Policy (CSP) bypass and a legacy API endpoint leaking API keys during a live hacking event, turning a basic finding into a $30,000 critical reward.

### Technical Details
To demonstrate credential exfiltration, the speaker walks through a lab environment featuring a modern web application architecture:
- **Inspecting Background Calls:** Opening the browser's Network tab reveals that loading the profile sends an asynchronous request to `/api/v1/api/me` (or `/me`), which returns a JSON object containing the user's name, email status, a JWT token, and an API key.
- **Crafting the Payload:** Instead of calling `alert(1)`, a custom JavaScript snippet is constructed using an `XMLHttpRequest` (or alternatively `fetch`) to issue a GET request to the internal `/me` endpoint. An event listener parses the JSON response, extracts the target `JWT` value, and transmits it via an outbound HTTP request to an external server controlled by the attacker (such as an interact.sh server, Burp Collaborator, or Apache server).
- **Payload Delivery:** The JavaScript code is Base64-encoded and wrapped inside an `eval(atob(...))` payload. Injected into the vulnerable input via Burp Suite, the script executes in the victim's session, queries the authenticated API endpoint, and forwards the sensitive JWT token to the attacker's listener.

### Takeaways
- **Never Stop at `alert(1)`:** Submitting a basic alert often results in an implied medium impact; investing extra time to demonstrate tangible harm like account takeover drastically increases bounty severity and payout.
- **Inspect Sensitive Workflows:** Test whether sensitive operations—such as updating an email address—require current password confirmation. If not, chain the email update directly with a forgot-password request.
- **Examine API Responses:** Thoroughly audit the network traffic of modern single-page and API-driven applications to identify legacy or standard endpoints that expose JWTs or authorization keys capable of granting complete API access.

talks.title: The Truth About Bug Bounties
talks.teaser: Explains that bug bounty success takes sustained effort, impact-focused reports and a personal methodology, not quick wins.
talks.summary:
This talk gives a candid look at bug bounties, arguing that the field is crowded but still open to newcomers who are willing to commit time. The speaker, who has worked on bounty platforms and as a hunter for about ten years, says that headline payouts hide the long stretches of learning and uneven results behind them. Comparing the path to streaming, the speaker notes that many well-known creators spent years with very small audiences before becoming successful.

The middle section focuses on hunting itself. The speaker stresses that every finding needs a clear answer to the question of what an attacker could actually do to a customer's infrastructure, since a theoretical flaw with no impact is unlikely to be rewarded. Even experienced hunters still receive duplicates and informative closures, and some disputes with triagers take days or weeks of back and forth before severity is recognised. Slow patching on long-running programs adds to the frustration.

The closing part covers motivation and advice. Passion is presented as what keeps a hunter going through dry spells, with money as a welcome side effect. The speaker encourages newcomers to learn from others' content and writeups, but to build a methodology that suits their own style and interests, and points out that new companies keep launching bounty programs.

talks.title: The Art of Finding Critical Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Shows how bug hunters use threat modeling and clear objectives to find high-impact vulnerabilities.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how experienced bug hunters find vulnerabilities with high or critical impact. The core idea is mindset: pick an objective, such as account takeover or remote code execution, instead of hunting a single bug class like IDOR, SSRF or XSS, then work backward through whatever chain of weaknesses reaches it.

Threat modeling comes next. Using Airbnb's program as an example, the speaker splits its data into guest and host sides and lists what would be sensitive on each, such as guest reservations, addresses and payment details, or the ability to alter host bookings. On the infrastructure side, hunters look at dev, API and DevOps hostnames, CI/CD pipelines and exposed GitLab instances, plus well-known backend software like Tomcat or IIS. The speaker also describes his own style: he moved away from heavy reconnaissance and automation toward mapping one core application and its API calls by hand.

Two examples illustrate this. Sam Curry's writeups involve API-focused work, where fuzzing and path traversal reach hidden routes and expose other customers' personal data. Justin's work centres on client-side research, including complex postMessage issues that can lead to account takeover. The closing advice is to set broad goals, like leaking a user's information, rather than searching one payload type across an application.

talks.title: Don't Make This Recon Mistake // How To Bug Bounty
talks.teaser: Shows how fuzzing for dated backup logs led to exposed source code and a file-read bug in a web app.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that hunters often give up when a target shows only a default error page or web server splash screen, and that careful content discovery can still turn up strong leads. It follows an introductory fuzzing lesson and is based on a bug the presenter found on a private bug bounty program. The method starts with a fuzzer, with ffuf used as the example, run against a common wordlist. A result that looks like a log directory is then explored further, with recursion and extension fuzzing to identify what the files are.

Next, the walkthrough builds a custom wordlist of dates in several formats across multiple years and fuzzes for dated log and backup filenames, filtering so only 200 responses are kept. The discovered paths are turned into a list of URLs and fetched with curl to see what each contains. In the example, a backup archive is downloaded and unzipped, revealing the source code of the exact application. Reviewing that code, with an LLM helping to summarise it, shows an admin preview page that takes a file parameter and returns the contents of arbitrary files, including a password file.

The takeaway is that fuzzing output should be examined rather than dismissed, and that treating discovery as a puzzle often reveals the real file names. Access to source code makes vulnerabilities much easier to spot. Practitioners should also keep date-based wordlists current each year, since older years stop being useful.

talks.title: What is Fuzzing (using ffuf)
talks.teaser: Shows how to use ffuf to find paths, extensions and parameters, and how to filter out noisy responses.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by defining fuzzing as sending unexpected or random input to a program to expose bugs. In bug bounty work this often means guessing directories, files, parameters or identifiers. The speaker introduces ffuf, a fast command-line fuzzer, and walks through its basic use against a practice target: a placeholder keyword marks the spot to fuzz, and a wordlist supplies the guesses.

The middle of the talk covers options that widen or sharpen a scan. Recursion makes the tool explore any folder it discovers, an extension flag appends formats such as .log to every wordlist entry, and raising the thread count speeds up the run. The speaker recommends a custom matcher that also keeps codes like 405 and 415, because APIs often answer with those instead of 200 or 403. A parameter fuzzing example then finds a debug parameter on an endpoint.

The final section deals with servers that return 200 for everything. Filtering by response size or word count removes the repeated noise, and the auto-calibration flag, -ac, learns that baseline automatically. The takeaway is to tune matchers and filters for each target, so that valid results are not buried among junk responses.

talks.title: REDACTED: $20,000 OAuth Bounty (FT. Nagli)
talks.teaser: Walks through how a hunter chained an OAuth flaw on a live event target into a one-click account takeover.
talks.summary:
Nagli, a top-ranked bug bounty hunter, joins to walk through a bounty he was paid on a HackerOne live hacking event. The target's sign-up left the new account unconfirmed, which blocked normal use. Attempts to get the account confirmed through response manipulation and password reset went nowhere, and redirect bypasses on the OAuth authorization flow failed too, including a subdomain test and an at-sign trick against the URL validator.

Turning to the JavaScript files, he found a client-creation function and an endpoint that was not linked from the main app. Testing it showed that it took a name and a redirect URL, that it needed a POST request with form data, and that the name was reflected back. Using an existing client ID, he created a client named after the legitimate application and pointed its redirect at a collaborator server he controlled. A victim who clicked Allow on that lookalike consent screen would send the authorization code to the attacker, which was enough to log in as them. The program rated it critical and paid $20,000, with an extra $5,000 for a later bypass of the fix.

The takeaways are that an unconfirmed or restricted account state still exposes features worth testing, that reading JavaScript and fuzzing for hidden endpoints can surface unusual implementations, and that a familiar app name makes a malicious consent prompt convincing. Turning the leaked code into a session cookie was not needed for this event.

talks.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Explained! // How to Bug Bounty
talks.teaser: Walks through finding reflected and HTML-injected cross-site scripting by testing parameters and escaping broken contexts.
talks.summary:
The video is a practical walkthrough of cross-site scripting (XSS), a flaw that lets an attacker inject JavaScript into a page so it runs in a victim's browser. The presenter explains that the impact can range from hijacking a session cookie to taking over an account through a stolen API key. The starting point is a basic test: inserting a harmless HTML tag to confirm that input is reflected and rendered, then adding an event handler that calls alert when the element is hovered or fails to load.

The main lesson is that context decides what works. Pasting a ready-made payload often fails because the input may sit inside a script block or an attribute, so the tester should first find where the value lands in the DOM and then close out of that context before injecting code. The demo shows a parameter reflected inside a script tag, where closing the tag let the payload run, and another reflected inside a quoted string, where closing the quote and commenting out the leftover code produced valid JavaScript. A referrer value that never appeared on the visible page still showed up in the script source, so unseen fields deserve checks too.

On a settings page, the form blocked special characters and sanitized quotes, which made it look like a dead end. Replaying the request through an intercepting proxy got around those browser-side restrictions, and a value placed inside a style block could close that tag and leak the rest of the page content. The takeaway is to test every input, including fields that reject characters in the browser, and to examine the context before escalating a plain HTML injection to script execution.

talks.title: This Is How You Setup Your Bug Bounty & Automation Box (Part 1)
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a bug bounty server with DNS records, HTTPS, and a consistent folder layout for recon output.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through building a personal server for bug bounty work. The presenter starts with a small Ubuntu cloud instance on DigitalOcean and uses the CloudPanel control panel to set up the web server and Let's Encrypt certificates. A domain's A record is pointed at the box, a PHP site is created, and HTTPS is enabled, because many third-party services refuse plain HTTP or raw IP addresses when testing issues such as SSRF.

Next, the DNS layer is covered. Extra records are created for the AWS metadata address, for 169.254.169.254 under a friendlier name, and for localhost, since filters often block the raw IP strings. Separate subdomains can host individual tools, such as an XSS listener, and internal private addresses can be mapped the same way.

The presenter then covers recon organization: a folder per target, a domains.txt file listing each company's domains, and tool outputs saved under a consistent name such as tool-output.txt so results can be searched across all targets. The web root also holds helper files, including XSS HTML and JavaScript files, redirect PHP pages for SSRF and open redirects, and XXE payloads. The main takeaway is to keep output formats identical across programs so a single search covers everything.

talks.title: 2024 Bug Bounty Recon Basics
talks.teaser: Walks through the basics of bug bounty reconnaissance, from subdomain discovery to content fuzzing and target prioritization.
talks.summary:
This talk is a recon primer for bug bounty hunters who want to find web application flaws by hand rather than leaning on automation. It is presented as the opening episode of a five-week program, meant to settle recurring questions about reconnaissance once and for all. The method follows a fixed sequence of steps, beginning with asset discovery.

Asset discovery uses SubFinder against a root domain, with Spotify as the example, to collect subdomains from many sources. Since some results may have no web server or may have lapsed, the next step is information gathering with httpx, which pulls page titles on ports 443 and 8443 and reports redirects. The speaker uses titles and hostnames to decide which assets look like sign-up or login flows. Examples include an ad-analytics host that appears to offer sign-in, a developer host that returns an HTTP error, and a fellowship page with a login.

Prioritization comes next, focusing on hosts that demand a sign-in and asking what functionality sits behind it. Content discovery follows, with a quick fuzzing pass aimed not at bugs but at reaching sign-up paths or APIs that may open up more features to test. Exploitation, the fifth step, means following leads found while working that functionality. The talk ends by asking viewers to choose a target program, paid or vulnerability disclosure, for the coming weeks.

talks.teaser: Lays out a free, step-by-step roadmap of fundamentals and practice platforms for aspiring bug bounty hunters.
talks.summary:
This video is a roadmap for people who want to become ethical hackers and bug bounty hunters, with the free resources to use at each stage. The speaker notes that the same path also fits web hacking, penetration testing, red teaming, and application security engineering. The starting point is networking and web fundamentals, including how DNS works and what happens when a browser sends an HTTP request, with a closing exercise of tracing that request end to end.

Next comes Linux, where OverTheWire's Bandit wargame teaches command-line basics, followed by scripting, where freeCodeCamp courses on bash and Python are recommended. The speaker suggests building a small automation project, such as a recon scanner, to apply those skills. For hands-on practice, the roadmap adds a cheap cloud server with a custom domain, the PicoCTF categories for finding an area of interest, and then web-focused wargames: OverTheWire's Natas, Hacker101 CTFs, Hacksplaining, and PortSwigger's Web Security Academy, which groups labs by vulnerability class.

The talk closes with a newer platform of realistic, scenario-based challenges built by the speaker and collaborators, aimed at learners who have finished the earlier resources. The main takeaway is to build fundamentals in order, practice with guided labs, and then move on to open-ended problems. Links to every resource mentioned were posted in the video description.

talks.title: I Tried 100+ Hacking Tools. These Are The Best!
talks.teaser: Ranks favourite bug bounty tools for subdomain discovery, port scanning, fuzzing, and JavaScript analysis.
talks.summary:
The video is a roundup of bug bounty tools picked from about a decade of hands-on testing, offered as a starting shortlist for newcomers. It follows a typical target workflow, beginning with asset discovery. Subfinder is named the top choice for quickly gathering subdomains, with Amass as the slower but more thorough runner-up. For port scanning, Nmap is preferred for its accuracy, while Naabu and Masscan are presented as much faster alternatives.

Next comes information gathering. httpx is chosen to probe a list of hosts and report details such as titles, response sizes and headers, which helps decide where to focus. For historic endpoints, waymore is favoured over waybackurls and gau, which are still described as good options. For proxying and fuzzing, Burp Suite is the main intercepting proxy, with Caido seen as a close rival and OWASP ZAP as a free option. For content discovery, ffuf is preferred over dirsearch because it can also fuzz parameters and file extensions.

For efficiency, the speaker recommends a diff-style tool to compare results from repeated runs and surface only new assets. For JavaScript, LinkFinder extracts endpoints and routes from script files, and sourcemapper rebuilds original source from webpack source maps. The closing point is that the tools matter less than understanding how they work and using them to save time.

talks.title: $1,000 👉🏼 $5,000+/month With Bug Bounties
talks.teaser: Outlines how bug bounty hunters can grow monthly earnings toward $10,000 through private programs and asset monitoring.
talks.summary:
The video is aimed at hunters who already earn some money from bug bounty platforms and want to scale toward a monthly target of around $10,000. The speaker argues that a concrete goal matters, since reaching it once makes it feel achievable again, and that luck only helps someone who keeps putting in sustained effort. Hunters can focus on whichever vulnerability classes suit them, whether business logic and authorization flaws or server-side issues such as IDORs and XSS.

The talk presents two main tactics. The first is earning invitations to private programs by performing well on a few good public or private programs, which also builds reputation on the platform. The second is becoming an anchor hacker on one to three programs, returning repeatedly to learn a platform's permissions and the recurring mistakes its developers make. Airbnb is given as an example of this approach, and the speaker notes that a familiar program can still produce findings during slow periods when new targets yield nothing.

The second half focuses on automation aimed at asset monitoring rather than mass template-based scanning, which the speaker considers saturated. Hunters can watch for newly issued domains so they reach fresh assets first, and track existing assets for change. One example is looping httpx against a root page to check its response size and sending a notification through a tool such as notify when it changes. The talk closes by encouraging hunters to find like-minded peers for shared learning and support during slumps.

talks.title: I Became A Million Dollar Hacker 😱
talks.teaser: Walks through how one bug bounty hunter reached $1 million in HackerOne payouts and the habits behind it.
talks.summary:
The speaker marks reaching one million dollars in bug bounty payouts on HackerOne. About a third of that total came in the first three years of his activity on the platform, and the rest came in the last two, with about half earned in the most recent year. He says a career break from bug bounties, including his time working at HackerOne, slowed progress early on, and that the sum was built over several years rather than in a single season. Roughly 60 percent of the earnings came from two programs, while the remainder came from many private programs.

The main changes he describes start with dropping heavy automation and broad recon in favor of going very deep on a few programs by hand. Collaboration with other hunters helped him learn and get through slow months. He also pushed into areas few people test, such as hardware and desktop applications, which produced bounties at live hacking events. Finally, he focused on one large program and took the effort to gain access to many of its applications, including joining calls and sometimes paying for access, which surfaced scope others had not reached.

He closes by urging hunters to stay within program rules, avoid anything illegal, and keep pushing past obstacles instead of giving up early.

talks.teaser: Compares popular cybersecurity certifications like CCNA, CompTIA, CEH and OSCP by career stage and job relevance.
talks.summary:
Beginners often struggle to choose among the many cybersecurity certifications available. This talk works through several popular options and suggests when each one fits a person's stage of career. It starts with networking foundations: Cisco's CCNA is presented as a common entry point that stays relevant because of Cisco's reach in networking. CompTIA's A+ and Network+ are described as good starting points for people without an IT background, and Security+ is highlighted as a credential that appears often in job listings.

The middle of the talk splits the options by career direction. CompTIA CySA+ is framed as a defensive, blue-team path, while PenTest+ covers offensive work such as scoping, scanning, exploitation and reporting. CEH is discussed as a broad ethical hacking certification that many employers ask for, with the caveat that it is expensive and much of its material can be learned free. OSCP is presented as a highly respected, hands-on offensive certification with a demanding 24-hour exam, and lower-cost alternatives such as TCM Security's PNPT are mentioned.

The closing advice is to build foundations with A+ and Network+ or CCNA, add Security+ for general security knowledge, and then choose a defensive or offensive path. Viewers are encouraged to search job listings to see which credentials employers actually request, as a practical way to decide where to invest their time and money.

talks.title: Easy $500 Vulnerabilities! // How To Bug Bounty
talks.teaser: Gives a beginner-oriented overview of five common web bug bounty vulnerability classes and how to hunt for each.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by setting expectations: bug bounty payouts of around $500 are reachable, but through steady practice rather than quick wins. It then previews five common web vulnerability classes and how to hunt for each, aimed at beginners.

Cross-site scripting comes first, and the speaker warns against pasting one payload into every field. Instead, testers should note where input lands in the page, such as a script tag, an input or a plain div, and escape that specific context. Cross-site request forgery is covered next, focusing on sensitive actions and how requests are authenticated, such as cookies or tokens that may be removed or reused. Insecure direct object references follow, where changing an identifier like a user ID can expose another user's data, with hashed IDs needing a way to leak the real value.

Authorization issues are described as a favorite area because fewer testers examine them. Testers map what admins, managers and regular users can do, then replay privileged requests using a lower-privileged session, ideally with two accounts in separate browsers. The final category is leaked credentials, found by identifying a target's third-party vendors, learning how they label API keys, and searching GitHub for the company's domain. The overall message is that these bugs need little specialized tooling, mainly an intercepting proxy and disciplined comparison across accounts.

talks.title: I Hacked Into Red Bull // Bug Bounty Stories
talks.teaser: Walks through chaining path traversal behind a reverse proxy to reach a Tomcat instance and its exposed Jolokia endpoint.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common setup: Apache Tomcat application servers often sit behind a reverse proxy such as nginx, and error pages or invalid paths can reveal that Tomcat is in the chain. The presenter covers how to check for the Tomcat manager interface, how a 403 can sometimes be bypassed, and how weak or default credentials can give access to it. Once logged in, a packaged JSP web application can be deployed to get command execution on the server, which is shown in a lab environment.

The middle of the talk focuses on cases where the Tomcat backend cannot be reached directly. By finding a path that the proxy forwards to Tomcat, then using semicolon-based path traversal, the presenter shows how the proxy and Tomcat can interpret the same URL differently. That reveals Tomcat's web root and additional content not visible otherwise, including a Jolokia endpoint. Jolokia was then used for a local file read, confirmed by reading the hosts file, and a diagnostic command was used to read Tomcat's users configuration. The credentials recovered from that file would let an attacker log in to the manager and deploy a shell. The presenter describes this as the chain used on a real bug bounty program, though the sensitive details were left out.

The closing takeaway is to test every path behind a proxy, compare how different paths respond, and treat small findings such as a leaked endpoint or a file read as leads that can be chained together. The presenter notes that the program asked for the research to stop at the report stage and not be pushed further.

talks.title: The Beginner's Guide to Blind XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
talks.teaser: Walks through placing and tracking blind XSS payloads so they fire in back-end admin views the tester cannot see.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces blind cross-site scripting, where a payload fires in a back-end view such as an admin panel that the tester never sees. The speaker explains that these payloads need a callback service, such as a self-hosted XSS Hunter-style server, that records the page DOM, a screenshot, cookies, referrer and user agent when the payload fires. A hosted alternative is mentioned, but it does not return the page source, which makes locating the injection point harder.

Using a deliberately vulnerable fake delivery website, the speaker places payloads in registration names, delivery notes, address lines and support tickets. Each field needs a guess about its context, such as an input tag, a textarea or a script block, and that guess determines which characters are needed to break out. Payloads are left unclosed so they survive simple filtering, and the speaker wraps them to cover several contexts at once. Order notes fired on the admin pending-orders page, and a payload in the user-agent header, injected with a Burp match-and-replace rule, fired in the customer metadata. A name field also fired in the admin users table, while an input-tag case was left as an exercise for viewers.

The takeaway is to assume that browser data and headers are collected, to test them as well as visible fields, and to keep a record of each injection point with its screenshot so a report can point to the exact location. The speaker also warns against flooding third-party support systems that may be out of scope.

talks.title: $0 👉🏼 $1,000/Month With Bug Bounties
talks.teaser: Gives newcomers a mindset, approach and program-selection strategy for earning steady income from bug bounty hunting.
talks.summary:
The talk sets a goal of earning roughly $1,000 to $2,000 a month from bug bounties as a stepping stone toward doing it full time. The speaker starts with mindset: approach hunting with a positive outlook, drop low-impact findings such as rate limiting or missing best-practice headers that do not show how a company or its customers would be harmed, and keep working around blockers instead of giving up, the way CTF players do.

Next comes the approach. Automated scanning across the whole ecosystem tends to surface lower-severity issues and gets crowded fast, so the speaker recommends that newcomers start manually with a small amount of recon, learn how to exploit each vulnerability class, and only then add automation. Manual hunting means mapping how a company's assets and APIs fit together and testing them one by one. Program choice is the third lever. Check recent activity on a platform, such as the 90-day stats for paid bounties, triaged reports and average payouts, and prefer active, large programs where a duplicate still shows progress. When a pattern of mistakes turns up, such as IDOR across an API, keep exploring that pattern and consider sharing it with friends who may build on it.

The talk closes by urging viewers to celebrate small wins when they hit a monthly target, spending part of the earnings as a reward to stay motivated.

talks.title: Bug Bounty Hunting Full Time
talks.teaser: Explains how to prepare financially and choose targets for a full-time bug bounty career.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that earning a living from bug bounties is achievable, but only after three things are in place: a budget, a financial runway, and a plan. The speaker describes leaving a senior executive role and realising that spending habits had grown along with salary. The advice is to list the true bare minimums, such as rent or mortgage, car payments, insurance and groceries, keep a small buffer for surprises, and then multiply that monthly figure by three to six months to set a savings target that covers the transition.

The second part covers the hunting itself. Bug bounty is high risk and high reward: days can pass without a finding, yet a single medium-severity bug can pay hundreds or thousands of dollars. The speaker suggests choosing large companies with many interconnected applications, and checking the average payout for medium findings to judge whether a program is worth the time. Hunters should look past the easy wins that scanners find, such as basic XSS or IDOR, and aim for business logic and authorization flaws. Rather than hopping between wide-scope programs, the speaker recommends committing to one program long enough to build momentum and understand how its applications fit together.

The talk closes with an example from a private program, where the speaker worked through sign-up requirements, such as needing a particular type of user, to reach applications other hunters could not access. The takeaway is that problem solving and persistence in getting past barriers can set a hunter apart. The speaker points viewers to a longer blog post with more detail on going full time.

talks.title: Hacking An Online Casino // Bug Bounty Example
talks.teaser: Walks through a CTF-style lottery app where hidden API endpoints allow account verification and admin access.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this walkthrough, the speaker demonstrates how they uncovered critical vulnerabilities in a major European online casino's lottery system. Because non-disclosure agreements and private bug bounty programs often prevent recording live targets, the speaker collaborated with Adam Langley to recreate the scenario as a Capture The Flag (CTF) challenge hosted on hackinghub.io. The demonstration illustrates that encountering an application with only a login prompt and no visible registration does not mean security testing has reached a dead end.

### Key Topics
- Overcoming restricted target interfaces with no apparent sign-up option.
- Endpoint discovery and API fuzzing with tools like ffuf and curl.
- Exploiting verbose API error messages that reveal required request parameters.
- Bypassing account verification workflows using exposed user tokens.
- Privilege escalation via leaked user enumerations and password brute-forcing to reach an unrestricted file upload.

### Technical Details
The attack began on a lottery application presenting only a login interface and a password reset link. Reviewing client-side JavaScript revealed initial authentication routes under the path `/api/v1/auth`.

1. **Endpoint Discovery & Parameter Identification:** Using `ffuf` with custom wordlists (referencing lists such as SecLists or Assetnote), the speaker discovered an unadvertised endpoint at `/api/v1/auth/new`. A `GET` request returned a `405 Method Not Allowed`, indicating that different HTTP methods were expected. Sending a `POST` request revealed verbose error responses specifying missing parameter fields, such as `username`, `email`, `password`, and `password2`. Supplying these fields successfully created an account.

2. **Manual Account Verification:** Logging into the newly registered account showed a status of "awaiting verification." Without receiving a verification email, the speaker inspected background traffic and identified a call to `/api/v1/users/me`. This response exposed the user ID and a `verification_token`. Authenticated fuzzing using the session cookie uncovered an endpoint at `/api/v1/verify`. Submitting a `POST` request with the required `verification_token` and `user_id` verified the account.

3. **Privilege Escalation and Admin Takeover:** Once verified, the application granted access to an internal interface leaking a list of all registered lottery usernames and identifying administrative accounts. By capturing the login request in Burp Suite and brute-forcing passwords (e.g., using lists like `rockyou.txt`), the speaker compromised an administrative account. Administrative access unlocked an unrestricted file upload feature, which allowed an attacker to upload a web shell and achieve remote execution on the target system.

### Takeaways
Security researchers should not abandon an assessment simply because there is no obvious public registration link. Hidden API endpoints, verbose error messages, and unauthenticated registration functions often leave paths to obtain an initial low-privileged session. Once authenticated, mapping secondary API routes and identifying information disclosure flaws can quickly escalate access to administrative compromise and full system control.

talks.title: API Hacking With ChatGPT!
talks.teaser: Shows how ChatGPT-generated path lists and Meg can uncover exposed Swagger and OpenAPI docs across a bug bounty scope.
talks.summary:
The video tackles a common bug bounty problem: wide-scope programs expose many APIs, and testing them blindly is inefficient. The presenter proposes finding leaked API documentation first. ChatGPT is used to generate a list of about fifty paths where Swagger files or API docs might be exposed, and versioned variants such as V3 paths are added where the list lacked them.

Next, subdomains gathered with a subdomain enumeration tool are fed to Meg, which requests each path on every host and saves the full responses into an output folder. To sort the results, the presenter asks ChatGPT what a Swagger YAML file looks like, then searches successful responses for the version string. Similar searches follow for OpenAPI version strings and for "Swagger UI" in page titles. The run produces about 447 hits, which are opened and reviewed to inspect the specs and the endpoints they list.

The key point is that exposed documentation is not a vulnerability by itself. It is a lead: the specs reveal endpoints, required parameters, and sometimes routes that need no authentication. Practitioners should then test for authorization flaws, such as reaching user lists without proper access checks, or for server-side issues, such as a webhook URL parameter that could allow SSRF.
