talks.title: #NahamCon2023: Forager: New Insights Into Leaked Secrets | @InsecureNature
talks.teaser: Shows how leaked API keys on GitHub and npm can be traced back to the employees and companies that posted them.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who created TruffleHog and leads Truffle Security, previews Forager, a tool set to launch soon that counts live credentials posted to GitHub and npm and links them to the companies that leaked them. He opens with a 2017 case in which a researcher used API keys that DJI employees had pushed to personal repositories to unlock restricted drone flight zones. Those keys were never in official company repositories, so finding them required connecting people to their employers.

The attribution method starts from commit email addresses, which GitHub does not verify. Using the events API, the researcher pulls the members of an organization, collects the emails they commit with, and follows those addresses to other accounts, including personal ones. Watching the platform-wide event stream then lets the pipeline attribute a secret in any commit to a likely employer. In one test, an AWS key planted in a new repository was used within 10 minutes, from several countries. Collected data suggested a live key appears on GitHub about every 10 minutes, usually in small, unwatched projects, and most leaks come from personal accounts rather than organizations. On npm, publishing a whole directory can sweep in backups and CI output. One package shipped a full production database, and git and npm ignore files do not work together.

The takeaway is that leaks outside official repositories matter as much as those inside them. Forager will show per-company counts of leaked key types, with raw details visible to employees of that company. Practitioners should review forks and personal repositories, check what a publish command includes, and scan older package versions, since sensitive files can persist there.

talks.title: #NahamCon2023: Hacking Root EPP Servers To Take Control of Zones | @infosec_au
talks.teaser: Shows how an XXE flaw and a file disclosure bug in registry software exposed domain registries and every domain they manage.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how domain registries, the operators at the top of a top-level domain's chain, can be compromised through their EPP servers. EPP is an XML protocol usually exposed on port 700 that registrars use to manage domains, so compromising it can reach every domain in the registry. Rather than testing DNS behaviour, the researchers scanned hundreds of hosts with a generic out-of-band XXE payload and received many callbacks.

Fingerprinting the callback hosts revealed a web login running CoCCA registry software, which many country-code TLD operators rely on. Reviewing the Java source showed the EPP server built its XML parser without disabling external entities, which enabled XXE. A pre-authentication servlet also concatenated a country parameter into a file path, giving local file disclosure. Chaining the two read arbitrary files, including the shadow file, which showed the service ran as root. Further files exposed an SSH key, encrypted backups of a registry, and a script that uploaded plain-text database backups for many TLDs to a cloud storage account.

Since the vendor was hard to reach, the team contacted the registry operator over WhatsApp and sent a written report. The operator confirmed that admin access to the web login let an attacker control any domain under that registry, and the software was patched. The takeaway is that small operators often depend on shared off-the-shelf software, so one flaw can become a single point of failure across many TLDs.

talks.title: #NahamCon2023: Securing Open Source Dependencies: It’s Not Just Your Code That You Need to Secure
talks.teaser: Explains how open source dependencies create third-party risk and how software composition analysis tools help manage it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that modern applications are assembled largely from open source code. Developers pull in direct dependencies, which in turn pull in many indirect ones they rarely inspect. Citing an annual industry study of commercial codebases, the speaker argues that most of a typical application is open source, that many codebases contain known high-risk vulnerabilities, and that license conflicts are common. These figures frame the problem as one of visibility, licensing and security rather than only custom code quality.

The middle of the talk uses real incidents to show the stakes. A small npm package being unpublished broke builds across much of the JavaScript ecosystem. The Equifax breach followed a remote code execution flaw in Apache Struts that had not been patched in time. The Log4j vulnerability showed why teams need a software bill of materials that lists every component they use. The speaker then explains software composition analysis tools, which generate that inventory, match components against vulnerability sources, and check licenses. Selection criteria covered include language support, the diversity of vulnerability data, whether the tool can tell if a vulnerable function is actually called, automated update pull requests, integration with pipelines, and reporting.

The closing section is a recorded demo in which npm audit is run against the intentionally vulnerable Juice Shop application. It reports dozens of vulnerabilities across more than twenty thousand packages, including a critical flaw that allows authentication bypass. The takeaway is that free or open source scanners are a sensible starting point, paid tools add needed features, and teams should scan dependencies routinely and patch on a regular cycle.

talks.title: #NahamCon2023: PCI DSS or PCI DISS?! | @Rhynorater
talks.teaser: Explains postMessage-based cross-origin flaws that leaked plaintext card data from payment iframes on real bug bounty targets.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how payment providers use PCI DSS compliant iframes to keep card data off merchant servers, reducing the merchant's compliance scope. It walks through how these embedded payment frames talk to the host page using the browser's postMessage API, and why the same-origin policy makes that cross-origin channel the focus of attacks. The speaker covers ways to locate message listeners, including browser developer tools and a message-tracking extension, and notes that a weak origin check, such as an unescaped dot in a regular expression, can let an attacker's domain through.

The middle of the talk covers several bug bounty cases. In one PayPal integration, a race condition during the payment flow let an attacker inject CSS that loaded per-character fonts from a remote server, leaking typed card numbers one digit at a time. A similar flaw was found on a food delivery provider's payment vendor. Another payment provider let an attacker overwrite transaction details such as price and the publishable key, redirecting payment to the attacker. A grocery provider's message handling enabled plaintext card capture through XSS and iframe replacement.

The closing takeaway is that postMessage handlers should be treated as client-side APIs and audited carefully, including checking every frame in each thread. The speaker says the combined work with two collaborators compromised about eight providers, with bounties in the upper five figures.

talks.summary:
The talk shows how to use Shodan to find exposed web panels and risky endpoints across an in-scope organization. A search on an organization's SSL certificate name lists its domains and IP addresses, while a hostname query suits narrower programs. Results are then narrowed with filters for HTTP title, status code, country and organization, plus negative filters that drop unwanted matches. Free accounts only reach two result pages, so the speaker changes the queries to see more.

Next, the flagged hosts are checked for liveness. Live domains are compared with their IP addresses, because a domain may sit behind a block while the raw IP still responds. Dead domains are checked on Web Archive for old endpoints. When an error page reveals Microsoft IIS, the speaker searches for ASPX endpoints using Google dorking and urlscan.io. Status codes 401 and 403 help point to login pages and restricted areas, which led to an admin directory in one case.

The main takeaway is that Shodan filters can map a large scope quickly, and testing against IPs can save time and avoid blocks. The speaker reports that this approach has uncovered critical issues, including unauthenticated access and the ability to create accounts. Practitioners should filter first, then verify each endpoint on both the domain and the IP.

talks.title: Hacker Interview: Ryan Montgomery AKA 0day
talks.teaser: A former treatment-center CEO and CTF champion describes his path into OSINT and online predator investigations.
talks.summary:
Ryan Montgomery, known as '0day,' is the #1-ranked player on TryHackMe (with nearly 2 million users) and co-founder of pentester.com, a rapidly growing cybersecurity platform. Before pivoting to cybersecurity, he operated three mental health and substance abuse treatment facilities for over seven years, managing 144 beds and approximately 120 employees. A defining achievement was his scholarship program, which provided free treatment to over 100 individuals without private insurance—addressing a personal gap he experienced while struggling with childhood addiction and lacking access to private facilities.

Ryan defines OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) as intelligence gleaned from publicly available sources: records, credentials, images, social media, and archived websites. He has integrated OSINT methodologies into pentester.com, which features Darkwatch (a database of 140 billion sensitive records including credentials, social security numbers, and home addresses) and Identity IQ (facial recognition using 120 facial measurements to locate where individuals appear online).

Ryan gained viral attention through recent activism targeting child exploitation. After discovering a forum-based website hosting such content, he reported it to authorities and media outlets—all refused to publish due to legal concerns. Through investigation, he identified the site owner as Nathan Larson, a Virginia politician who ran for Congress twice, and found that Frederick (founder of The Pirate Bay) was knowingly hosting it. Six months later, Larson was arrested in Denver with a kidnapped 12-year-old.

Unable to accept institutional inaction, Ryan partnered with Dustin Lampro, an undefeated professional MMA fighter (also appearing on The Ultimate Fighter), to work with adult decoys posing as children online. When suspected predators arrive for meet-ups, Ryan and Dustin confront them using preloaded OSINT (names, jobs, family, criminal histories) before police arrive and make arrests. Ryan employs reverse image searching, employee databases, and deep OSINT to identify individuals from minimal information.

A viral podcast clip describing the exploitation content spread over 100 million times across platforms, leading to major podcast appearances including Project Veritas and the Shawn Ryan Show. Khloé Kardashian reshared his content to 307 million followers. Ryan plans to partner with nonprofits working alongside law enforcement for increased prosecutions and potential trafficking ring investigations. He is not monetizing these efforts.

Ryan addressed criticism from detractors who excavated his MySpace history from ages 13–14, when he struggled with substance abuse and used typical emo-era usernames. Now nearly 30, he emphasized that personal growth means learning from teenage mistakes, and his current actions demonstrate his commitment to helping others.

talks.title: Hacking with Google Dorking!
talks.teaser: Shows how Google search operators can surface login pages, subdomains, and parameterized URLs as bug bounty leads.
talks.summary:
The video targets people who have just started bug bounty hunting and are unsure how to find a target and a starting point for testing. The presenter argues that Google search operators are a practical way to build leads before any testing begins. The walkthrough starts with the site: operator to limit results to a single domain, then uses a minus sign to drop noisy subdomains that flood the results.

From there the talk layers other operators. The inurl: operator finds keywords in URLs, such as api or login, and intitle: narrows results to pages whose titles contain a term. In the example this surfaced a Jira instance on an IBM subdomain, a tool that is usually internal but is sometimes exposed to partners. The filetype: and ext: operators search for specific extensions. A PHP query returned a login page, while a JSP query returned nothing in the example. Searching a domain can also reveal cached pages, which may show settings or dashboards that are reachable without logging in. Searching inurl with an equals sign lists indexed URLs that carry parameters, which the presenter suggests as candidates for cross-site scripting, SQL injection, and SSRF testing.

The main takeaway is that results are often sparse, so operators should be combined and adjusted until something useful appears. Each lead still needs manual checking before it can become a valid finding, and the presenter recommends running these searches as a routine step for any new target.

talks.title: Free Web Application Hacking Resources // Ethical Hacking
talks.teaser: Surveys free and paid platforms, labs, and disclosed-report sites for learning web application hacking.
talks.summary:
This video is a guided tour of resources for learning web application hacking, aimed at people who want to become penetration testers, red teamers or bug bounty hunters. It follows on from an earlier roadmap video and focuses mostly on free options. The suggested path starts with TryHackMe's web fundamentals and introduction to web hacking rooms, then Burp Suite basics and the OWASP Top 10 material. PortSwigger's Web Security Academy comes next, organising reading and labs by vulnerability type. Hacker101 follows as a step that makes the learner assess unfamiliar applications without being told which bug classes to look for. OWASP Juice Shop is presented as a deliberately vulnerable application that can be used online, through TryHackMe, or run locally.

The paid options cover TryHackMe's premium rooms, Hack The Box, with its retired machines and a web category filter, Pentester Lab, which includes CVE-based exercises, and CTFChallenge, whose challenges are modelled on real bugs. For reading, HackerOne's Hacktivity and Bugcrowd's disclosed reports show how other hunters found, reported and were rewarded for issues. Disclosure-tracking accounts on social media are also listed. The speaker mentions his own paid course as an option for learners who want direct instruction.

The talk closes by arguing that certifications such as CEH or PenTest+ are not necessary to prove web hacking skill. The speaker suggests that testing authorised bug bounty and vulnerability disclosure programmes and listing those results on a resume shows practical ability more clearly.

talks.title: Finding Your First Bug
talks.teaser: Makes the case for moving from tutorials to real bug bounty hunting, with advice on approach and which bug classes to learn first.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many newcomers stay stuck in a loop of watching videos and finishing practice labs without ever submitting a real finding. The speaker recalls how earlier hackers learned by testing real targets, such as vulnerability disclosure programs and open source projects installed locally, and reporting what they found. Unlike a CTF, a bug bounty target has no known answer, so the hunter has to rely on their own method and judgment.

The middle of the talk focuses on mindset and approach. Instead of asking which payload someone used, the speaker suggests asking how they found the flaw, since spraying payloads without understanding them rarely works. The recommended approach is to get deeply familiar with a product: read its documentation, use every feature, and map out functionality that is less visible, because those areas tend to hold bugs and attract fewer duplicate reports. Starting on vulnerability disclosure programs is suggested, followed by picking recently listed programs on HackerOne. A few valid reports there can lead to private invitations, where competition is lower.

To build skill, the speaker advises mastering a small set of common bug classes first, such as cross-site scripting, CSRF and IDOR, before adding server-side request forgery, authorization issues and authentication bypasses. The closing message is to stop postponing and begin hunting now, because the skills only develop through doing the work.

talks.title: Bug Bounty Changed My Life!
talks.teaser: Shows how bug bounty findings built one hunter's resume and income, and lays out a starter plan for new hunters.
talks.summary:
The speaker describes starting bug hunting around late 2013, while still in college and frustrated with the coursework on offer. Public write-ups from established researchers, including a remote command execution on Yahoo, pushed them to try programs themselves. Early disclosure programs gave them findings to list on a resume, which led to a first job as an application security engineer at Hulu. Payouts mattered too: a handful of SQL injection bounties on Yahoo in early 2014 added up to about $9,000.

The middle of the talk compares those early years, when practice meant intentionally vulnerable apps and word of mouth, with today's learning platforms and larger competition. The first vulnerability took about three months, so the speaker suggests a three-to-six-month goal. Concrete steps include tracking how daily time is spent, cutting back on gaming and going out, and setting a regular hacking schedule. Joining a Discord community to find an accountability partner is also recommended, along with starting on vulnerability disclosure programs, where there is less competition.

The closing advice is that one early finding, whether from a disclosure program or a paid program, can earn an invitation to private programs on platforms such as HackerOne and Bugcrowd and build momentum. The talk is aimed at people who want to become pentesters, red team members, or full-time hunters, and it presents hacking practice as a habit that improves with consistent effort.

talks.title: I MADE $100,000 IN TWO MONTHS!
talks.teaser: Shares how a bug bounty hunter earned about $100,000 in two months through manual testing across two platforms.
talks.summary:
The video recounts a bug bounty run that brought in roughly $100,000 over the first two months of 2023, with about $82,000 from HackerOne and about $20,000 from Bugcrowd. The creator says timing and luck played a large part, since a private HackerOne program and a long-running Bugcrowd program paid out when the creator happened to look at them. Splitting effort between a primary and a secondary platform is presented as a practical way to organize the work.

The method was fully manual, with no reconnaissance tooling. The creator worked in Burp Suite and the browser's network tab, reading JavaScript files to find admin functionality that a standard user account should not reach. Authorization flaws were the most common issue, leading to IDORs, cross-site scripting and some SQL injection. One notable case was an SSRF on a large retailer's production server that was escalated to remote code execution, the largest single payout at about $12,000, which was shared with a collaborator. The creator also stresses looking for repeated coding mistakes across all of a company's applications, since the same developers often make the same errors.

The closing section covers the downsides. Client travel left the creator hacking in airports and on planes, which led to burnout and a stall after February. The advice is to set a goal with enough time for rest, and to accept stopping once that goal is reached.

talks.title: How To Use Shodan For Bug Bounty & Recon
talks.teaser: Shows how to use the Shodan CLI with jq, httpx and xargs to map an organization's hosts, ports and SSL assets.
talks.summary:
The video starts from a penetration test where the presenter needed to scope a client's many domains and IP addresses quickly. The argument is that raw Shodan CLI output is only useful once it is processed, so the walkthrough sets up the CLI with an API key and compares the two files a domain lookup produces: a lighter JSON file and a fuller host file that includes HTTP status, server details and IP information.

The middle of the talk moves into filtering. Using jq, the presenter pulls specific fields such as hostnames, IP strings, ISP and organization from the saved data. Organization searches are then limited to IP, port and HTTP title, and port filters such as excluding 80 and 443 are used to surface unusual services. The output is cleaned up with tr so it can be fed into httpx to grab titles and follow redirects, with nuclei shown only as an example of passing the data to another tool.

The final section covers SSL certificate searches for a domain and a search by autonomous system number. Hostnames from an ASN search can reveal domains beyond the target's main one, which are then deduplicated with sort. The presenter closes by looping those domains back into Shodan searches with xargs to collect IPs and ports. The takeaway is that Shodan results are a starting point, and since indexed data can be older than desired, live probing should confirm what is still exposed.

talks.title: WHY YOU SUCK AT HACKING // How To Bug Bounty
talks.teaser: Offers aspiring bug bounty hunters advice on building deep knowledge, sustained effort, and focused, structured practice.
talks.summary:
The talk is a motivational guide for hunters who struggle to land a first valid bug bounty finding or keep receiving informative or duplicate reports. The speaker argues that progress depends on three things beyond raw ability: knowledge, consistent effort, and focus supported by structure.

On knowledge, the speaker warns against copy-pasting payloads without understanding them, since they fail when the injection point differs. Hunters should learn why issues such as XSS, SSRF and IDOR occur and how developers fix them, which helps in finding ways around those defenses. Free training platforms are presented as sufficient for building this depth. On effort, the speaker cites a well-known hunter's tweet suggesting 16 to 18 hours on one program before expecting a first finding, because mapping an application's functions and threat model takes time. Relying on automated one-liners is discouraged in favor of manual testing.

For focus, the speaker recommends stepping away from the phone during work blocks and setting a timed goal. The suggested plan is to choose one bug class, study its labs and payload construction, then hunt it on a disclosure or bounty program until several real findings are filed. Only after that should a second class be added, gradually building a personal methodology for approaching web applications.

talks.title: Web Pentest & Hacking Roadmap // How To Bug Bounty
talks.teaser: Lays out six skills to learn, in order, before starting web hacking and bug bounty work.
talks.summary:
This video presents a web hacking roadmap for newcomers who want to move into bug bounties or web penetration testing. The host argues that these foundations are useful beyond bounty work, so he starts with the basics of how websites function. He walks through what happens when a browser requests a domain, the role of DNS, the request and response path, and how the back end responds. He suggests setting up a simple web server and pointing a domain at it to see these pieces working together.

Next he covers Linux basics and curl, which he calls his most-used command. curl lets you make requests without a browser, set headers such as cookies and authorization, and pull data from web APIs. Third on the list is a scripting language, such as bash, PowerShell or Python, mainly for automating repetitive tasks and manipulating data like JSON. Only after these come the core web vulnerability classes. He explains that knowing how databases work helps with SQL injection and that network knowledge helps with SSRF. He recommends being able to explain each bug class clearly to others, including how to fix it.

He warns against leaning on automation before you understand the fundamentals. He suggests light manual recon first, building a list of assets and interesting applications, and automating later. The final skill is JavaScript, which lets you read front-end code, find endpoints, and work out which HTTP methods and parameters they expect. He points to LinkFinder for locating endpoints. He closes by restating the six skills in order as the path to success in bug bounty hunting.

talks.title: #NahamCon2022EU: Managing a Bug Bounty Program From a Hacker's Perspective by @0xlupin
talks.teaser: Shows how a European marketplace runs its bug bounty, from scope and reward tables to triage and hunter invites.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a senior security engineer at the European home improvement marketplace ManoMano, traces the company's bounty history. The security team began offensive testing in 2019 and launched a bounty on a French platform that December. In 2021 the program moved to HackerOne to draw a larger pool of testers and widen the scope.

The talk walks through the program's policy choices. Personal data of customers, sellers and employees is in scope, a stance tied to the company's GDPR obligations. A hard-coded reward table prices known bug classes, such as remote code execution on the marketplace at 10,000 dollars, while clickjacking reports are discouraged. Other findings fall on a sliding scale for web and mobile issues. Hunters are encouraged to demonstrate real impact and chain bugs, since the team raises rewards for escalations.

On the operations side, the team aims to answer quickly, works with hunters in a Slack channel, and lets hunters with a medium or higher report invite two peers. Severity starts from CVSS but is adjusted for data exposure, log evidence of exploitation, how long the flaw existed and how hard the fix will be. The speaker also describes bonuses for useful Nuclei templates, paid retests and memes. The takeaway is that clear communication, transparent severity decisions and close collaboration with testers helped build a loyal community.

talks.title: Does Cybersecurity Require Programming?
talks.teaser: Explains when programming is needed for security work versus scripting, and which languages newcomers should learn first.
talks.summary:
The video takes up a common debate in infosec: whether you need to code to get into cybersecurity. It separates programming, which covers languages like C, C++ and Rust used for building software and low-level work such as binary exploitation or kernel research, from scripting, which automates repetitive tasks, with Python often cited as an example. The host draws on short clips from two guests from his livestream series, who both argue that coding is not strictly required for roles like penetration testing, bug bounty hunting or security analysis, but that basic scripting makes the work far easier.

For newcomers, the suggested path starts with bash or PowerShell, learning how to manipulate text, use loops and functions, and pass the output of one tool into another. Python comes next because of its libraries for making HTTP requests and its use in web frameworks, and JavaScript follows for web testing, since it helps explain how sites exchange data with the browser. The host shares his own workflow, where a short loop runs one command across a thousand domains instead of typing it over and over.

The closing takeaway is that deeper programming becomes necessary for exploit development, Linux kernel work, or auditing widely used open-source software, where scripting alone leads to a dead end. Languages such as C, Rust or PHP are suggested for that path. The overall message is that coding is not required at the start, but understanding how systems work makes it much easier to progress.

talks.title: I QUIT RECON... and made $10,000 in bounties!
talks.teaser: Shows how to find IDOR and hidden API endpoints by using a web app as a normal user and reading its JavaScript.
talks.summary:
The speaker explains a 30-day experiment of setting aside reconnaissance and returning to hands-on testing of web applications. Looking back at past talks and bounty work, most of the speaker's findings had come from signing up for applications, logging in, and browsing the core product rather than from asset discovery. Within the first week of the experiment the speaker earned about $10,000 in bounties, and the speaker says this renewed their enjoyment of the work.

The walkthrough uses a test Airbnb host account with two listings as a stand-in for a real target, and the speaker notes the demo is not about any actual Airbnb vulnerability. The method is to watch network traffic in the browser's developer tools, search for an object's ID across the captured calls, and see where that ID is referenced. Creating a second account with its own listing makes it easier to test whether one account can read another account's data by swapping IDs. The speaker also follows API paths by version and endpoint name, checks JavaScript files for further endpoints and parameters, and tries related queries such as listing lookups by category.

A second example from a recent test involved a JavaScript file that called admin-only API routes. The server only checked for a valid session, so a regular non-admin user could load data meant for administrators. The speaker recommends using a proxy such as Burp Suite to review request history, and tools that pull endpoints out of JavaScript files. The main takeaway is to understand an application's functionality and its authorization checks before running automated scanners.

talks.title: The 3 Tools You Need // How To Bug Bounty
talks.teaser: Walks through three core tools for web bug bounty work: asset discovery, content brute forcing, and intercepting proxies.
talks.summary:
The video argues that a small set of tools covers most of the early work in web bug bounty and ethical hacking. The presenter groups them into three categories: asset discovery, content discovery, and proxy tooling. He notes that the same approach fits penetration testing and scoped engagements, not only open bounty programs.

For asset discovery, the presenter runs Subfinder against a domain with all sources enabled and shows which data providers contributed results. He says free passive sources are enough for small targets, and that paid API keys mainly raise query limits. For content discovery, he recommends ffuf as a fast directory and parameter brute forcer, and mentions a slower Python alternative that he considers more accurate. He adds that port scanning is often unnecessary, though directory brute forcing is worth doing even on a single application.

For proxies, he scopes Burp Suite to one target domain and uses the intercept and history views to find background API calls that the browser does not show. He sends requests to Repeater to modify them and check the responses. He pays for a commercial Burp tier but uses mainly Repeater, with occasional Intruder runs. Free options such as ZAP or browser developer tools also work. The main takeaway is to learn a few tools well and automate only slow, repetitive chores, so more time goes into finding vulnerabilities.

talks.title: How to Bug Bounty
talks.teaser: Gives newcomers a roadmap of free learning resources, practice platforms and mentorship advice for starting bug bounty hunting.
talks.summary:
This beginner-oriented talk explains how to get started in bug bounty hunting. The speaker came to the field from a general computing background with no formal security training, and he presents a set of free resources and practical advice he wishes he had known at the start.

For learning, he recommends security content creators on YouTube, then hands-on practice. PicoCTF builds fundamentals such as browser developer tools, curl, regular expressions and headers. PortSwigger's Web Security Academy offers articles and labs on vulnerability classes including XSS, CSRF and SSRF. Hacker101, run by HackerOne, offers small applications where you hunt without being told which bug to find, and earning enough points can bring private program invitations. On mentorship, he describes three useful people: someone ahead of you, a peer at your level to collaborate with, and a newer learner you can teach, since teaching deepens understanding.

His main advice is to set concrete goals and metrics, and to get strong in a few bug types such as XSS, IDOR and SSRF before expanding. He advises avoiding automation early so the underlying concepts are learned. Start with a large target or a vulnerability disclosure program, dig deep, and move on when progress stalls, aiming for a few valid reports that lead to platform invitations.

talks.teaser: Coverage of How Hackers Run For The Money! from the conference program.

talks.title: What Should You Do After Recon?!
talks.teaser: Explains how to triage reconnaissance results by HTTP status code and keywords to pick which assets to test first.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at what to do once reconnaissance is finished. The speaker argues that automation does not replace hacking, since much good research comes from manual fuzzing and walking through application workflows. He describes two styles: staying in a terminal running endpoint discovery, or registering on large applications and dissecting their features and JavaScript, and suggests blending both.

His method starts with custom Nuclei templates that fingerprint applications like Jira or Jenkins, rather than default templates everyone runs, and with light information gathering via httpx, recording response code, size and title across an organisation's assets. Each status code then gets its own approach. A 200 with a title such as dashboard or login is worth registering for and testing. A 300 redirect to single sign-on may guard valuable data and calls for bypass attempts. A 401 suggests trying sessions from other applications or default passwords. A 403 invites path tricks and contextual directory brute forcing, and a 404 is approached through subdomain keywords such as API, leading to Swagger or YAML specifications.

Finally, assets are prioritised, starting with 200 responses and keywords like dashboard, customer and login, then moving to 404 results containing API, dev, internal or CI-related names. The main takeaway is that no status code is a reason to stop, and that experience sharpens these judgements.

talks.title: The DeFi Money Heist
talks.teaser: Walks through three DeFi smart contract flaws: missing role checks, arbitrary token repayment, and a denial-of-service via deposits.
talks.summary:
This episode covers three vulnerabilities in decentralized finance (DeFi) smart contracts, each shown with a small example contract. The first concerns authorization. A token contract restricted its mint function to accounts holding the minter role, but a separate public function for passing that role had no access check. Calling it to assign the role to his own address let an ordinary account print tokens. The takeaway is to search the code for role-related names and to check whether sensitive functions such as withdraw or delete have any required statement or modifier.

The second case involves a lending contract. Borrowers deposited collateral and repaid loans through a payoff function that accepted a token address as an argument. Because the repayment token was not restricted, the presenter deployed a custom ERC-20 token, repaid the loan with it, and recovered the real collateral without paying anything. The root cause is accepting arbitrary tokens instead of hard-coding the assets the protocol trusts. The presenter also noted that collateral prices can fall sharply, which can force liquidation, although this was discussed rather than demonstrated.

The third case is a denial-of-service flaw in a savings contract. The deposit function let a caller register a deposit for any address, so an attacker could block known users from making their own deposits. Because blockchain activity is public, the attacker can collect those addresses easily. The presenter linked this to auctions, where blocking past bidders could let an attacker win an item cheaply. Auditors should look for functions that let one user change another user's state.

talks.title: #NahamCon2022EU: Till REcollapse: Fuzzing the Web for Mysterious Bugs by @0xacb
talks.teaser: #NahamCon2022EU: Till REcollapse: Fuzzing the Web for Mysterious Bugs by @0xacb.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at NahamCon 2022 EU, André (known online as @0xacb or master of mystery), co-founder of Ethiack and ethical hacking professor at the University of Porto, introduces techniques and tools for black-box fuzzing of regular expressions. Modern web applications heavily rely on regular expressions for input validation, sanitization, and normalization, but implementations across languages frequently suffer from subtle edge cases and inconsistencies. André demonstrates how systematic byte-level fuzzing around key regex positions can bypass strict security controls and lead to severe security vulnerabilities like account takeover and web cache deception.

### Key Topics
- **Regex Implementations and Edge Cases**: Developers often copy-paste regexes from external sources without comprehensive testing, or use automated generation (e.g., GitHub Copilot) that introduces bypasses like unescaped dots (`.`) matching arbitrary characters. Furthermore, common constructs such as the end-of-string anchor (`$`) behave inconsistently across languages (e.g., JavaScript rejects trailing newlines, Python allows a single newline before the end, and Ruby matches regardless of subsequent lines unless configured differently).
- **Validation vs. Extraction Flaws**: Applications often validate full user inputs against a regex pattern but subsequently process the unextracted raw input rather than matched groups, allowing attackers to inject trailing or unvalidated bytes.
- **The REcollapse Methodology**: Black-box fuzzing of unknown backend regexes by systematically injecting byte values (`0x00` through `0xFF`) into three pivot locations:
  1. *Starting and termination positions* (probing anchor assertions).
  2. *Separator positions* (probing delimiters, special characters, and group boundaries).
  3. *Normalization positions* (fuzzing characters, especially vowels, that get transformed or canonicalized by backends).
- **The `recollapse` Tool**: A helper tool developed by the speaker that generates mutated input lists based on these pivot rules and supports different encodings (raw, URL-encoded, JSON bodies) and multi-byte fuzzing. It is designed to pipe wordlists into scanners like Burp Intruder or ffuf.

### Technical Details
- **Open Redirect to Account Takeover Demo**: Illustrates taking a validated domain (`example.com`) redirect parameter and fuzzing separator positions with single bytes. The author identifies that an `@` character followed by domain manipulation (`example.com@evil/.com`) bypassed filtering, which could be chained with an integer/decimal IP host to leak sensitive authentication tokens to an attacker-controlled server.
- **Web Cache Deception Case Study**: On a red-acted target API endpoint (`/wp-json/v1/user`), typical cached extensions (`.css`, `.pdf`, `.js`) yielded `404` errors. By fuzzing bytes prior to the extension, the author discovered that `%23` (`#`) or `%3F` (`?`) before `.pdf` (e.g., `%23.pdf`) caused the backend API to return a `200` response containing a user API token while the caching layer treated it as a cacheable static asset (`X-Cache: HIT`), enabling token theft.
- **Shopify / OAuth Zero-Interaction Account Takeover**: Demonstrates exploiting normalization quirks across OAuth identity flows (specifically involving `accounts.shopify.com` and a third-party app, `teller.app`). While the email change endpoint rejected unusual characters, the sign-up endpoint accepted a mutated character (such as a special unicode `i` or `a` character). When the identity provider forwarded the account via OAuth, the downstream application normalized the email into the victim's canonical address, granting unauthorized access without user interaction.

### Takeaways
- **Developers**: Ensure regular expressions are strictly tested and fuzzed across target runtime libraries. When validating inputs, explicitly extract matched substrings rather than processing raw strings.
- **Security Researchers**: Black-box fuzzing of locked-down input fields frequently exposes language-specific regex quirks, differential parsing across endpoints, or normalization discrepancies. Minor input modifications and single-byte variations can escalate into critical vulnerabilities.

talks.title: How to Directory Brute Force Properly
talks.teaser: Shows how to tailor directory brute force wordlists and targets to a server's stack and subdomain context.
talks.summary:
Many people run directory brute force with the same generic wordlist against every target, which wastes time and misses what is actually hosted. The video argues that results improve when wordlists match the server's technology stack, such as ASPX files on a Windows server or PHP on Linux, and when the scan is shaped by what the asset is for.

The approach starts with a broad pass using a combined all-purpose list that checks for common names across languages, filtering for useful response codes such as 301, 302, 401 and 405. If nothing useful comes back, the subdomain name becomes the source of ideas. A host with API in its name suggests testing route names like api, v1 or v2, along with combinations of words drawn from the hostname. In the example, the broad list returned nothing of interest, but keyword variants surfaced redirects and an exposed swagger.yaml specification, which could reveal the API's routes.

The takeaways are to collect wordlists from public sources such as SecLists and Assetnote, organize them by file extension, and build a personal list from files and leaks found during testing. When a lead appears, such as a PHP file, run an extended scan using only that extension. Choosing the list and extensions to fit the asset's context, rather than reusing one list, is the core lesson.

It breaks a hostname into subdomain, root domain and top-level domain, then shows how organisations add extra labels to separate products, APIs, internal tools and environments such as dev or QA. Smaller firms often use dashes inside one name instead of separate zones, which changes what to look for.

The method starts with a list of known subdomains gathered by enumeration tools. That list is fed to altdns along with a set of keywords such as admin, dev, api and app, which generates about 165 candidate names. Shuffledns then resolves those candidates using a list of resolvers. In the demonstration, nine candidates were valid, adding names such as appdev, dashboard and admin-api to an original list of seven.

The presenter argues that this permutation approach is a lighter alternative to full subdomain brute forcing, which is often not worth the effort for large organisations. The main aim is to find development and staging sites, which are more likely to expose files, folders or source code that were never meant to be public. The practical takeaway is to tailor keyword lists to the naming conventions of each target to widen the attack surface.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this session, host Ben invites packet analysis expert Chris Greer to break down the fundamentals of Wireshark, examine packet capture (pcap) data, and understand how TCP network traffic reveals security-relevant activities. Building on a previous discussion about how Nmap functions, the episode focuses on viewing network traffic from both defensive and offensive security perspectives, highlighting why both red and blue teamers need to understand what tools transmit onto the wire.

### Key Topics
- **Wireshark User Interface and Architecture**: Wireshark is an open-source, widely adopted packet analysis tool available at wireshark.org. It features a three-pane layout: a top summary pane listing packets line by line, a bottom-left pane detailing decoded protocol fields, and a bottom-right pane presenting raw packet data in hexadecimal and ASCII.
- **Profiles and Display Filters**: Wireshark supports custom profiles to tune columns and visibility depending on the task (such as troubleshooting versus cybersecurity analysis). It also provides a display filter bar and quick-access filter buttons to isolate protocols such as TCP, UDP, specific IP addresses, or combinations of criteria.
- **Nmap Port Scan Signatures**: Network reconnaissance leaves specific protocol artifacts. A stealth SYN scan generates distinctive TCP parameters that differ from normal TCP traffic patterns.

### Technical Details
Chris analyzes a captured stealth SYN scan targeting services like FTP and port 8080 to demonstrate how Nmap fingerprints itself on the wire:
- **Conflicting TCP Window and MSS Values**: In a default Nmap SYN packet, the TCP receive window size is advertised as 1024 bytes. Simultaneously, Nmap provides a TCP Maximum Segment Size (MSS) option of 1460 bytes. Telling the destination host that the maximum segment per packet is 1460 bytes while declaring a total receive buffer limit of only 1024 bytes is contradictory behavior rarely seen in standard real-world TCP stacks, serving as an immediate signature of an Nmap scan.
- **Wireshark Filter Construction**: Chris shows how to drag and drop packet fields directly into the filter bar to build detection queries. He constructs a filter combining the specific window size and the SYN flag: `tcp.window_size_value == 1024 and tcp.flags.syn == 1`. He explains that running this filter across large traffic volumes (such as terabytes of traffic) identifies default Nmap SYN scans with near certainty.

### Takeaways
- **Offensive Awareness**: Red teamers and penetration testers must know what their scanning tools transmit on the wire. Relying on default scan settings without customization creates obvious signatures that trigger alerts or get IPs blocked.
- **Defensive and Internal Detection**: Blue teamers and analysts can use targeted TCP filters to catch unauthorized port scanning and lateral movement within an internal network—such as identifying a compromised internal device or printer scanning adjacent network hosts behind IDS/IPS defenses.
- **Future Focus**: Deep dives into custom filter creation and the top 10 recommended Wireshark filters are planned for the subsequent episode.

talks.title: HACKERS ARE HIJACKING WEBSITES! // Subdomain and DNS Takeover
talks.teaser: Shows how dangling subdomain records and Route 53 name server delegations can be hijacked to serve content from a victim's domain.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how attackers take over subdomains and DNS delegations. A classic subdomain takeover happens when a CNAME points to a third-party service that no longer has an owner, for example because the organization was never registered, a record contains a typo, or the resource was deleted and can be claimed by a new user. The presenter notes that many well-known cases have since been patched after years of bug bounty reports, but that some variants still work. The main focus is a more serious case: taking over an entire name server delegation, such as a zone hosted on AWS Route 53.

The walkthrough uses a demo domain the presenter controls. Using host and dig, the presenter separates a missing record from one that returns SERVFAIL, which means the name exists but points to something unreachable. A dig trace from the root then reveals that the domain had been delegated to four Amazon name servers. A tool was then used to repeatedly create and delete hosted zones in Route 53 until one zone matched one of the target name servers, at which point the zone appeared in the AWS console. The presenter finished by adding a proof-of-concept record that pointed to a server they controlled and confirmed the subdomain resolved to it.

The key lesson is that matching even one name server is enough to control the zone's records. The presenter also warns that typos in name server records and expired domains used as name servers can be claimed in similar ways. Defenders should audit their DNS delegations and dangling records, and check whether any domains their name servers depend on have lapsed.

- **CVSS Scoring & Attack Complexity**: Evaluating the issue against the CVSS rating framework, the vulnerability initially appeared lower in priority due to high attack complexity. talks.title: OWASP Top 10 in 10 Min! (Kinda)
talks.teaser: Walks through each OWASP Top 10 2021 web risk category in short form, with examples and bug bounty angles.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security researcher and Hadrian VP of Research and Community Ben Sadeghipour (nahamsec) provides an accessible, rapid walkthrough of the OWASP Top 10 (2021 edition). Drawing from his background educating non-technical team members and working in bug bounty, he breaks down each vulnerability category, sharing practical explanations, common exploitation scenarios, and relevance to bug bounty hunters.

### Key Topics
The presentation centers on the ten categories defining the OWASP Top 10 (2021):
- **A01: Broken Access Control**: Gaining unauthorized access to data or functionality that belongs to another user or role (e.g., viewing other employees' salaries or PII via Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR), API parameter fuzzing, or tampering with JSON cookies and JWT tokens).
- **A02: Cryptographic Failures**: Failures in protecting data in transit or at rest, such as sending cleartext data, lacking proper HTTP headers, or failing to use HTTPS.
- **A03: Injection**: Flaws allowing execution of arbitrary code or queries, grouping server-side execution (SQL injection, remote code execution/command injection) and client-side execution (cross-site scripting / XSS, XXE).
- **A04: Insecure Design**: A category introduced in 2021 focusing on flaws in business logic rather than pure implementation vulnerabilities, such as bypassing item quantity limits or tampering with prices and coupons.
- **A05: Security Misconfiguration**: Leaving exposed debug or unnecessary functionality, unneeded open ports, default files, or default/guessable credentials on deployed applications (e.g., Apache Tomcat defaults).
- **A06: Vulnerable and Outdated Components**: Exploiting known vulnerabilities or zero-days in widely used platforms (such as Apache Struts 2, Heartbleed, Jira, GitHub Enterprise, Jenkins, or Grafana) using public proofs of concept.
- **A07: Identification and Authentication Failures**: Compromising user accounts via brute-forcing passwords, credential stuffing against breaches, session fixation, token exposure in URL bars, or session reuse.
- **A08: Software and Data Integrity Failures**: Risks stemming from untrusted code, unverified software updates, dependency confusion (highlighting research by Alex Birsan), or CI/CD pipeline tampering, illustrated by the SolarWinds supply chain attack.
- **A09: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures**: Inability to detect attacks or malicious activity in real-time due to absent logging for failed logins or server traffic.
- **A10: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)**: Tricking the server into generating unintended network requests, enabling attackers to interact with internal infrastructure, query cloud metadata services (e.g., AWS keys), bypass firewalls/VPN boundaries, or read local files.

### Technical Details
The speaker highlights various testing approaches and tools throughout the talk:
- **Fuzzing and Exploitation**: Mentioning tools like `ffuf` and `wfuzz` for finding API endpoints and brute-forcing parameters, and `nuclei` for scanning outdated components.
- **Logic Attacks**: Evaluating whether an application's business rules can be inverted or broken (e.g., ordering 150 units of an item limited to 15, or manipulating $29.99 pricing down to $0.99).
- **SSRF Exploits**: Leveraging internal network access from vulnerable apps to reach cloud provider metadata services (such as AWS/Azure), internal APIs, or internal web consoles.

### Takeaways
For newcomers and bug bounty hunters seeking hands-on practice, the speaker recommends OWASP Juice Shop (available as a Docker image), Hack The Box retired machines, and TryHackMe dedicated rooms. While noting structural differences and personal preferences favoring the 2017 list, the speaker emphasizes that the OWASP Top 10 remains an essential framework for identifying critical vulnerabilities and understanding web application security risks.

talks.teaser: Guest interview on Live Recon covering a security career path, CTF design, recon mindset, and tooling choices.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this live stream episode of Live Recon, host Ben (NahamSec) is joined by co-hosts Jason Haddix and STÖK to interview prominent cybersecurity content creator and Hack The Box contributor IppSec. The conversation spans IppSec's early background in gaming, hardware, and systems administration, his transition into offensive security, and the core philosophies guiding his approach to reconnaissance, CTFs, and career development. The discussion also touches on the practical differences between bug bounties and CTFs, favorite testing tools, and managing mental health, routines, and boundaries in the tech industry.

### Key Topics
- **Background & Entry into Tech**: IppSec details his start in hardware technician work in 2006, transitioning into Linux, Solaris, and Windows systems administration, as well as early experiences with AOL/AIM hacking, StarCraft casting, and game hacking.
- **Networking vs. Certifications**: The speakers discuss the value of college, training, and certifications. IppSec emphasizes that while he attends training like SANS and NetWars for networking and learning, he generally skips certification exams. He notes that showing continuous improvement and demonstrating soft skills are far more critical for bypassing the "HR firewall."
- **CTFs vs. Bug Bounties**: The panel compares CTFs to bug bounties. IppSec explains why he prefers CTFs and deep technical problem-solving over bug bounties, citing the risk of burnout, repetitive payload spraying, and toxic competitive dynamics tied to financial incentives. In contrast, STÖK and Jason present perspectives favoring real-world external attack surface discovery and deep target analysis.
- **Reconnaissance Philosophy**: IppSec describes reconnaissance as an art rather than an automated science. Rather than flooding targets with automated scanners, he focuses on spotting subtle anomalies, reading documentation, and analyzing what tools do *not* report.
- **Tools and Automation**: The participants discuss preferred tools for directory busting, web fuzzing, and proxying, evaluating options like Burp Suite, Wfuzz, ffuf, Gobuster, and Feroxbuster.
- **Mental Health, Burnout, and Setting Boundaries**: The stream concludes with an open dialogue on imposter syndrome, daily routines, social anxiety, depression, and the vital career skill of learning to say "no" to overwork.

### Technical Details
- **Pattern Recognition & Recon**: Drawing from real-time strategy (StarCraft) mechanics, IppSec compares recon to identifying missing elements and subtle discrepancies. For instance, finding an Nginx or Apache server setting a `JSESSIONID` cookie can hint at an underlying Tomcat instance with URL misconfigurations that scanners miss.
- **Host & Artifact Forensics**: Leveraging blue team and incident response experience, IppSec points out how timestamp precision (sub-second or millisecond cutoffs versus 32-bit representations) and file creation clusters around specific targets (e.g., `user.txt`) can expose backdoor files and challenge author actions.
- **Specific Vulnerability Case Studies**:
  - *WordPress MFA Bypass*: In a Hack The Box machine named "Press," IppSec bypassed MFA via legacy XML-RPC functions allowing post editing, leveraging the PHP Anywhere plugin to achieve code execution.
  - *PHP/Laravel Type Juggling*: Exploiting loose equality checks (`==`) in Laravel APIs that accept JSON payloads in the request body even during `GET` requests, allowing authentication/flag validation bypass via `{"flag": true}`.
  - *MFA Token Brute-Forcing*: Bypassing rate-limiting IP blacklists in Laravel APIs by rotating `X-Forwarded-For` headers alongside sequential numeric fuzzing.
  - *IPv6 Link-Local Pivoting*: On the "Sneaky" box, calculating `fe80::` link-local addresses derived from ARP table MAC entries to pivot across local broadcast domains.
  - *ProcFS Inspection*: Bypassing blind web issues using Local File Inclusion (LFI) by reading `/proc/sched_debug` or `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` to discover running services (such as knockd) or intercepting active reverse shells.
- **Tool Preferences**:
  - *Burp Suite*: Primarily used for Repeater without extensions or Collaborator.
  - *Fuzzers*: Preference for Wfuzz over ffuf or Burp Intruder when multi-parameter fuzzing and header injection are needed without custom wordlists; choosing Gobuster for targeted non-recursive scans and Feroxbuster for recursive exploration.

### Takeaways
- Reconnaissance is most effective when driven by curiosity and reading between the lines rather than relying on noisy, automated scanning pipelines that produce alert fatigue.
- Deep struggles during CTFs build lasting technical retention and problem-solving intuition ("spidey sense") far better than superficial successes.
- Soft skills, networking, and demonstrating a trajectory of self-improvement open more doors than stacking advanced certifications alone.
- Establishing firm boundaries—especially saying "no" to excessive workload—is critical for preventing burnout and sustaining long-term passion in cybersecurity.

talks.title: Critical Bounties via Leaked API Keys (FT TruffleHug)
talks.teaser: Shows how leaked API keys in public code become critical bug bounty findings, using TruffleHog to scan repositories.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why leaked credentials matter to bug bounty hunters, penetration testers and red teamers. Developers often hardcode API keys, configuration secrets and SSH keys into code, and those secrets can end up in public repositories, especially when a project is open-sourced and the keys are never removed. The speaker suggests learning how third-party services name their keys, since that naming makes them easier to search for. He outlines three approaches: searching for known key names, looking for APIs meant only for internal use, and running a secret scanner.

The main demonstration runs TruffleHog through Docker against a GitHub organization, limited to verified results so that only working credentials are returned. A call with one of the tool's co-founders explains the verification process. For each credential type, the tool matches a fixed string and a pattern, then makes a non-state-changing API call, such as Amazon's caller identity lookup, to confirm the key is live. Some services need workarounds: Slack webhooks are checked with a malformed request so that no message is posted. The speaker also logs in with a found credential to see what it can reach, while stressing that nothing should be changed.

The closing advice is to review private invitations and public programs whose scope covers many digital assets, scan their code for secrets, and report findings to the program. A live key may still reach data the company does not consider important, so severity has to be settled in conversation with the company. Practitioners should prefer reporting and asking permission before using a found credential.

talks.title: How to Identify and Exploit CVE-2021-43798
talks.teaser: Walks through finding exposed Grafana instances and exploiting the unauthenticated path traversal in CVE-2021-43798.
talks.summary:
The speaker introduces CVE-2021-43798, an unauthenticated path traversal in Grafana that lets an attacker read most files on the host, depending on the account the instance runs as. Because the flaw was still a zero-day, he warns that bounty programs may decline payment or delay it. The demo runs against a lab instance he installed himself.

Identification comes first. A default Grafana usually listens on port 3000, redirects unauthenticated requests to a login page, and shows a Grafana title and version string. Manual checks include the redirect location header and page source, while searches can use hostnames, favicon hashes and keyword matches in historical subdomain data. For bulk work, he runs httpx against a list of hosts on ports 443 and 3000 with response saving and host-redirect following, then greps saved responses for the Grafana fingerprint.

For exploitation, the traversal goes through a built-in plugin path, such as the alert list or annotations list plugins, so the attacker needs a plugin that is not disabled and then climbs out of the plugin folder to request /etc/passwd. He confirms this in Burp Suite Repeater and then uses Intruder with a payload list of plugin paths, turning off payload encoding, to find which plugins respond with 200. For scale, he feeds the host list into meg with the same paths, filters 200 responses containing root, and lists the hosts that appear vulnerable. The takeaway is to check which plugins are present and to follow each program's rules for reporting.

talks.title: Live Recon on Rockstar Games With @zseano​
talks.teaser: Follows a bug hunter probing Rockstar Games' main web app for open redirects, CSRF gaps and risky SVG uploads.
talks.summary:
In this livestream recon episode, the guest zseano is given Rockstar Games as the target by a chat poll. Rather than starting with subdomain scanners, he works through the main public web application first, mapping sign-in and sign-up flows, noting how return URL parameters are handled, and reading earlier disclosed reports to see which bug classes the site has already shown. His stated aim is to learn how the site behaves before choosing what to test.

He then works through several leads in Burp Suite. A return URL on the login flow suggests open redirect bypasses, with ideas for encoded characters, relative paths and alternate hostnames. An account update request appears to rely on client-side validation and has no visible anti-CSRF token, while a sign-up request does carry a verification token, which he expects to be enforced on other endpoints. An emblem editor accepts SVG data that can be stored and displayed, so he explains that the impact depends on whether the file is served from the company's own domain. He also demonstrates an archive-based workflow, feeding Wayback Machine URLs through a local redirect script to find old endpoints that still respond.

The episode closes with practical advice. Understand how the production application works before automating anything, check whether earlier fixes are complete, test alternate content types and file handling, and keep testing within program rules. He also recommends removing XSS payloads after testing and treating recon as a way to understand a target, not only as asset discovery.

talks.title: Live Recon and Distributed Recon Automation Using Axiom with @pry0cc
talks.teaser: Shows how the Axiom framework spins up cloud instance fleets to spread recon scans across many hosts at once.
talks.summary:
Pry, the author of Axiom, joins a livestream to show how his bash-based framework spins up temporary cloud instances and spreads reconnaissance work across them. It promises speed and low cost: a fleet of fifteen small instances can finish scans far faster than one machine, and the speaker quoted about 21 dollars for a two-hour run on a fleet that size. Chat voted on targets through polls, and the demo ran mostly against Spotify, with a larger Microsoft run for the bigger scans.

The walkthrough started with fleet creation from a prebuilt base image that already held common recon tools. Subdomains pulled from Chaos were resolved across the fleet with DNSX and probed with httpx, with input files split between instances and results pulled back to the local machine. Other modules included a distributed nmap run over common ports that produced XML and an HTML report, meg fetching robots.txt and another path across hosts in about half a minute, screenshots with go-witness, and a URL collection run. A round-robin proxy over SSH tunnels rotated the source IP per request. The speaker noted that nmap at scale strained the local host, and that a large wordlist fuzzing run was avoided on Microsoft.

The main takeaway is that modules are simple JSON definitions naming a command, its input and output, and how results merge, so users can add their own tools while arguments pass straight through to them. Fleets should be created in batches because DigitalOcean rate-limits API requests. The speaker described plans for a rewrite beyond bash, better logging, multi-cloud support, and possible GPU-based work, while stressing that the framework is meant to extend an operator's own workflow rather than hide it.

talks.title: Live Recon and Automation on Shopify's Bug Bounty Program with @TomNomNomDotCom
talks.teaser: Follows a live recon workflow against Shopify's bug bounty scope, from subdomain discovery to archived JavaScript and GitHub code.
talks.summary:
A live stream let chat choose Shopify as the target, and the speaker starts by turning the wildcard domains in the bounty scope into a large list of subdomains. Probing that list for live web services and saving each root response gives a baseline of what normal looks like. Unusual response headers stand out against thousands of similar ones: a canary marker on one host, a unique server timing header on the docs subdomain, and pod identifiers that suggest Kubernetes and consistent hashing by source IP. These oddities become the leads to follow.

Next, the speaker looks at historical data from the Wayback Machine to find old URLs and endpoints that no longer appear on current pages. Archived versions of a JavaScript file are fetched to show how it changed over time. URL lists are filtered against the program's scope, and reflected query parameters and a redirect are tested for behaviour. Browser-console scripts pull result links from Google and GitHub searches, the matching repositories are cloned, and git history is dumped to search for in-scope URLs in old commits.

The main lesson is that recon is mostly information gathering: learn what normal looks like for a system, then look for differences. Historical data often reveals older, less-reviewed code. Scope filtering and simple command-line pipelines turn large outputs into short lists worth reviewing by hand. The speaker closes by stressing persistence, since most of the thousands of items reviewed are unremarkable and knowing when to move on matters.

talks.title: NahamCon2021 - Putting Your Mind to It: Bug Bounties for 12 Months - @zseano
talks.teaser: Shows how to study web features and bug classes, then sets a 12-month plan for bug bounty hunting on one large program.
talks.summary:
Z Seano (Sean), founder of bugbountyhunter.com, delivers a strategy-focused talk on sustained bug bounty hunting over 12 months. He emphasizes that with proper methodology, dedication, and patience, anyone—experienced or inexperienced—can discover vulnerabilities and earn bounties.

Core Philosophy: Understand Features, Not Just Bug Types
Seano argues against "spraying payloads everywhere." Instead, hunters should understand how website features work: login flows, account updates, token exchanges, developer tools, and mobile apps. For example, recognizing that SSO token exchanges enable open redirect attacks, or that IDOR vulnerabilities appear in profile edits and permission systems, sharpens targeting.

Methodology: Start Harmless, Then Test Intelligently
Rather than immediately testing malicious payloads, begin with what the application expects. For an open redirect parameter, test the legitimate domain first, then explore variations: subdomains, different encodings, trailing slashes, relative paths. Similarly, for XSS, inject harmless HTML before script tags to confirm reflection and understand filtering. This reveals how the application handles input and what bypasses are possible. Seano notes that understanding SQL injection requires only testing a single quote first to confirm vulnerability; XXE testing should start with basic DOCTYPE replacements.

Selecting and Committing to Programs
Seano recommends choosing programs with large scope and interactive features (login, upload, post content). Spend 6–12 months on a single target to deeply understand its architecture, code reuse patterns, and potential issues across subdomains or teams. Example: Google's .com and .cn versions may be separate codebases, each harboring different vulnerabilities. He cautions against relying on bug bounty platform invites; instead, hunters should proactively access public programs like Google VRP without needing formal invitations.

Leverage Disclosed Write-Ups
Seano emphasizes studying published vulnerability reports (e.g., Sam Curry's Apple disclosures) to identify endpoints, parameters, bug types, and developer fixes. Since developers reuse code, similar vulnerabilities often appear elsewhere. After finding one IDOR in a specific path, test that pattern across the entire application. Read disclosed reports carefully, follow the hacker's steps, and test for bypasses—the original fix may contain weaknesses.

The 12-Month Google VRP Challenge
Seano sets a concrete task: Hunt on Google's Vulnerability Reward Program for the next year. Steps include:
- Catalog all disclosed Google VRP write-ups, documenting endpoints, parameters, vulnerability types, and fixes
- Map Google subdomains and in-scope services (Gmail, Google Drive, Google Ads, etc.)
- Test login flows consistently across subdomains and platforms (desktop, mobile, Android, iOS user agents)
- Investigate permission and role systems, verify they work correctly across platforms
- Write comprehensive notes to identify patterns and recognize similar code

Speaker Credentials: Self-taught developer from age 11–12, web application hacker who achieved BugCrowd rank 2 by focusing on one program for 8–9 months. Sponsors bugbountyhunter.com, which teaches vulnerability identification and runs "hack events" mentoring members on live bug bounty programs.

Key Takeaways: Websites follow common patterns; mastering one program's logic accelerates finding bugs on others. Understanding features, systematic testing, extensive notes, and 6–12 months of focused effort yield far better results than casual scanning or random payload spraying. The sky is the limit for those committed to the process.

talks.title: NahamCon2021 - Hacking IIS - @infosec_au
talks.teaser: Shows practical ways to attack Microsoft IIS servers, from virtual host discovery to file disclosure and view state RCE.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why IIS servers are a rich target. Case-insensitive paths make content easy to find, short-name scanning can reveal partial file and folder names, and debug mode can expose stack traces and full paths. Debugging scripts may leak session tokens, and a series of Telerik bugs has led to remote code execution. The first practical section covers hosts that answer with a generic Microsoft HTTP API 2.0 404. The speaker suggests taking a hostname from the SSL certificate, setting it in the Host header, and mapping it in the hosts file so the real application responds. Scans should then be run again against that application.

The middle of the talk covers virtual host hopping and file disclosure. On a development-looking IIS server, brute-forcing Host headers revealed an internal SQL Server manager that was not reachable from outside. In ASP.NET applications, a local file disclosure bug can be used to read web.config and global.asax, which name the DLLs to download from the bin folder. Those DLLs can then be decompiled with dnSpy. The web.config also contains machine keys, which the speaker says can enable view state deserialization and RCE. For XXE with no outbound HTTP, a fragment identifier trick makes the parser error include partial file contents. Short-name results can be expanded by fuzzing the remaining characters after a known prefix, and Crunch can generate wordlists when pure brute force is needed.

The closing section points to further reading, including the Assetnotes video channel, Soroush's blog, and an upcoming short-name scanner. The main takeaway is that a single file read on IIS can often lead to much more serious impact, so testers should keep enumerating hosts, files and keys.
