talks.title: NahamCon2021 - Better Report Writing for Faster Triage Times - @FarahHawa
talks.teaser: Offers practical tips for writing bug bounty reports with clear reproduction steps, proof of concepts and impact.
talks.summary:
Farah Hawa, a triager at Bugcrowd, explains why some bug bounty reports sit in triage for days or weeks. The main cause she identifies is back-and-forth questioning, which usually traces back to unclear reproduction steps or an impact that is not defined. She advises against long paragraphs, against including cookies, tokens or credentials in a report, and against copying generic report templates that add unnecessary detail.

For reproduction steps, she recommends short, clear steps that are easy to follow, plus a proof of concept even when it is simple, such as a link for a reflected or stored XSS, a GET-based open redirect, or an HTML page for a POST-based CSRF. Videos should be avoided where possible; if used, they should be short, edited to remove dead time, clear in resolution, and password-protected. Other tips include inline screenshots, direct endpoint URLs, the vulnerable HTTP request, and whether the user was authenticated. With several user roles, she advises stating each role and which user is the attacker and which is the victim, with each user's steps kept separate.

The final section covers impact through an attack scenario that answers who would exploit the bug and why. It should describe the attacker's starting position, the assumptions made about the victim, and any prerequisites for the attacker or the application, since each extra assumption lowers the impact. She closes with checklists for writing reproduction steps and showing impact.

talks.title: NahamCon2021 - Career and Community Building with Bug Bounties by @vickieli7
talks.teaser: Panelists share how bug bounties shaped their careers, community ties and time management, with advice for newcomers.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with how each speaker first got into bug bounties. One joined a live hacking event through a mentorship scheme, another learned on a trip abroad by picking a single bug class, and a third started with a Singapore challenge and Hacker101 training. Early finds included access control flaws and a race condition.

Bounties also opened doors. The speakers described a welcoming community where experienced hunters share techniques at private events, and where writing up findings and making videos deepened their knowledge. One said her teaching videos helped her land an academic post, and another moved from bounty hunting into incident response. Their advice was to network through meetups and approach companies with a clear story.

On time management, speakers described blocking calendar hours, scheduling breaks and capturing ideas away from the screen. They agreed bounties are not a quick way to get rich, that persistence and a chosen niche matter, and that free training such as PortSwigger's Web Academy is a strong starting point.

talks.title: Live Recon and Google Dorking on the Department of Defenses Vuln Disclosure Program with @thedawgyg
talks.teaser: Walks through a live recon session on a military disclosure program, covering Google dorking, subdomain discovery and web triage.
talks.summary:
This livestream had chat vote on a target, and a U.S. Department of Defense disclosure program won. A guest hacker showed how he starts recon on a .mil domain. He used Google to search for PHP files across hosts, then ran amass for subdomain enumeration and Aquatone for port scanning and screenshots. The approach was to use search results to learn which file extensions and technologies a site uses before choosing what to brute force. Directory brute forcing on the live target was skipped for safety, so the demo focused on the search and triage steps.

The Google dorks were the core of the session. He used site and filetype-style queries, then inurl queries for admin, API, login, and SSRF-prone parameter names such as image or source URL fields. He also searched intitle and document types like xlsx and pdf, since setup files and screenshots can expose demo logins or tokens. For a 403, he treated it as a sign that content exists and worth more digging, while he usually skipped 401s because they flood brute force output. On a Tomcat manager page, he only tried a few default username and password pairs and avoided real credential brute forcing. For APIs, he tried case variations of paths and sent malformed JSON to get the server to list expected parameters. He preferred Turbo Intruder for fast, scripted requests when dirsearch became noisy.

The main takeaways were practical. Google results often reveal folders, technologies, and error pages that brute forcing would take much longer to find. A sibling domain from the same company can hint at the stack on a target that is harder to read. Recon data should be organized by company and asset, and subdomain lists should be monitored over time because hosts can appear briefly and then disappear.

talks.title: Live Recon on Snapchat with @ITSecurityGuard (amass, FFUF, SecurityTrails Demo)
talks.teaser: Walks through organization-wide recon on Snapchat, from domain discovery to directory brute forcing with amass and ffuf.
talks.summary:
The stream starts with a target picked by viewers: Snapchat, chosen for a live recon session. The hosts begin with the program's disclosed activity on HackerOne, which lists several owned domains, then use a domain intelligence service to expand that list into associated domains, including corporate and development hosts. The discussion stresses that a company with a single brand can hide many of its assets across unrelated-looking domains.

The middle of the session covers automation. The guest runs amass against each root domain using a config file with API keys, stores results in per-domain folders, and uses its diff feature to spot hosts added over time. He keeps only resolving names to avoid false positives and explains that ASN-based scanning matters less for younger cloud-hosted companies. Directory discovery with ffuf follows, using custom wordlists, filtered status codes and a realistic user agent. Hosts that sat behind CloudFront were examined by their IP addresses, and a newer app's JavaScript was reviewed for endpoints, with Burp used to crawl and analyze parameters.

The takeaways are practical. Check every IP behind a domain, monitor assets continuously, and build wordlists by pruning real-world lists rather than running huge generic ones. Avoid discarding 400 responses, since GraphQL endpoints often return them. The session shows how a recon workflow moves from a list of domains to candidate targets worth deeper testing.

talks.title: @Farah Hawa Talks About Learning How to Code, Javascript, Creating Content, Mentorship and more!
talks.teaser: @FarahHawa Talks About Learning How to Code, Javascript, Creating Content, Mentorship and more!.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this live stream interview, Farah Hawa, an Application Security Engineer at Bugcrowd, part-time bug bounty hunter, and YouTube content creator, discusses her transition into infosec, her learning methodologies, and her approach to web application security. Coming from a non-technical educational background with a degree in mass media, Hawa shares insights into how structured self-study, mentorship, and content creation accelerated her career in application security and triage.

### Key Topics
- **Non-Technical Transition to Infosec**: Hawa graduated with a bachelor's degree in mass media. Encouraged by her father to explore cybersecurity rather than general software engineering, she transitioned into web application testing through hands-on internships.
- **Mentorship and Learning Strategy**: Her second internship at AppSecure under Anand Prakash provided a pivotal learning environment where her mentor guided her to research root causes autonomously rather than spoon-feeding answers. She also credits content creator Vickie Li's accessible blog posts as a major inspiration.
- **Content Creation and Networking**: Hawa began posting bug bounty findings and educational resources on LinkedIn and YouTube. This visibility led to collaborations with Bugcrowd and an eventual invitation from Michael (Codingo) to join Bugcrowd as an Application Security Engineer.
- **Certifications and Career Advice**: Holding a Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH) certification, Hawa clarifies that while it served as an HR filter and personal commitment tool, it offered minimal practical value for web hacking skills. She recommends OSCP over CEH for foundational hands-on security concepts.
- **Mental Health and Industry Evolution**: Hawa discusses managing burnout through consistent, incremental daily effort rather than overworking, alongside addressing imposter syndrome. She predicts the bug bounty landscape will move toward customized, crowdsourced penetration testing models (such as Bugcrowd's Next-Gen Pen Tests).

### Technical Details
- **Coding for Hackers**: Hawa practiced coding across JavaScript, PHP, Python, and SQL using Codecademy and The New Boston. While not strictly mandatory for all bug bounty hunting, she emphasizes that understanding JavaScript, server-side languages, and database query mechanics enables hunters to visualize backend request processing and evaluate vulnerability impact.
- **Core Study Resources**: Practical training combined PortSwigger Web Security Academy, *The Web Application Hacker's Handbook*, and hands-on labs like PentesterLab.
- **Methodology & Recon**: Rather than relying solely on extensive subdomain enumeration, Hawa prioritizes deep application analysis. She documents every feature and workflow exhaustively using Notion to uncover logical flaws and access control bypasses. Her recon stack includes Amass, cert.sh, Dirsearch, Wayback URLs, LinkFinder, and Google Dorking for exposed sensitive organizational data.
- **Burp Suite Setup**: Alongside core features (Scope tab and HTTP history), she highlights Turbo Intruder for race conditions, HTTP Request Smuggler, INQL for GraphQL analysis, and JSON Web Token extensions.

### Takeaways
- Beginners should master web fundamentals (HTTP, headers, cookies, browser security) before attempting vulnerability exploitation.
- Starting with swag-only or Hall of Fame programs found via Google Dorking helps build foundational skills and confidence without the intense competition of large public programs.
- Knowing JavaScript is critical for understanding Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) context and demonstrating real business impact over simple popup alerts.

talks.title: The Act of Balancing by @ChloeMessdaghi
talks.teaser: Explains what burnout is and how information security workers can recognize, prevent and talk about it.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a series of relatable scenarios: an overloaded inbox, friends' calls going unanswered, swings in emotion, constant procrastination, and fatigue. The speaker frames these as signs of burnout, which she describes as prolonged stress leading to emotional, physical and mental exhaustion, and contrasts it with ordinary stress, which a break can relieve. She notes that information security workers are at particular risk because they are on call and online around the clock.

The middle covers prevention and coping. Recommended steps include self-awareness about how work and stress affect your mood and habits, regular exercise, a balanced diet and good sleep, and a weekly day offline with no devices or social media. Keeping a written to-do list is presented as a way to stop looping on tasks overnight. She also covers workplace conversations: telling a manager about burnout, asking for time off, and putting requests and follow-ups in writing so there is a paper trail. She suggests listing what you enjoy and dislike about your job to decide whether it still fits.

The closing message is that you cannot support others while you are depleted, so you should put yourself first and ask for help. She points listeners to peer and crisis resources when they feel isolated, and reminds them to check regularly whether work and personal life are in balance.

talks.teaser: Shows how to build target-specific wordlists from archived URLs, HTML, JavaScript and public code datasets for bug hunting.
talks.summary:
The talk makes the case that popular public wordlists are useful but generic and heavily used, so they tend to surface the same results everyone else already finds. Wordlists are presented as a way to make guessing attacks practical, covering subdomains, paths, usernames, API method names and parameters. The speaker favours small, hand-curated lists and target-specific lists that include terms a generic list would miss.

The middle of the talk covers sources for target-specific data: Burp Suite project history, Wayback Machine archives, sitemaps and Google search results. A browser extension is shown that pulls URLs from result pages into a local companion server while paging through results. Paths are then split into segments with unfurl, sed and sort. To find vocabulary unique to a target, the speaker compares words from the target's HTML against an unrelated document, using comm to suppress common terms. Fetched JavaScript files are also mined for parameter and endpoint names.

The final section uses BigQuery datasets of public GitHub repositories and HTTP Archive data. One query finds files containing PHP info output, and another collects nginx configuration files to find location blocks vulnerable to the alias off-by-slash traversal issue. The speaker warns that queries can cost real money, so estimated sizes should be checked and sample tables used first. The takeaways are to keep a short curated list, build lists for each target, and set spending limits.

talks.title: How to Use Amass Efficiently by @jeff_foley
talks.teaser: Shows how to run OWASP Amass efficiently, from tuning data sources and resolvers to writing custom Lua data source scripts.
talks.summary:
This NahamCon workshop walks through OWASP Amass, a tool for attack surface mapping and asset discovery. Amass runs a cyclic process in which each data source's results feed the next round, so a full run can take a long time, and a timeout flag can cap it. The session covers the configuration file, the output directory, and the local graph database, which can be turned off at the cost of tracking and visualization. It also contrasts the enum subcommand for subdomain discovery with intel for expanding scope, and shows exporting stored results as D3 graphs.

Next comes control over data sources. Include and exclude flags select which sources run, and passive mode with a single source is useful for testing. Outside passive mode, a name source must be paired with an infrastructure lookup source to get network and ASN data. Brute forcing is off by default and accepts a custom wordlist. For speed, the presenter suggests validating a large public resolver list, sampling a smaller set such as 25 to 100 resolvers, and raising the maximum DNS query setting to match.

The final section covers the Lua scripting engine. A script must define its type and name, and callbacks such as vertical handle domain requests. The example wraps the assetfinder tool as an external data source, which Amass loads and runs in passive mode. The question period covers active versus normal mode, a planned DNS subcommand, distributed agents, and resolver reliability. The main takeaway is that Amass can be tuned for coverage, speed and noise, and extended with custom sources.

talks.title: Practical Attacks Using HTTP Request Smuggling by @defparam
talks.teaser: Walks through practical HTTP request smuggling attacks, from session hijacking to response queue poisoning.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces CL.TE and TE.CL desync attacks, in which a front-end and a back-end server disagree on where one HTTP request ends, leaving attacker-supplied bytes stuck on a shared back-end connection. It explains how far a desync can reach: an open desync can affect any visitor, an IP desync only clients sharing the attacker's address, and a self desync only the attacker's own traffic, though it can still bypass front-end controls. The speaker also describes a Python tool written to test for desync safely, without disturbing neighbouring connections.

The case studies show escalation beyond the basic finding. On one site, a self desync reached an endpoint listed in robots.txt that the front end normally blocked, exposing an administration panel. On a mobile API, an open CL.TE desync allowed a JSON parameter to be moved into the request line, which the server honoured, letting the attacker add themselves as an account owner. Converting a JSON invite form to URL-encoded fields caused a victim's full request, including a session token, to be stored in an invitation email. In a lab demo, a smuggled absolute URL steered a redirect so that a victim's headers were sent to an external host.

The final demo covers response queue poisoning, where a smuggled complete request splits the back-end stream so that responses reach the wrong clients, exposing personal data and session tokens. The speaker stresses that this is far more damaging than hijacking, since later requests on that back-end connection stay out of sync and other users can receive each other's data. The takeaways are to check robots.txt and request-line handling for hidden endpoints, to try to escalate stored reflections, and to keep testing within program rules and on low-traffic infrastructure.

talks.teaser: Walks through a bug bounty recon workflow, from seed domains and ASN lookups to subdomain discovery, port scanning and takeover checks.
talks.summary:
This talk is the reconnaissance half of the Bug Hunter's Methodology, split out from the longer presentation, with the application analysis half still in progress. The speaker starts with project tracking, keeping each target and its sites in mind maps with notes on roles, logging, technology and interesting endpoints. The discovery work then begins with seed domains taken from bug bounty scope pages, company acquisitions found through CrunchBase, autonomous system lookups on bgp.he.net, and reverse WHOIS searches. Using the Twitch and Tesla examples, the speaker shows how each step widens the list of related domains and IP ranges.

The middle of the talk covers subdomain enumeration in several layers. Burp Suite and command-line spiders pull links out of HTML and JavaScript, while passive sources such as search engines, certificate datasets, security databases, GitHub code searches and Shodan add more names. The speaker also describes scanning cloud provider ranges for TLS certificates that mention a target, multi-resolver brute forcing and permutation scanning, which once helped him reach a host behind a web application firewall and find an origin server. Later steps include masscan port scanning, default credential checks against remote administration services, GitHub dorking, screenshot triage and subdomain takeover checks with subover and nuclei.

The closing section covers automation with interlace and a tiered comparison of recon frameworks, from simple scripts to commercial platforms. The main takeaway is that recon is iterative: newly found seeds should be fed back into the workflow, and combining several sources finds assets that any single one would miss.

talks.teaser: ​@LiveOverflow Talks About the Importance of CTFs, Hacking, Creating Content for Hackers, and more!.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this livestream interview, host NahamSec interviews Fabian, the security researcher and educator known as LiveOverflow. They explore Fabian's background in computer science, how he transitioned from developer to web application penetration tester, his views on Capture the Flag (CTF) competitions versus bug bounties, and his journey into content creation on Twitch and YouTube.

### Key Topics
- **Entry into Security & Education:** Fabian began programming as a teenager and encountered SQL injection early on, but his formal pursuit of cybersecurity began during his dual-study bachelor's degree after playing the Stripe CTF. He later earned a master's degree in computer science and obtained the OSCP certification (under the BackTrack era).
- **CTFs vs. Real-World Assessment:** Fabian explains why he creates content highlighting both the positives and negatives of CTFs. While CTF challenges can occasionally be unrealistic or reliant on guessing, high-weight competitions (found via ctftime.org) foster transferable foundational problem-solving skills, especially when studying write-ups.
- **Approach to Web Application Security:** As a freelance pentester, Fabian specializes in code-assisted web application assessments, relying heavily on source code review rather than automated reconnaissance or brute-forcing.
- **Bug Bounties vs. Pentesting:** Fabian discusses why he has avoided bug bounties, contrasting the unpaid, duplicative subdomain and TLS enumeration of external bug hunting with structured penetration testing where clients provide source code and routes.
- **Content Creation & Workflow:** Inspired initially by watching GeoHot stream CTF challenges on Twitch, Fabian launched LiveOverflow to give others the experience of looking over a professional's shoulder. He later shifted from live streaming to scripted, edited YouTube videos.

### Technical Details
- **Tooling:** Fabian primarily relies on Burp Suite for web testing alongside custom Python scripts to test endpoints and parameters. He seldom relies on scanners like Nmap, masscan, DirBuster, or Wfuzz because his engagements are source-code assisted.
- **Languages:** Fluent in Python and C, Fabian also uses C# (from game development in Unity) and reads many languages during white-box code reviews.
- **Vulnerabilities & CTF Highlights:** Fabian notes memory corruptions as his favorite vulnerability class. Memorable CTFs mentioned include Stripe CTF, Real World CTF in China, and CCC (C3) on-site CTFs, alongside CTF teams like Sauercloud and ALLES!.

### Takeaways
- **Understand Underlying Systems:** Rather than memorizing bug labels like IDOR, security practitioners should understand fundamental application design and access control models.
- **Learn by Observing:** Watching experienced practitioners work—including their editor choice, terminal habits, and thought processes—accelerates technical learning.
- **Embrace Curiosity and Balance:** Turning casual activities (such as analyzing mobile game APIs or exploring game engines) into technical learning projects helps sustain interest without succumbing to external pressure or burnout.

talks.teaser: Shares a bug hunter's recon workflow, tool habits and attack-surface mindset drawn from years of Yahoo and bug bounty work.
talks.summary:
Naffy, a long-time bug bounty hunter, recounts how he started hunting on HackerOne in 2013 and found early issues on Yahoo, where exposed hosts and forgotten admin panels were common. He credits strong web fundamentals, steady daily time on targets, and peer exchange over any secret tooling.

The core of the interview is his recon workflow. He runs Nmap with HTTP title grabs against newly seen hosts, checks certificate and internet-scan data for fresh assets, and brute forces content on hosts he has not tested. He also enumerates virtual hosts by sending known subdomains in the Host header to ingress points. Case examples include a redirect to a hostname with no DNS record, which led to an old admin panel that allowed a shell, and a path traversal through an API route that reached an off-the-shelf product's paths and several critical issues before the app was taken offline. He uses Burp Intruder with public wordlists and sorts responses by status code and length to spot deviations.

He closes by warning about diminishing returns, the value of stepping away from a target, and reading specifications such as RFCs to find unexpected behaviour. He stresses that testing requires permission, that tools miss edge cases so you should understand what they do, and that consistent practice and collaboration matter more than any single technique.

talks.title: Mayonaise Talks About His Recon Workflow, How to Learn Different Topics, and How to Bug Bounty!
talks.teaser: Walks through a bug bounty hunter's recon pipeline, endpoint discovery habits, and advice on learning and sustaining the work.
talks.summary:
The guest, a bug bounty hunter who started in late 2018 after a career in data analytics and marketing, joins the host for a wide-ranging interview. He explains how his analytics background shapes his habit of watching for anomalies and grouping related assets, and why he focuses on a few large programs with wildcard scopes.

The center of the talk is his recon workflow. Root domains feed a passive subdomain enumeration step, then a resolver pass confirms which hosts are live. Each run is diffed against the last so only new hosts move on. Historical URLs are pulled for each group of related environments, such as dev, QA, UAT and production, because a path leaked in one often shows up in another. Looping shell workers process small chunks so the pipeline never sits idle. For brute forcing, he generates custom permutations by combining product words with environment names, and he checks a short list of high-value endpoints such as Swagger pages during content discovery.

Later sections cover learning and staying sustainable. He recommends mastering one bug class, then replicating a finding across many hosts, asking targeted questions, and staying patient. Coding is not strictly required if you can read JavaScript and HTML for endpoints. When stuck on an endpoint, he steps away and returns with fresh ideas. He also discusses long hours, recognizing burnout, imposter syndrome, and the value of certifications as training.

talks.title: Creating Wordlists for Hacking, Pentesting & Bug Bounty Hunting Using Seclists, Bigquery, and More!
talks.teaser: Shows how to build custom wordlists from SecLists, BigQuery, Wayback Machine data and Burp sitemaps for recon.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how to build personal wordlists for content discovery during bug bounty work and penetration tests. The presenter sorts wordlists by theme, covering directory names, common file names, extension-specific names, paths tied to third-party software with known CVEs, a last-resort group of rarely seen paths, and lists built for one specific target. He suggests merging these into a few groups based on how much data each has and how often it will run.

Usage falls into two cases. The first is early recon on a newly opened scope: after scanning subdomains and reviewing screenshots, run a quick list of the most common files and directories. The second is brute forcing a page that shows a default or forbidden response, where hidden content may sit behind it and a themed list can reveal what the site is for.

For sources, SecLists provides a baseline, including the raft lists and CMS-specific paths. BigQuery can query GitHub's public dataset for the most common file names by extension, exported as CSV and trimmed with cut. Wayback Machine URLs can be filtered in a terminal to reveal folder and endpoint naming patterns, and Burp's sitemap can be processed the same way with bash. The closing advice is to keep a history of collected data and keep adding to it, since a personal list becomes more useful over time.

Working in teams was described as a way to combine different experiences, cover more ground quickly, and push each other to submit only impactful findings.

To keep up, they recommended reading disclosed reports, following researchers and newsletters, replicating new techniques in labs, and competing in CTFs. talks.teaser: @Mrtuxracer Talks About Monitoring Endpoints, Binary Exploitation, Continuous Recon and More!.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Mrtuxracer (Julian), a full-time bug bounty hunter and HackerOne MVH (Master of Bug Bounty Hunting) belt holder, discusses his endpoint monitoring methodology, binary exploitation expertise, educational path, and professional insights into competitive bug bounty hunting.

## Key Topics

**Continuous Endpoint Monitoring & Reconnaissance**
Julian's approach differs from traditional subdomain-focused recon. He uses three to four automated programs to continuously monitor endpoints discovered in JavaScript files rather than hunting new subdomains. His custom tool daily fetches and analyzes JavaScript files, compares content length and response times, and alerts him via Slack and email when changes occur. Upon alerts, he manually investigates exploitability.

**Parameter Discovery & Wordlist Building**
He relies heavily on fuff for brute-forcing HTTP requests. His wordlists use two-tiered approach: a baseline containing common paths (git directories, config files, backups) and target-specific lists built by extracting frequently-occurring words from source code. While leveraging Seclists, he extensively customizes. He notes 90% of his work uses fuff.

**Binary Exploitation & Reverse Engineering Background**
Julian transitioned from reverse engineering (10 years ago) to web app security after discovering PayPal's bug bounty program, earning his first $500 for an XSS. He prioritizes three binary exploitation areas: privilege escalation, file import fuzzing, and custom URI handler exploitation. He recommends Coralan tutorials for foundational processor/memory concepts, then assembly language before pursuing binary bounties. He recently discovered 10-11 zero-days earning multiple CVEs.

**Education & Certifications**
Self-taught with no university degree, Julian earned OCP (Offensive Security Certified Professional) after one year of study. He's pursuing OCE and recommends OCP for those with fundamentals but not beginners. He emphasizes the "try harder" mindset is valuable despite pentest-to-bounty methodology differences (pentest involves pivoting; bounties don't allow this).

**Initial Reconnaissance Workflow**
For new targets, Julian uses Sonar project data, Subfinder, and Nmap for subdomain enumeration and port scanning. He screenshots all HTTP services, analyzes Nmap metadata and HTTP titles, then focuses on interesting hosts. He performs vhost enumeration by testing dead/unresolved subdomains against live IPs, discovering hidden hosts. He extracts Google Analytics UIDs to identify additional company assets.

**Technical Tools & Methodology**
Primary toolkit: Burp Suite Pro (describes as "best investment ever"), fuff, Python, nmap with custom NSE scripts, Sonar, Subfinder, and custom-built tools. He writes Burp extensions and Python scripts for automation. For RCE discovery, he uses "catch-all payloads" (sleep, DNS lookups) but acknowledges no universal rule exists.

## Takeaways

**Learning & Knowledge**
Curiosity and self-directed learning (Google, reading, documentation) matter more than formal credentials. He learned everything through hands-on experience, not CTFs. Proper Googling skills and independent problem-solving are essential for beginners.

**Work-Life Balance**
Julian maintains 20-60 hours weekly depending on motivation and program interest. He prevents burnout through sports (fitness), vegetarian lifestyle, and side interests (stocks, card games). Yearly income goals matter more than monthly targets due to bounty variability.

**Beginner Guidance**
Understand browser security fundamentals (same-origin policy) before attempting exploitation. Avoid pursuing bug bounties solely for money. Learn XSS, CSRF, SSRF fundamentals first. Wordlists and methodologies are proprietary assets representing years of work—don't expect them to be shared.

**Industry Outlook**
He hopes larger institutions (insurance, banking) adopt bug bounty programs in the next 3-5 years. Transitioning from pentesting to bounties isn't difficult since reconnaissance methodology overlaps; the difference is bounties skip network pivoting.

A major theme is using GitHub for recon. He searches repositories for leaked keys and passwords, and later for hostnames and endpoints that developers or third-party vendors publish, which standard wordlists often miss. Instead of one large list, he builds a small wordlist for each target from its naming patterns, the disallowed paths in robots.txt, and a few common paths for each technology. He also describes a case where a leaked privileged access management login led to a high-severity payout, and says that incident later led him to step back from publicly sharing GitHub findings.

His takeaways are that scripting and chaining existing tools matters more than being a strong coder, that a repeatable process can still produce results with limited time, and that newcomers should learn web fundamentals before chasing public write-ups. He also argues that collaborating with other hunters speeds up finding and escalating bugs, and that hunters should focus on the vulnerability classes they are strongest in.

talks.title: Exploiting a Server Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in WeasyPrint to hack Lyft & HackerOne’s $50M CTF
talks.teaser: Shows how injected HTML in a receipt PDF generator led to SSRF, internal file reads, and cloud metadata access via WeasyPrint.
talks.summary:
The speaker describes finding a server-side request forgery by accident. While testing an expense feature in a delivery and ride-share app, they put an HTML tag into an expense note. Months later, an automatically emailed expense PDF rendered that tag as a large heading, which showed that user-supplied markup reached the PDF generator. Early attempts to load remote images failed because of quoting mistakes. Once those were fixed, an out-of-band image request leaked the server header, identifying WeasyPrint as the backend.

With WeasyPrint identified as an open-source project, the researchers read its source code. They found that most outside resources such as images, iframes and objects were blocked, but the link tag was still allowed. A tag that attaches files was also usable: embedded files were pulled into the output PDF, and an unexpectedly large PDF revealed that a local file had been attached by accident. Using the same technique, they could request internal and external HTTP endpoints and capture the responses inside the generated PDF, then decompress it with PDF tools to extract the data. This gave them access to AWS instance metadata keys and the ability to read files on the internal network.

The same flaw was later reused in a large CTF run by Lyft and HackerOne, where many participants exploited it within hours or even minutes. The main takeaways are to identify the rendering backend early using out-of-band requests, to review the source of open-source components in use, and to sanitize user-supplied HTML before it reaches a document generator.

talks.title: Learning Server Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Basics Using Portswigger's Web Security Academy
talks.teaser: Walks through PortSwigger's basic SSRF labs, covering internal access, filter bypasses and open redirect chaining.
talks.summary:
The stream walks through the first set of Server-Side Request Forgery labs from PortSwigger's Web Security Academy. Each lab has a stock checker feature that makes a backend request to an address the user supplies. The first lab shows that the stock API is reachable only from the server, so swapping the URL to localhost reaches an admin panel where a user can be deleted. The second lab requires finding the internal admin host by scanning a private address range on port 8080 in Burp Intruder, and the presenter warns against aggressive scanning on live programs.

The later labs add defenses. A localhost blacklist is bypassed by changing the capitalisation of the admin path, which the filter does not match. A whitelist that only accepts the stock host is bypassed by embedding the internal address after a permitted host name and double URL encoding it. The last lab chains an open redirect in the next-product path with the stock check, so the trusted redirect forwards the request to the internal admin page.

The takeaway is to test SSRF early by aiming at localhost and internal hosts, then try common filter bypasses such as alternate host spellings, encoding and redirects when direct requests fail. Check every redirect parameter, since one can turn a trusted endpoint into a request forwarder. The stream closes with a plan to cover blind SSRF in a later episode.

talks.title: Setting Up Your Ubuntu Box for Pentest and Bug Bounty Automation
talks.teaser: Walks through provisioning a cloud Ubuntu server, creating a non-root user, and wiring recon tools into aliases and scripts.
talks.summary:
The talk is a how-to for building a personal Linux workstation in the cloud for recon and bug bounty work. The presenter starts by provisioning a small Ubuntu droplet on DigitalOcean, choosing a region and plan, and then connecting over SSH from Windows through a terminal. Before doing anything else, the presenter recommends creating a separate non-root user and granting it sudo rights, so that elevated privileges are used only when a task needs them.

Next, the presenter clones a personal tools repository that installs common recon and bug bounty utilities, including Go-based tools. To cut down on typing, a directory brute-forcing command is wrapped in a bash alias that takes the target and the file extension as parameters. The presenter then turns a reusable step, a certificate transparency subdomain lookup, into a standalone executable in the bin folder so that scripts can call it. The difference between aliases and commands is explained, since scripts cannot see aliases.

The final section covers organisation. Each target gets its own folder under a recon directory, and tool output is saved into dated text files so older results can be found later. A sample script loops over discovered subdomains, runs curl on each one, and saves every response under a file named after the domain. The takeaway is a consistent folder layout and scripted workflow that keep results easy to find and compare across targets.

talks.title: Live Bug Bounty Recon Session on Verizon Media's Yahoo.com W/ @Securinti
talks.teaser: Live Bug Bounty Recon Session on Verizon Media's Yahoo.com W/ @Securinti.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This livestream session features a live bug bounty reconnaissance workflow targeting Verizon Media's Yahoo assets, followed by an in-depth guest interview with prominent bug bounty hunter Inti De Ceukelaire (@securinti / Inti). The host spends the first half of the stream troubleshooting server infrastructure and writing Bash automation to query HTTP response codes and headers into a MySQL database (`reconDB`). The second half transitions into a wide-ranging discussion with Inti covering his hacking background, bug bounty philosophy, discovery of logic flaws, recon approaches, and collaboration dynamics at live hacking events.

### Key Topics
- **Live Recon Automation**: Building Bash scripts to take discovered alive domains from `httpprobe`, probe HTTP/HTTPS ports (80 and 443) using `curl`, collect response codes, and store the output in MySQL tables.
- **Hacking Journey & Philosophy**: How Inti got started in security via a PlayStation Portable crash bug and Google's Hall of Fame, embracing an "uncertified" path focused on curiosity and reading documentation rather than formal certifications.
- **Deep Recon vs. Surface Automation**: Inti's preference for manual core-target analysis, reading client-side JavaScript, and using the Wayback Machine to identify legacy endpoints and architectural changes.
- **Logic Flaws & Escalation**: Identifying non-technical, application-logic vulnerabilities (e.g., Ticket Trick, gift card discount loops, grouping/blocking privilege escalation) and escalating low-severity findings (P4/P5, HTML injection, CSS injection) into higher-impact bugs.
- **Community, Mental Health & Collaboration**: Managing burnout through vacations and structured routines, collaborating at live hacking events with peers (such as Jack Cable and Jobert Abma / cable-jey), and friendly rivalries with Team Sweden and Frans Rosén.

### Technical Details
- **MySQL & Bash Recon Pipeline**: The streamer resolves local MySQL socket configuration issues on Linux before querying `domains_data` where `alive = 1`. A custom Bash loop queries each domain with `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}"`, checking port 80 first. If a `000` status returns, it re-attempts the request via HTTPS on port 443 with `-k` (insecure) and records the resulting status code into a newly created `headers` table.
- **Wayback Machine & JS Archaeology**: Inti explains his technique of using the Wayback Machine to fetch historic JavaScript files and analyze diffs. Finding remnants of deprecated software in JavaScript provides hints about backend systems, undocumented endpoints, or lingering legacy services.
- **Chaining Logic Flaws**: Inti highlights that logic flaws typically arise from combining individually secure components. Examples discussed include abusing newsletter discounts to continually repurchase gift cards at a discount, exploiting Facebook group admin assignment logic by blocking all group members to force solitary membership, and intercepting password resets through misconfigured email/bounce flows that bypass standard web authentication.

### Takeaways
- Deep, manual source code reading (especially JavaScript) often uncovers vulnerabilities that automated broad-scope scanners miss.
- Understanding the expected operational workflow of an application allows researchers to find high-impact logic flaws by doing the inverse of what developers anticipated.
- Beginners do not need specialized programming backgrounds or security certifications to succeed; persistence, reading documentation thoroughly, and asking specific, well-researched questions are far more valuable.

Hosted by NahamSec on a Sunday stream, this session pairs an interview with Tomnomnom and a live recon demonstration against Yahoo. Tomnomnom explains how he started bug bounty hunting, why he wrote his tools in Go, and why he prefers checking one path across many hosts over noisy scanning that trips rate limits and monitoring. The conversation also touches on his first bounty, collaboration, and keeping motivation without burnout.

His recon method starts with subdomain enumeration, then Google and GitHub dorking, feeding discovered domains into archived URL sources, and hunting internal indicators such as intranet hostnames that leak into public repositories. During the demo he gathers subdomains, separates raw domains from hosts that answer on web ports, and explains why dead hosts stall tools with fixed concurrency. He then runs meg for PHP info files with a per-host delay, and triages responses by sorting sizes and file types with find and shell filters.

He also previews an experimental fetcher that controls delay between launches rather than fixed concurrency, a tokenizer that builds wordlists from discovered domains, and a recursive DNS brute forcer that skips branches returning NXDOMAIN. The key takeaways are to keep tools small and pipeable, pace requests to stay under the radar, and treat tooling as a means while skill comes from practice.

talks.title: Using BurpSuite's Intruder to find bugs and solve Bug Bounty Notes & Hacker101 CTFs
talks.teaser: Shows how Burp Suite Intruder can fuzz HTTP headers to find a hidden XSS sink in a Bug Bounty Notes challenge.
talks.summary:
The streamer works through a Bug Bounty Notes challenge aimed at finding cross-site scripting. The endpoint accepted a debug parameter but returned nothing useful for GET or POST requests, so the streamer reasoned that the input might arrive through an HTTP header instead. After setting up Burp Suite and its proxy, they loaded a list of common header names into Intruder as payloads and placed a marker on a test header value.

Sorting the Intruder results by response length surfaced the Referer header, which reflected the supplied value inside a script tag. A payload that closed the quoted string and called alert confirmed the XSS, and the challenge was submitted. The stream then moved to Hacker101 CTF challenges on a blog application. Techniques shown included enumerating numeric post IDs with Intruder to expose a hidden post, and testing a weak admin login. A later challenge involving PHP include behaviour was attempted but not finished before the stream ended.

The takeaway is that when an input shows no obvious reflection, systematic fuzzing of headers and parameters, combined with sorting results by response length, can reveal where user input lands in a page. Enumerating object IDs with Intruder is also a practical way to find content that the interface does not link to.

talks.title: Struggling with Hacker101's GraphQL CTF and solving an XSS challenge from Bug Bounty Notes!
talks.teaser: Struggling with Hacker101's GraphQL CTF and solving an XSS challenge from Bug Bounty Notes!.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this live stream recording, the speaker works through Hacker101's "BugDB v3" GraphQL CTF challenge after encountering technical issues, including 100% CPU usage and unrecorded footage of an earlier cross-site scripting (XSS) exercise. Racing against a tight time limit before having to log off and travel to AppSec DC Global, the speaker collaborates with live chat participants (notably C1, DC, Elliot, and Cody) to understand the target application's GraphQL schema, identify an arbitrary file read vulnerability, and locate the hidden flag.

### Key Topics
- **Live CTF Troubleshooting**: Dealing with system resource constraints, resetting broken challenge instances, and working against strict personal time limits.
- **GraphQL Reconnaissance and Schema Exploration**: Querying users, bugs, edges, nodes, and attachments to understand data models and identify query/mutation capabilities.
- **File Traversal / Arbitrary File Read**: Using mutations on attachments to point to internal server file paths instead of uploading user content.
- **Source Code Review via File Inclusion**: Reading local Python source files (`main.py`, `model.py`, `schema.py`) to discover backend architecture and references to internal databases.

### Technical Details
- **Target Identification**: The challenge revolves around a Hacker101 BugDB v3 instance built on Python/Flask with a GraphQL API.
- **Schema Enumeration**: Querying through `users` -> `bugs` -> `attachments` revealed fields including `id` and `fileName`.
- **Exploiting Attachment Mutations**: The speaker utilized a `modifyAttachment` mutation. By targeting attachment ID 2 and manipulating the `fileName` parameter with directory traversal sequences (e.g., `../main.py`), the backend fetched and stored server-side files into the attachment rather than taking user-supplied input.
- **Source Code Reconnaissance**: Inspecting the contents loaded into the attachment revealed source code from `main.py`, which imported local modules like `schema` and `model`. Examining `model.py` uncovered a reference to an SQLite database (`level18.db` / level 18 database).
- **Extracting the Flag**: Fetching the contents of the referenced database file into the attachment and inspecting the raw text allowed the speaker to locate the flag string directly.

### Takeaways
- GraphQL CTFs often require careful inspection of input arguments in mutations that may interact directly with the local filesystem.
- When path traversal or file inclusion is identified in source-code driven challenges, traversing to entry point files like `main.py` and reviewing local application imports (`model.py`, `schema.py`) is an effective method for discovering critical backend assets and databases.
- The XSS challenge mentioned in the title was noted as missing from the recording due to high CPU load at the start of the stream.

talks.title: Live Bug Bounty & Recon Session on Yahoo's Bug Bounty Program w/ @TheDawgyg
talks.teaser: Follows a live recon session on Yahoo's bug bounty scope, from subdomain discovery to directory brute-forcing and asset mapping.
talks.summary:
This live-streamed session follows NahamSec and guest DoggyG as they do reconnaissance against Yahoo's bug bounty program. They start with broad subdomain enumeration across Yahoo's root domains, then probe the discovered hosts to see which ones respond and capture screenshots of live web services. Long-running scans are left going in the background while they move between staging and beta hostnames, check DNS records, and review the results as they arrive.

The middle of the stream covers directory brute-forcing against the more interesting hosts, with attention to redirects and to 403 versus 404 responses. On one staging admin-style path, access was denied until a double-slash variant changed the response, and the pair treated that as a bypass worth exploring further. DoggyG explained his own approach: pulling copyright strings from a page to find related domains, using WHOIS-based lookups to expand a company's domain list, searching public GitHub gists for leaked hostnames and debug logs, and reading hostname naming patterns to find internal systems. He builds per-target wordlists from public collections rather than relying on one huge list.

The takeaway is that asset discovery drives the rest of the work, and that good recon depends on manual investigation and creativity more than on any single tool. The guest also noted that Yahoo's program does not permit public disclosure of reports, and that newer hunters learn most by reading disclosed reports and building their own payload collections.

talks.title: Live Bug Bounty Recon Session on Yahoo (Part 1
talks.teaser: Walks through a bash-driven subdomain recon pipeline built against Yahoo's bug bounty scope, from certificate data to live hosts.
talks.summary:
This stream opens a structured recon session on Yahoo's bug bounty program, which was then run under Verizon Media. The host starts by checking the program scope and removing domains marked out of scope, such as certain Taiwan, AOL CDN and Hong Kong properties. Subdomains are then gathered from certificate transparency data using wildcard queries against crt.sh and certspotter, with the host noting that certspotter returned far more records for the same queries. A cheap cloud server is used so the work can run in the background inside a terminal session.

The middle of the session focuses on triage. Names containing keywords such as ops, corporate, internal, API, dev, staging, UAT and admin are pulled out first, because the host considers them the most likely to expose sensitive or non-public systems. Results are appended to text files, deduplicated, and passed through an HTTP probe to separate responding hosts from dead ones. Across the session the list grew to several thousand names, and roughly 700 were live after probing. A screenshot tool was then run against the live hosts, though memory limits on the small server caused some failures, and a simple Python web server was used to browse the captures.

The main takeaway is the method rather than any single finding. Understanding how a large company names and structures its infrastructure helps guide keyword-based enumeration, and shell loops and aliases can chain tools into a repeatable pipeline. The host stresses that the results still need manual review, and that vulnerability testing against the discovered hosts was deferred to later sessions.

talks.title: The Truth About Recon (Bug Bounty Tips)
talks.teaser: Presents a bug bounty recon approach that adapts to program scope, using asset discovery, content gathering and fuzzing.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that recon should change with the bug bounty program. When only one asset is in scope, the presenter studies what the application is built to do, which user roles exist, and what each role can reach. The focus is on separating public information from private, checking whether data is exposed without logging in, and mining JavaScript files for hidden or restricted endpoints that can then be fuzzed.

For programs that list many domains and subdomains, the presenter splits the work into three buckets. Asset discovery gathers as many subdomains as possible using enumeration tools and search services. Content gathering maps folders and endpoints, adds directory brute forcing, and builds screenshot galleries to spot interesting hosts. Fuzzing then targets those endpoints, with each one examined in a proxy to learn its purpose. Supporting habits include bash aliases for long tool commands, searching error messages online, and keeping dated folders of scan output. Fingerprinting products like GitLab or Jenkins by their headers and paths helps find similar weaknesses across targets.

The closing message is that no single correct method exists. The presenter recommends building one bucket at a time, making each reliable before moving on, and eventually combining them into a single command.
